docs.title: The Project Management Knowledge Atlas
docs.text:
The Project Management Knowledge Atlas is a connected PMP study and project-management reference. It explains how processes, artifacts, decisions, authority, and information flows work together instead of presenting them as isolated definitions.

It is an independent learning resource, not official PMI material or a substitute for current PMI standards, examination guidance, or organizational governance.

Current status

docs.title: Active review stage
docs.text: The Atlas is being reviewed for coverage, source traceability, cross-page consistency, and editorial quality. Treat it as a structured study aid under active review, and verify consequential claims against current PMI and organizational sources.

docs.title: Six complementary viewsRoles, Responsibilities, and AuthorityProject Lifecycle GuideMaster Project SequenceProcess ReferenceArtifact ReferenceDecision Guides
docs.text:
Clarify who acts and decides

Separates performance, ownership, decision, approval, acceptance, verification, and escalation across predictive, adaptive, Scrum, Kanban, and hybrid contexts.

Begin with the project story

Explains how work unfolds from need and authorization through planning, execution, monitoring, acceptance, transition, closure, and benefits handoff.

Follow the integrated flow

Shows the end-to-end flow of processes, artifacts, handoffs, decisions, and the major transformations from business need to value.

Study process mechanics

Provides detailed pages for the 49 named processes, with their purpose, position, relationships, and practical context.

Understand project records

Explains documents, registers, baselines, records, examples, and downloadable templates used to preserve project information and decisions.

Reason from a situation

Connects scenario and exam-style questions to authority, artifacts, applicable processes, likely next action, and escalation.

docs.title: How to use the Atlas
docs.text:
1. Start with the Project Lifecycle Guide for the overall story.
  2. Use the Master Project Sequence to see the integrated flow.
  3. Open Process Reference pages for process-level mechanics.
  4. Check Roles, Responsibilities, and Authority to identify who acts, decides, approves, accepts, verifies, owns, or receives escalation.
  5. Use the Artifact Reference when you need to understand or create a project artifact.
  6. Use Decision Guides for scenario and exam-style reasoning.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: These principles exist to ensure the Atlas reads as though it were written by a single author.

docs.title: Principle 1 — Explain Before Naming
docs.text:
Introduce the concept before introducing PMI terminology.

Readers should understand the idea before memorizing the vocabulary.

docs.title: Principle 2 — Explain Why Before How
docs.text:
Every process exists to solve a project problem.

Explain the problem first.

Then explain the mechanics.

docs.title: Principle 3 — Relationships Matter More Than Lists
docs.text:
Do not present processes or artifacts in isolation.

Always explain:

  • what created it
  • what depends on it
  • what it influences next

docs.title: Principle 4 — Write for Understanding
docs.text:
The goal is not memorization.

The goal is comprehension.

If readers understand the relationships, recall becomes easier.

docs.title: Principle 5 — Use Plain Technical Language
docs.text:
Write clearly and precisely.

Avoid unnecessary rhetorical flourish.

Avoid unnecessary metaphors.

Avoid repetitive stylistic constructions.

Use emphasis sparingly.

docs.title: Principle 6 — One Idea Per Section
docs.text:
Each section should answer one primary question.

Avoid mixing multiple concepts into the same discussion.

docs.title: Principle 7 — Diagrams Replace Paragraphs
docs.text: When a relationship can be shown more clearly with a simple diagram than several paragraphs of text, use a diagram.

docs.title: Principle 8 — Respect PMI Terminology
docs.text:
Use official PMI terminology when referring to processes and artifacts.

Explanatory text may use simpler language, but should never invent competing terminology.

docs.title: Principle 9 — Distinguish Facts from Commentary
docs.text:
Clearly separate:

  • PMI guidance
  • Atlas explanation
  • Practical advice
  • Exam tips

Readers should always know which perspective they are reading.

docs.title: Principle 10 — Write Beyond the Exam
docs.text:
Every chapter should remain useful after certification.

Readers should be able to use the Atlas while managing real projects.

docs.title: Closing Statement
docs.text:
The Atlas is intended to explain project management as an interconnected system of decisions, information, processes, and artifacts.

Every chapter should help readers understand not only what project managers do, but why each activity exists and how it supports the project as a whole.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: The Atlas explains project management through relationships between processes, artifacts, decisions, and information rather than presenting isolated definitions.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: Readers understand projects more easily when they see how information flows from one process to another.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: Every chapter should explain what a process creates, what depends on it, and why it exists.

docs.title: Alternatives Considered
docs.text:
• Presenting isolated definitions for each concept.
  • Structuring the book strictly by PMI chapter taxonomy.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Each process introduces its purpose before discussing mechanics.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: Understanding purpose improves retention and helps readers answer situational questions.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: Every process page begins with Purpose and Why This Process Exists.

docs.title: Alternatives Considered
docs.text:
• Starting with procedural steps before purpose.
  • Presenting mechanics only.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Narrative sections present processes in logical dependency order rather than strictly following PMBOK chapter organization.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: The PMBOK is a reference standard; the Atlas is a learning and navigation aid.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: The Atlas may present processes in an order that differs from PMBOK while preserving PMI terminology and technical accuracy.

docs.title: Alternatives Considered

• Following PMBOK chapter order exactly.
  • Organizing content purely by memorization categories.

docs.title: Decision: Maintain a Neutral Technical Voice
Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: The Atlas uses clear technical prose and avoids unnecessary rhetorical flourishes.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: Readers should focus on concepts rather than writing style.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: Prefer concise explanations, numbered lists, and diagrams. Avoid repeated stylistic constructions and unnecessary metaphors.

docs.title: Alternatives Considered
docs.text:
• Using a more narrative or literary tone.
  • Adding frequent rhetorical devices for emphasis.

docs.title: Decision: Separate Lifecycle Narrative from Process Mechanics
Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: The Project Lifecycle Guide owns cross-process sequence, concurrent work, handoffs, feedback, and changing project conditions. Process pages retain process purpose, mechanics, authority, and direct relationships; artifact pages retain artifact structure and states; Decision Guides retain scenario choices.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: The Confluence source contains a useful end-to-end narrative but repeats process and artifact detail. Explicit ownership preserves the relational value without creating a second Process Reference.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: Lifecycle order, phase emphasis, links, deferrals, shared terminology, and provenance are registered in definitions/lifecycle.yaml. Generated lifecycle regions and navigation must remain current. Lifecycle prose summarizes and links rather than reproducing full ITTO catalogs.

docs.title: Alternatives Considered
docs.text:
• Copying each Confluence chapter into a public page.
  • Expanding the Master Project Sequence until it also served as the detailed lifecycle guide.
  • Maintaining process and artifact links independently in every chapter.

docs.title: Decision: Preserve the Closure and Benefits Boundary as Source-Limited
Status
docs.text: Accepted pending source resolution

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: The Atlas distinguishes formal project closure from continuing benefits ownership and requires an explicit handoff. It does not assert that all benefits must be realized before closure or that closure ends benefits responsibility.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: The Confluence snapshot places benefits measurement after formal closure, while the former Master Project Sequence wording defined project completion through realized value. The registered primary-source material does not resolve that boundary.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: The unsupported absolute statement was removed. Post-project benefits authority, measurement, and sustainment remain deferred until current PMI or framework sources are registered and reviewed.

docs.title: Alternatives Considered
docs.text:
• Treating the Confluence wording as authoritative PMI guidance.
  • Retaining the former absolute completion statement.
  • Omitting benefits ownership from transition and closure entirely.

docs.title: Projects, operations, programs, and portfolios
docs.text:
A project is temporary work undertaken to create a particular product, service, result, capability, or change. Temporary means it has a beginning and an end; it does not mean the work must be short. The result may continue long after the project team finishes.

Operations are the continuing activities that keep an organization functioning. A customer-service team handling cases each day is performing operations. A temporary effort to replace that team’s service platform is a project. The project ends after the replacement is delivered and transitioned, while the service continues in operations.

A program coordinates related projects and other work when managing them together can produce benefits that separate management would miss. A portfolio groups projects, programs, and sometimes operational work so leaders can select and balance investments against strategy, risk, capacity, and funding. A project manager manages an authorized project; program and portfolio decisions may change priorities or funding outside that project manager’s authority.

These distinctions matter because the same work can be viewed at different levels. ServiceBridge may be one project inside a broader customer-experience program, which may itself compete for funding within a transformation portfolio. The project still needs its own purpose, authority, scope, plans, and closure conditions.

docs.title: Why the Atlas uses a sequence
docs.text:
The sequence shows how project information changes. It is not a claim that every project follows one rigid, linear lifecycle.

A need is examined before resources are committed. Authorization then gives the work a legitimate starting point. Planning develops enough detail for coordinated action. Delivery produces results and evidence. Monitoring compares actual conditions with approved expectations. Change control protects commitments that cannot be altered informally. Verification, acceptance, transition, and closure make different decisions about the finished work.

Several parts repeat. Requirements can be clarified after planning begins. Risks are identified throughout the work. Adaptive teams refine a backlog and learn from increments. Hybrid projects may use iterative product delivery inside fixed funding, contractual, regulatory, or milestone boundaries.

docs.title: Governance and project management
docs.text:
Governance establishes who may make important decisions, which evidence those decisions require, and where exceptions are escalated. Project management organizes and coordinates the authorized work within those rules.

The two are connected but not interchangeable. A project manager may prepare an impact analysis, recommend a response, and coordinate approved work. That does not automatically allow the project manager to approve more funding, change a contract, waive a compliance requirement, accept a deliverable for the customer, or close the project. Those decisions belong to the roles named by the organization’s governance model.

The process, artifact, role, and decision pages linked below explain each part of this sequence in detail. The July 2026 course and registered source snapshots support the named relationships; where the Atlas explains how those relationships work in practice, it identifies that explanation as synthesis rather than PMI wording.

docs.title: Why Projects Exist
docs.text:
Projects exist because organizations need to move from an observed need to a durable result. The transformation framework in this section helps readers see that project work is not a collection of isolated activities. It is a sequence of changes in state, each one answering a different project question and creating new conditions for the next stage.

This framework is a conceptual map. It is not a new PMI methodology. It is a way to organize the Atlas around the major transitions that occur as a project moves from a business need to realized value.

docs.title: The Six Project Transformations
docs.text:
The six transformations describe how a project evolves from an initial opportunity or problem to an outcome that creates value. They also show why artifacts matter. Each transformation produces or updates artifacts that make the next stage possible, and each transformation creates a new level of clarity, commitment, or accountability.

The framework is useful because it helps readers connect sequence, artifacts, and decisions. It also clarifies that project work is often iterative and concurrent rather than strictly linear. A project may plan, execute, and adjust in parallel as uncertainty is reduced and new information appears.

docs.title: Planning Process Group Reference Order
docs.text:
The Atlas uses the following canonical order to reference and navigate the 24 processes in the Planning Process Group. This ordering gives each process a stable position; it does not claim that planning must occur once in a rigid chronology. Planning processes overlap, iterate, and may be revisited as project information changes.

docs.title: Planning Quality Before Work Begins
docs.text:
Quality planning is part of the project sequence because a project needs agreed standards before it can manage execution consistently. This section is positioned after requirements and scope information have emerged, because meaningful quality planning depends on knowing what the project is intended to achieve.

The process answers a practical question: what standards will define acceptable work, and how will the team measure them? In the Atlas sequence, this activity supports later quality management and inspection work by establishing the criteria that will be used during execution and review.

The transformation is not a separate method from the rest of the project. It is part of the broader movement from stated need to deliverable reality. Once the project has defined the quality expectations, later work can proceed with clearer measures for evaluation, verification, and acceptance.

For the complete process reference, see Plan Quality Management. Related artifacts include Quality Management Plan, Quality Metrics, Quality-Control Measurements, Verified Deliverables, and Accepted Deliverables. A dependency view is available in the Plan Quality Management dependency map, and a decision guide for inspection failures is available in A Deliverable Fails Quality Inspection.

docs.title: Transformation 1 — Business Need → Business Decision
docs.text:
A project begins with a business need, problem, or opportunity. The first transformation asks whether the organization should act on that need and commit resources to a project response.

The starting condition is an identified need. The resulting condition is a business decision to proceed, defer, or stop. The problem being solved is whether the opportunity is worth pursuing under current constraints. The principal decisions concern priority, feasibility, strategic fit, and expected value.

The primary artifacts involved are the business case, the initial project charter, and related strategic documentation. This transformation enables the next stage by creating the authority to move from intention to formal project initiation.

docs.title: Transformation 2 — Business Decision → Authorized Project
docs.text:
Once a decision has been made to proceed, the organization must establish the project as an authorized effort. This transformation turns a decided direction into an organizational commitment.

The starting condition is a business decision to proceed. The resulting condition is an authorized project with defined sponsor support and an initial mandate. The problem being solved is whether the effort is formally recognized as a project that can be governed. The principal decisions involve sponsor approval, high-level scope boundaries, and initial expectations for delivery.

The primary artifacts involved are the project charter, governance arrangements, and any initial stakeholder alignment materials. This transformation enables planning by giving the project a recognized starting point and a basis for formal coordination.

docs.title: Transformation 3 — Authorized Project → Planned Project
docs.text:
The third transformation turns an authorized project into a planned project. Planning does not mean every uncertainty has been eliminated. It means the project has enough structure to guide work, make tradeoffs, and manage risk.

The starting condition is an authorized project. The resulting condition is a planned project with defined scope, schedule, cost, quality expectations, and approach. The problem being solved is how the work will be carried out and how success will be measured. The principal decisions involve scope definition, approach selection, resource allocation, and risk posture.

The primary artifacts involved include the project management plan, scope statements, schedule information, and other planning outputs that define how the work will proceed. This transformation enables execution by converting intent into an actionable course of action.

docs.title: Transformation 4 — Planned Project → Executed Project
docs.text:
Execution brings the plan into practice. This transformation answers whether the project team can deliver the planned outcomes under real conditions.

The starting condition is a planned project. The resulting condition is an executed project with work being completed, monitored, and adapted. The problem being solved is how to deliver value while managing change, uncertainty, and performance concerns. The principal decisions involve prioritization, issue resolution, change handling, and coordination across workstreams.

The primary artifacts involved include work performance information, change records, status reporting, and updated planning artifacts. This transformation enables the next stage by producing evidence of progress and a basis for acceptance.

docs.title: Transformation 5 — Executed Project → Accepted Solution
docs.text:
The fifth transformation moves the project from delivery activity to formal acceptance. This is the point at which the project team and the requesting organization determine whether the solution is acceptable.

The starting condition is an executed project. The resulting condition is an accepted solution, where deliverables have been reviewed and the customer or sponsor accepts the outcome. The problem being solved is whether the work completed meets the intended need in a way that is acceptable to the receiving organization. The principal decisions involve validation, acceptance criteria, transition readiness, and formal closure of delivery obligations.

The primary artifacts involved include acceptance criteria, validation records, transition materials, and formal acceptance documentation. This transformation enables value realization by creating the conditions for the solution to be used rather than merely delivered.

docs.title: Transformation 6 — Accepted Solution → Business Value
docs.text:
The final transformation connects the accepted solution to business value. The Atlas currently treats formal project closure and continuing benefits ownership as distinct concepts, but the registered source set does not yet resolve exactly when benefits realization should define project completion.

The starting condition is an accepted solution. The resulting condition is realized business value. The problem being solved is whether the accepted outcome produces the intended benefit. The principal decisions involve adoption, measurement, operational integration, and ongoing accountability for results.

The primary artifacts involved include benefits tracking information, operational handoff materials, and performance measures that connect delivery to realized outcomes. The project must make continuing ownership explicit at transition; detailed post-project authority remains deferred pending source verification. See Verification, Acceptance, Transition, and Closure.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The six transformations provide a conceptual map for understanding how projects move from need to value. They help readers see that project work is an interconnected sequence of decisions, artifacts, and transitions. The Atlas uses this structure to explain why each stage exists, what it produces, and what follows next.

flowchart LR
    A[Business Need] --> B[Business Decision]
    B --> C[Authorized Project]
    C --> D[Planned Project]
    D --> E[Executed Project]
    E --> F[Accepted Solution]
    F --> G[Business Value]

docs.title: Reusable Resources
docs.text:
Every published artifact page includes an editable blank template and a filled Atlas example. Narrative and approval artifacts use DOCX; registers, logs, matrices, measures, estimates, and schedules use interoperable CSV. The examples share the fictional ServiceBridge Modernization context so requirement, risk, issue, change, deliverable, acceptance, transition, closure, and benefit records can be followed across pages.

Some artifacts use one common example because their decision purpose and structure do not materially change across delivery approaches. Their pages still explain differences in timing, ownership, granularity, formality, approval, storage, and update cadence.

An accepted deliverable is a verified deliverable that the authorized customer or acceptance role has formally approved.

Acceptance confirms that the result satisfies the agreed acceptance conditions and that the person with authority is willing to accept it. Technical conformance supports that decision but does not replace it.

DRAFT — Pending Editorial Review

docs.title: How acceptance occurs
docs.text:
Validate Scope presents verified deliverables, requirements, acceptance criteria, and supporting evidence to the designated acceptance authority. The decision and any conditions are recorded.

If accepted, the deliverable can move toward transition, release, payment, phase completion, or closure as the project requires. If rejected, the reason is documented and routed through clarification, correction, defect handling, contract administration, or change control.

For ServiceBridge, the accessibility and integration tests pass, so the portal is verified. During acceptance, customer-service leadership finds that an agreed supervisor workflow is missing. The result can be technically verified yet rejected because it does not satisfy the approved acceptance conditions. The team must determine whether the workflow is an omitted requirement, a defect, or a new request before acting.

docs.title: Why the authority matters
docs.text:
The project manager coordinates the acceptance process but does not automatically accept on behalf of the customer. A quality specialist verifies evidence but does not automatically own the business acceptance decision. Contracts, governance, product ownership, and organizational policy determine the authorized role.

Acceptance is not transition. A result can be accepted before operations are ready to receive it. Acceptance is also not project closure; remaining deliverables, obligations, procurements, records, or transition work may still be open.

Adaptive teams may accept backlog items or increments frequently. The Product Owner’s decisions operate within the organization’s actual product, contract, compliance, and acceptance authority. Hybrid projects may combine iterative product acceptance with formal release or project-level sign-off.

On the exam, verification precedes acceptance, and acceptance precedes or supports transition and closure.

docs.title: Delivery approach applicability
docs.text: ◎Common across approaches Predictive treatmentThe same core record supports predictive decisions; formality, approval, baselining, and storage are tailored. Adaptive equivalent or treatmentThe same core record supports adaptive decisions with timing, ownership, granularity, and update cadence tailored to the team. Hybrid treatmentThe same core form can cross governance and delivery cadences when ownership and decision rights remain clear. Why these badgesThe canonical artifact resource provides one common example because the decision purpose and structure do not materially differ by approach.

A separate Formal Acceptance Record was evaluated and consolidated here. Acceptance evidence is part of the accepted state and should not be split into a parallel record that can drift from the deliverable decision.

An agreement is the binding record of obligations and rights between parties. Use this page to interpret the contract boundary around seller work: the procurement statement of work describes what is needed, source selection chooses a seller, and the agreement records the negotiated scope, price, schedule, acceptance, change, remedy, and closure terms. Project team members may administer work within delegated limits, but only authorized representatives can bind the organizations.

For ServiceBridge, an iterative release arrangement can allow backlog detail to evolve while keeping the funding ceiling, accessibility evidence, acceptance role, and commercial change route explicit. A backlog decision does not silently amend the agreement.

docs.title: What an assumption is
docs.text:
An assumption is something the project temporarily treats as true for a decision or plan even though complete proof is not yet available. Assumptions exist during initiation because authorization must occur before every requirement, estimate, supplier condition, technical fact, and stakeholder response is known. The danger is not uncertainty itself; it is allowing an untested belief to behave like a fact without an owner or consequence.

An Assumption Log makes those beliefs visible and testable. It records what is assumed, why the belief appears reasonable, who can validate it, when validation is needed, what method and evidence will be used, and what happens if it proves false. This transforms hidden uncertainty into managed project information.

docs.title: Contents and rationale
docs.text:
The assumption statement must be specific enough to test. Its basis records the evidence or reasoning available when the assumption was made. An owner is the person able to coordinate validation—not necessarily the person who first stated it. A validation method and due date keep the assumption from remaining indefinitely open.

The impact if false links the belief to scope, schedule, cost, quality, risk, procurement, stakeholder, benefit, or transition consequences. Status and result fields show whether the assumption is open, validating, confirmed, disproved, superseded, or closed. Related risks, decisions, dependencies, and changes preserve traceability when validation changes the project’s direction.

docs.title: Validation and lifecycle
docs.text:
Assumptions are captured from needs assessment, the Business Case, benefits planning, agreements, charter development, stakeholder discussions, estimates, technical analysis, and environmental conditions. The project manager coordinates the log, but specialists, sponsors, functional leaders, sellers, product roles, and operational owners validate assumptions within their authority and expertise.

During planning, assumptions shape estimates, requirements, approaches, and reserves; they should be tested before irreversible commitments where practical. During execution, new evidence may confirm or disprove them. A disproved assumption is not automatically a formal change request: first assess the consequence. If a controlled baseline, contract, funding decision, or other reserved commitment must change, route the appropriate decision through its governing process.

Predictive work may review assumptions at planning gates and control dates. Adaptive work often converts uncertain beliefs into hypotheses, spikes, experiments, prototypes, or early increments. Scrum and Kanban do not prescribe an Assumption Log, though their feedback practices can supply validation evidence. Hybrid work can connect rapid experiments to formal milestone, contract, compliance, and funding decisions.

docs.title: Nearby concepts
docs.text:
A fact is supported as true for the current decision. A constraint limits available options, such as a law or fixed deadline. A dependency is a reliance between work, parties, decisions, or conditions. A risk is uncertainty that may affect objectives; an assumption can be a source of risk when its failure would matter. A decision selects an action or position from available information. These concepts can be related without being synonyms.

For example, “the statute requires seven-year retention” is a constraint when verified. “The selected platform supports compliant retention without customization” is an assumption until tested. Reliance on the seller’s configuration is a dependency. The possibility that the capability fails and delays acceptance is a risk. Selecting an extension after analysis is a decision.

docs.title: ServiceBridge worked example
docs.text:
ServiceBridge assumes that active customer records can be mapped to the cloud platform with acceptable quality before the transition window. The basis is a preliminary sample and seller documentation. The migration lead owns validation through a rehearsal and control-total reconciliation by the planning checkpoint. If false, migration scope, schedule, cost, acceptance evidence, and the 2027-11-19 transition may be affected.

The related risk is that migrated-record quality delays acceptance. If rehearsal evidence disproves the assumption, the team analyzes correction, phased migration, additional tooling, or schedule options. The project manager can coordinate analysis but cannot exceed the USD 2.4 million authority, change the seller agreement, or move an acceptance decision unilaterally; those consequences go to the appropriate sponsor, change, procurement, and acceptance authorities.

docs.title: Failure modes
docs.text:
Unstated assumptions create surprise because stakeholders discover too late that they planned from different beliefs. Vague entries such as “resources will be available” cannot be tested. Entries without owners or dates remain permanent uncertainty, while marking an assumption “confirmed” without recording evidence creates false confidence.

Another failure is converting every unknown into a risk entry without clarifying the underlying belief, or treating every disproved assumption as automatic scope change. A useful log keeps statements testable, validates them at decision-relevant times, and routes consequences according to authority.

docs.title: Exam distinctions
docs.text: Assumption is not fact, constraint, risk, dependency, issue, or decision. A false assumption can create or change a risk; once an uncertain event occurs it may become an issue; and a response may require a change request only when a controlled commitment is affected. The charter contains high-level assumptions, while the Assumption Log maintains fuller validation information through the lifecycle.

docs.title: Sources and synthesis status
docs.text: The verified conception source supports initial assumptions, charter and assumption-log relationships, ownership, validation, and later planning use. Existing Atlas relationship and decision data supports links to risk and change. The detailed distinctions, ServiceBridge validation path, and failure modes are Atlas synthesis constrained by those sources; no universal assumption status set, experiment method, or approval workflow is asserted.

docs.title: Benefits Handoff Record
docs.text:
On this page
  1. Definition and purpose
  2. Creation, updates, and authority
  3. Typical content
  4. Lifecycle and state
  5. Relationships and downstream use
  6. Delivery approach applicability
  7. Illustrative example

A Benefits Handoff Record transfers responsibility for measuring and sustaining expected benefits after project work or formal closure.

Projects often create a capability before the organization can observe its full benefit. ServiceBridge can launch a new platform and close the project before six months of operational response-time data exist. Without a handoff, the measure, owner, and follow-up decision can disappear when the project team is released.

docs.title: What the record needs to preserve
docs.text:
The record identifies each benefit, its owner, baseline, target, measurement method, data source, expected realization period, dependencies, disbenefits, review dates, reporting route, and action or escalation threshold.

The baseline shows the starting condition. The target defines the expected improvement. The method and data source make the measure repeatable. The owner remains accountable after project closure. Review dates prevent “measure later” from becoming no measurement at all.

For ServiceBridge, the operations director owns the target of reducing average response time from 48 hours to 12 hours within six months of launch. The record identifies the service-data source, monthly reviews, adoption dependencies, and the governance route if performance does not improve.

docs.title: Relationship to other records
docs.text:
The Business Case explains why the investment should be made. Benefits management information defines expected value and how it will be measured. The Project Charter authorizes the project at a high level. The Benefits Handoff Record confirms who continues the measurement and response after transition or closure.

The final report can state what the project delivered and which early outcomes are known. It should not claim that a future benefit has been realized without evidence.

The registered sources do not resolve one universal rule for whether benefit realization defines project completion. The Atlas therefore separates formal closure from continuing benefits ownership and preserves that source gap explicitly.

Predictive, adaptive, and hybrid projects can all require benefit follow-up. Delivery cadence may change when capabilities are released and measured, but it does not remove the need for an owner and evidence.

On the exam, distinguish project outputs from benefits, the project manager from the post-project benefit owner, and formal closure from later benefit realization.

docs.title: Definition and purpose

docs.title: Plain-language meaning and function
docs.text:
A Benefits Management Plan explains what valuable outcomes the project is expected to enable, how those outcomes will be measured, who owns them, when they may appear, and what must continue after project delivery for them to be sustained. It prevents “delivered the outputs” from being treated as automatically equivalent to “created the intended value.”

An output is something the project produces, such as a portal, migrated records, training, or a transitioned service. An outcome is the changed condition that follows when people use those outputs. A benefit is a measurable improvement valued by the organization or customer. The project can finish before the benefit is fully realized because adoption, operating performance, policy change, or market response may continue after transition.

docs.title: Contents and rationale
docs.text:
Each benefit needs a clear statement, a baseline or current condition, a target, a measure, a data source, and a realization horizon. Without the baseline, an improvement cannot be distinguished from prior performance. Without a target and measure, “better service” cannot support an accountable decision. Without a trustworthy data source, a reported benefit may be advocacy rather than evidence.

The plan identifies a benefit owner because project authority is temporary while benefit ownership often continues in operations, product management, or the sponsoring organization. It also records dependencies, assumptions, risks, possible disbenefits, enabling changes, review cadence, and handoff conditions. These elements explain why a technically correct output may still fail to create value—for example, if training is incomplete, adoption is low, a policy dependency is unresolved, or the measure cannot be collected.

docs.title: Creation and ownership
docs.text:
Benefits planning draws from the Business Case, charter objectives, strategy, customer and operational needs, expected product outcomes, and feasibility evidence. The sponsor, business owner, benefit owner, operations owner, product leadership, finance or measurement specialists, customers, and project team negotiate what can reasonably be attributed to the initiative and what remains outside project control.

The project manager coordinates enabling work and provides project evidence but does not automatically own post-project realization. The sponsor sustains strategic sponsorship and ensures ownership is assigned. The benefit owner accepts the measure, dependencies, review schedule, and follow-through needed after handoff. Governance decides what level of benefit shortfall, delay, or changed assumption requires correction, reconsideration, or escalation.

docs.title: Lifecycle and realization
docs.text:
Benefits are identified during investment evaluation and clarified during authorization and planning. Project decisions use them to compare scope, release, quality, schedule, cost, and change options. During delivery, increments or demonstrations can provide early evidence, but preliminary signals should not be confused with sustained realization.

Transition moves responsibility for using the capability and collecting measures to the receiving owner. Closure can occur when the project’s completion and handoff conditions are met even though later benefit reviews remain scheduled. The benefits information then remains under operational or governance ownership, and the project record should identify unresolved dependencies or risks rather than quietly abandoning them.

Predictive work may define measures and realization reviews early against an approved investment case. Adaptive work can treat benefits as hypotheses, use increments to test value, and revise product direction when evidence changes. Scrum does not prescribe a Benefits Management Plan, and product value accountability does not erase organizational benefit ownership. Hybrid work can combine iterative value evidence with formal funding, transition, and post-project review commitments.

docs.title: ServiceBridge worked example
docs.text:
ServiceBridge delivers a cloud service platform, accessible appointment portal, validated migration, and operations training. Those are outputs. The intended outcomes are that customers can complete appointments through an accessible self-service path, staff can work from reliable records, and operations can sustain the service. The planned benefit is a measurable reduction in service time without sacrificing accessibility, retention, or availability obligations.

The Director of Customer Operations is the benefit owner. The plan records the current service-time baseline, a 30 percent improvement target, the operational reporting source, and review points after the 2027-11-19 transition. Dependencies include staff adoption, complete training, reliable production data, accessible workflows, and support capacity. Risks include low adoption, data-quality defects, and operating workarounds that bypass the new process.

The Service Modernization Program Manager ensures the portal, migration, training, measurement capability, and handoff evidence are delivered within the project. The benefit owner accepts the ongoing measurement responsibility. If the project closes on 2027-12-17, that closure does not assert that the 30 percent benefit has already been sustained; later reviews determine realization.

docs.title: Failure modes
docs.text:
Benefits plans fail when they rename deliverables as benefits, choose measures after results are known, omit baselines, or assign ownership to a temporary project role with no post-project mandate. They also fail when every positive organizational trend is attributed to the project despite other causes.

The consequence is an initiative that can report completion while no one can determine value. A useful plan keeps measures proportionate, documents assumptions and attribution limits, names a durable owner, and connects transition evidence to later review rather than inflating certainty.

docs.title: Exam distinctions
docs.text: The Business Case supports the investment decision; the charter authorizes the project and states high-level objectives; the Benefits Management Plan defines benefit measures, ownership, timing, and sustainment; project deliverables are outputs; operational outcomes and benefits may follow later. Product value decisions and benefit-realization governance can interact without being identical.

docs.title: Sources and synthesis status
docs.text: The verified conception and closure sources support benefit definition, ownership, realization timing, transition, and post-project measurement. The output–outcome–benefit explanation, ServiceBridge walkthrough, failure modes, and cross-approach treatment are Atlas synthesis constrained by the registered scenario and official adaptive-framework boundaries; the Atlas withholds any claim that one benefit formula, template, or ownership model is universally prescribed.

docs.title: Plain-language meaning and function
docs.text:
A Business Case is the decision argument for investing in an initiative. It explains the problem or opportunity, compares credible options—including doing nothing where that is feasible—and shows why the recommended option is expected to create sufficient value under the organization’s constraints and uncertainty. Its central question is not “How will the team manage the project?” but “Should this organization commit attention and resources to this change?”

That question requires more than an attractive solution. Decision-makers need to understand the current condition, the consequences of inaction, strategic alignment, expected benefits and disbenefits, costs, feasibility, major risks, assumptions, dependencies, and the people who will own the result. A proposal can be technologically possible but operationally unworkable, financially unattractive, legally unacceptable, or misaligned with strategy.

docs.title: What it contains and why
docs.text:
The need or opportunity establishes the condition that warrants a decision. Alternatives analysis prevents the preferred solution from being treated as inevitable and reveals tradeoffs among no action, process change, purchase, build, incremental discovery, or other options. Strategic alignment explains why the initiative deserves priority relative to other uses of resources.

Expected benefits, costs, and timing let decision-makers judge value rather than outputs alone. Feasibility examines whether the option can realistically work across technical, operational, financial, legal, schedule, organizational, and resource dimensions appropriate to the context. High-level risks, assumptions, and dependencies show where the conclusion is conditional rather than certain. The recommendation then connects evidence to a decision instead of merely repeating the preferred option.

docs.title: How it is developed
docs.text:
Business-case development normally begins with a needs assessment that compares the current state with a desired future condition. Sponsors, business owners, customers, operational representatives, finance, legal or compliance specialists, technical experts, procurement authorities, and potential project leadership contribute different evidence. Estimates at this stage should be proportionate to the decision; false precision can make an immature proposal look more certain than it is.

The evaluating authority may approve, reject, defer, request more evidence, authorize discovery only, or select a different option. The project manager can contribute feasibility, delivery, dependency, and risk information, but does not normally decide that the organization should invest unless that authority is explicitly assigned.

docs.title: Lifecycle and decision use
docs.text:
The Business Case precedes or supports charter authorization. A favorable case creates a reason to authorize; it does not itself necessarily authorize project execution. The Project Charter records the authorization, high-level boundaries, sponsor, and project-manager authority. The Benefits Management Plan develops how expected value will be measured, owned, transferred, and sustained.

The case can be revisited when feasibility evidence changes, costs or benefits materially shift, strategic priorities move, a major risk emerges, or continued investment no longer appears justified. Revisiting the case is not a ritual rewrite at every status meeting. It is a governance response when the original investment logic may no longer hold.

Predictive governance may seek a comparatively developed case before authorizing detailed planning. Adaptive governance may authorize a small discovery, experiment, or release to test the riskiest value and feasibility assumptions before committing to a full solution. Hybrid governance can use fixed funding, compliance, or contract boundaries while allowing product scope to evolve from evidence.

docs.title: ServiceBridge worked example
docs.text:
Northstar Public Services documents fragmented appointment and customer-service processes, avoidable delays, accessibility gaps, and weak record traceability. It compares four options: retain the current process, improve procedures without replacing the platform, purchase and configure a cloud service, or build a custom system. Doing nothing avoids near-term investment but preserves service and compliance exposure. Procedure-only improvement is less costly but cannot supply the required accessible portal, availability, migration, and auditable-retention capability.

The recommended cloud-service modernization is estimated within the authorized USD 2.4 million boundary and can deliver the four registered ServiceBridge deliverables. Expected outcomes include accessible self-service, validated records, stronger availability and retention controls, and a measurable reduction in service time after transition. The case recognizes migration quality and seller capacity as major risks, assumes operational participation and usable source data, and requires compliance evidence before release.

The recommendation is conditional: authorize ServiceBridge Modernization with the Chief Customer Officer as sponsor, require detailed planning and procurement controls, and retain explicit exit criteria if migration feasibility, compliance evidence, or seller capacity becomes unacceptable. The case supports the charter; the sponsor’s charter approval supplies the project authorization.

docs.title: Failure modes
docs.text:
A weak Business Case starts with a preferred product and works backward to justify it. It omits no-action consequences, hides disbenefits, treats optimistic benefits as guaranteed, or presents early estimates as a cost baseline. The result is selection bias and a project that can deliver outputs without solving the actual need.

Another failure is orphaned value: the case promises benefits but names no operational owner, measure, or realization horizon. A completed project then has no accountable recipient for determining whether value occurred. The corrective practice is evidence-based comparison, explicit uncertainty, named benefit ownership, and governance that can stop or redirect investment.

docs.title: Exam distinctions
docs.text: The Business Case justifies an investment; the charter authorizes a project; the Benefits Management Plan explains how benefits will be measured and sustained; and the Project Management Plan explains how project work will be managed. Feasibility supports a decision but does not itself authorize. Approval of a case may lead to rejection, discovery, conditional authorization, or full authorization depending on governance.

docs.title: Sources and synthesis status
docs.text: The July 2026 course supports the Business Case as a documented feasibility study that establishes benefits and provides a basis for further authorization, and it distinguishes the preceding business-needs information. The verified conception source supports alternatives, feasibility, strategic alignment, risks, assumptions, and downstream charter use. The ServiceBridge comparison, failure modes, and approach-specific decision patterns are Atlas synthesis; no claim is made that PMI prescribes one financial technique, document format, or approval path for every initiative.

docs.title: Change Log
docs.text:
On this page
  1. Definition and purpose
  2. Creation, updates, and authority
  3. Typical content
  4. Lifecycle and state
  5. Relationships and downstream use
  6. Delivery approach applicability
  7. Illustrative example
  8. References

The Change Log records change requests from submission through decision, implementation, verification, and closure.

It gives the project one traceable view of what was requested, who decided, what commitments were affected, whether the approved work was completed, and whether the result was verified.

docs.title: The states must remain distinct
docs.text:
A requested change is awaiting a decision. An approved change has authorization but may not yet be implemented. An implemented change has been performed. A verified change has evidence showing that the approved result was achieved. A closed entry preserves the full path and any remaining conditions.

Collapsing these states creates false reporting. A dashboard that counts approval as completion can claim progress before the team has performed or checked the work.

For ServiceBridge, the change log links an encryption request to its impact analysis, approval by the designated authority, revised design and test work, implementation owner, security-test evidence, baseline updates, and closure date.

docs.title: How the log relates to other records
docs.text:
The Change Request contains the proposal and analysis. The Change Log tracks its lifecycle. Approved changes can update the Project Management Plan, baselines, project documents, contracts, backlog items, deliverables, or other controlled records. Work performance reports may summarize change status for stakeholders.

The log does not replace the configuration record that identifies product versions, the Issue Log that manages current problems, or the decision record that may hold detailed rationale. Links connect these records without confusing their purposes.

In adaptive work, the log should cover changes that cross a controlled boundary rather than every normal backlog refinement. Hybrid projects may connect iterative delivery changes to formal contract, compliance, release, funding, or baseline decisions.

On the exam, approval does not equal implementation, and implementation does not equal verification.

docs.title: Change Requests
docs.text:
A change request is a documented proposal to modify a project commitment, result, plan, document, process, or course of action.

Submitting a request does not approve the change. The request creates a record that can be analyzed and sent to the person or group with authority to decide.

docs.title: What a useful request explains
docs.text:
The request identifies the proposed change, reason, requester, urgency, affected scope or result, and known effects. Impact analysis then examines schedule, cost, quality, resources, risk, benefits, contracts, compliance, operations, and stakeholders as applicable.

These elements prevent a decision based only on the apparent benefit. A “small” ServiceBridge encryption change may affect seller work, performance, testing, compliance evidence, cost, and the launch date. The decision-maker needs those effects before approving it.

Requests may propose corrective action, preventive action, defect repair, or an update to a controlled plan, baseline, document, or deliverable. The correct classification helps route the request, but it does not determine approval by itself.

docs.title: What happens after submission
docs.text:
The authorized change role approves, rejects, defers, or requests more information. An approved request becomes an approved change. It is communicated, assigned, implemented, and verified. A rejected request does not authorize work. The Change Log preserves the decision and later implementation status.

The project manager may approve changes within delegated limits but does not have universal authority over baselines, funding, contracts, compliance, personnel, or product decisions.

Adaptive teams can refine or reorder uncommitted backlog work without treating every adjustment as a formal change request. Changes to controlled commitments still follow the applicable authority route. Hybrid projects must state which decisions remain within the team and which require integrated control.

On the exam, analyze before acting, use the approved process, and do not implement a requested change merely because it seems beneficial or urgent.

Closed procurement is the documented state reached after the buyer confirms that contractual obligations, claims, payments, records, and required acceptance or termination actions have been handled under the agreement. It is not the same as project closure: one contract may close while other project work continues, and project closure cannot erase an unresolved seller obligation.

For ServiceBridge, the procurement authority reconciles final invoices, confirms delivery and contractual acceptance evidence, resolves an open claim, and archives the agreement record before marking the procurement closed. The project manager supplies project evidence, but commercial closure follows the authority named by policy and agreement.

docs.title: Evidence must connect an obligation to a decision
docs.text:
Compliance evidence and traceability is the controlled record that connects an applicable obligation to the work that addresses it, the evidence that demonstrates conformance, and the authority that decides whether the evidence is sufficient. It exists because a policy, law, security rule, accessibility standard, or contract clause cannot be managed reliably as an isolated note. The team must know where the obligation came from, which deliverable or process it affects, who owns the response, and what evidence will support release or acceptance.

The record normally identifies the obligation and source, interpretation, affected requirements and work, evidence location and version, responsible owner, reviewer or approving authority, status, exceptions, and retention needs. Those fields create a chain that can be followed in both directions. A tester can find the requirement behind a test, while an auditor can start with an obligation and locate the approved evidence. The record is not the evidence itself and does not grant an exception; it indexes evidence and preserves the relevant decision trail.

For ServiceBridge, a seven-year retention obligation affects data design, migration tests, operating procedures, and the transition package. The compliance lead records the source and interpretation, the team links test results and configuration evidence, and the authorized reviewer records sufficiency or a required correction. If evidence fails, the issue and any controlled change follow their own processes. Predictive work may establish the matrix early; adaptive teams update it with each increment; hybrid delivery links iteration evidence to formal release gates.

docs.title: Definition and purpose
docs.text:
Connects an obligation to requirements, controls, tests, evidence, findings, approvals, and retention without defining an unsupported universal compliance framework.

Obligations need an auditable path to implementation and evidence without inventing a one-size-fits-all compliance system.

docs.title: Cost Baseline
docs.text:
The Cost Baseline is the approved, time-phased budget used to measure and control project cost performance.

“Time-phased” means the approved budget is distributed across the periods in which the work is planned. This allows the team to compare the value of planned and completed work with actual cost at a particular status date.

docs.title: What is included and excluded
docs.text:
The baseline is built from approved cost estimates for the project scope. It includes contingency reserve for identified uncertainty within that scope. It excludes management reserve, which is held for unforeseen work that is still within project scope.

The total of the cost baseline is Budget at Completion, or BAC. The total project budget is the cost baseline plus management reserve. A Charter funding boundary, an early estimate, BAC, available cash, and total authorized funding can therefore be different values.

These distinctions matter because performance must be compared with the correct reference. Using management reserve as though it were ordinary baseline budget would hide the fact that the project needed governance-held funds for unforeseen work.

docs.title: How the baseline is created and controlled
docs.text:
The team aggregates estimates from the approved scope, accounts for schedule timing and funding constraints, adds authorized contingency treatment, and reconciles the result with the project’s financial boundary. The designated authority approves the baseline under the Project Management Plan.

For ServiceBridge, approved migration, configuration, integration, testing, training, and transition costs are time-phased. Contingency for identified migration uncertainty is included. Any management reserve is shown outside the baseline and released only through the organization’s authority process.

Actual cost and earned value are compared with the baseline during Control Costs. A forecast such as Estimate at Completion predicts where the project may finish; it does not silently replace the baseline. An approved change may update the baseline, after which the change record and baseline version preserve the decision history.

Predictive and hybrid projects commonly use a formal cost baseline where scope and financial control require it. Adaptive product teams may manage funding by release, horizon, or stable team capacity, but project-level financial commitments and governance still need an explicit reference where the organization requires control.

On the exam, distinguish estimate from baseline, BAC from total project budget, contingency reserve from management reserve, and forecast from approved baseline.

docs.title: An estimate explains expected cost and its basis
docs.text:
A cost estimate is a quantified assessment of the money expected to be needed for project work. It exists so the team can compare options, test affordability, build a budget, and understand uncertainty before money is committed. A number without scope, assumptions, units, date, method, and confidence is not a usable estimate because another reader cannot tell what it includes or when it should be revised.

Estimates may be prepared for activities, work packages, control accounts, releases, or the project. Supporting detail explains the estimating method, resource rates, quantities, exclusions, assumptions, risks, range, and source data. Analogous estimates use comparable history; parametric estimates apply a valid unit relationship; three-point estimates represent uncertainty; bottom-up estimates aggregate detailed components. The method should match the available information and required decision. An estimate is not the cost baseline: estimates inform the budget, while the approved time-phased cost baseline becomes the performance reference.

For ServiceBridge, the migration team estimates 8,000 records at a validated rate of 12 minutes per record, adds specialist review, and documents the expected error range. The project manager combines that estimate with other work and identified contingency during budgeting. If trial migration shows 18 minutes per record, the estimate changes and the budget effect is assessed; the baseline changes only through the applicable authority. Predictive work often estimates more detail earlier, adaptive work refines near-term items and forecasts releases, and hybrid work combines both horizons.

docs.title: Deliverables
docs.text:
On this page

  2. Creation, updates, and authority

A deliverable is a product, service, or result produced by the project.

Deliverables are the things the project is responsible for creating. They may be physical, digital, documentary, operational, or decision-related. A configured platform, migrated data set, approved design, training package, and transition package can all be deliverables.

docs.title: What the record needs to establish
docs.text:
A deliverable record identifies the result, version, related requirements, producer, completion evidence, known exceptions, and current state. These details keep different versions from being confused and connect the result to the scope and requirements it is meant to satisfy.

“Completed” means the delivery team has produced the result according to its working definition of completion. It does not automatically mean that quality control has verified it or that the customer has accepted it.

For ServiceBridge, the team completes a migration package containing transformed records, reconciliation results, exception files, and execution notes. That package is a deliverable. Quality control still needs to inspect the evidence and test the result before its state can become verified.

docs.title: The deliverable state sequence
docs.text:
1. The delivery team produces a deliverable.
  2. Control Quality inspects or tests it.
  3. Conforming work becomes a Verified Deliverable.
  4. Validate Scope presents verified work to the authorized acceptance role.
  5. Approval creates an Accepted Deliverable.
  6. Accepted results are transitioned and included in closure evidence as appropriate.

A failed check can return the result for correction. A verified result can still be rejected during acceptance if it does not satisfy the agreed acceptance conditions or the wrong result was produced.

Adaptive teams may produce a usable increment containing several completed backlog items. The Definition of Done establishes the shared quality commitment for the increment. Product review and formal organizational acceptance remain context-dependent decisions.

On the exam, do not use completed, verified, and accepted as synonyms. Each state requires different evidence and authority.

docs.title: The final report explains what the project actually achieved
docs.text:
A final report is the project-level account of performance, results, significant decisions, and remaining responsibilities prepared for closure. It exists because scattered status reports do not provide one reliable conclusion about what was authorized, what was delivered and accepted, how performance compared with the plan, and what continues after the project ends.

The report normally summarizes objectives and outcomes, accepted deliverables, schedule and cost results, quality and risk results, major changes, procurement status, lessons, transition status, unresolved obligations, and benefits ownership. Each element supports a closure decision or future organizational learning. The report does not itself accept deliverables, transfer operational ownership, close a contract, or authorize project closure. It assembles evidence from those decisions and makes omissions visible to the closure authority.

For ServiceBridge, the project manager reports that the portal and migration were accepted, the release occurred three weeks later than the original baseline after an approved accessibility change, and USD 80,000 of management reserve was used through authorized governance. The report names the operations owner for two open support actions and the benefit owner for later adoption measurement. The sponsor uses this report with acceptance, transition, procurement, and archive evidence to decide formal closure. Incremental delivery may produce release reports throughout the work, but adaptive and hybrid projects still need a coherent project-level conclusion when the authorization ends.

docs.title: Closure is an authorized decision, not a feeling that work is finished
docs.text:
A formal closure record documents that the person or body with closure authority has reviewed the required evidence and authorized the project or phase to close. It exists because teams can finish delivery while contracts, records, transition actions, finances, or ownership decisions remain open. The record makes the boundary decision explicit and prevents later uncertainty about whether the project still has authority, resources, or obligations.

The record identifies the project or phase, closure basis, approving authority and date, accepted or terminated scope, transition status, procurement and financial status, unresolved items and their owners, archive location, resource release, and any conditions attached to closure. These fields show both what ended and what continues elsewhere. A final report informs the decision; the closure record captures the decision. Accepted deliverables and an operational handoff may be prerequisites, but neither automatically closes the project.

For ServiceBridge, the sponsor reviews customer acceptance, the operations receipt, the seller’s final settlement, the final report, and a list of two support actions transferred to operations. The sponsor signs the closure record, the project manager releases the remaining team, and the records custodian archives the controlled files. Benefit measurement continues with its named owner; that continuing work does not silently keep the project open. A terminated project uses the same discipline to identify completed work, assets, liabilities, and continuing ownership. Adaptive releases may close incrementally, while project-level authorization still requires its own closure decision.

docs.title: Definition and purpose

Formal closure is an authority decision, not merely the absence of remaining project tasks or the realization of every benefit.

docs.title: An impediment record makes blocked flow actionable
docs.text:
An impediment record captures a condition that obstructs or slows the team’s work and tracks the action needed to remove it. It exists because a blocker mentioned in a daily conversation can disappear from attention even while its delay grows. Recording the condition, affected work, owner, urgency, escalation route, and resolution evidence makes the obstruction visible until flow is restored.

An impediment differs from a risk because it is affecting work now rather than describing an uncertain future event. It can also be an issue, but the impediment view emphasizes blocked flow and removal. A defect describes nonconforming work; a change request proposes an alteration; neither is automatically an impediment. The team should avoid creating duplicate records when one issue log or work board can carry the needed fields and traceability.

For ServiceBridge, the portal team cannot complete integration tests because the shared identity environment is unavailable. The team marks the affected backlog items, records when blocking began, assigns the platform lead, and sets an escalation threshold of one business day. When the restoration estimate exceeds that threshold, the project manager escalates the dependency and updates the release forecast. The record closes only after access is restored and the affected work can proceed, not when someone promises to investigate. Adaptive teams may keep impediments on a visible board; predictive and hybrid projects may use an issue log, provided current impact and removal ownership remain clear.

docs.title: Definition and purpose
docs.text:
Makes work blockers or flow constraints visible so the team can resolve or escalate them; an impediment may also be managed as an issue.

Work that is blocked or slowed needs immediate visibility even when the team has not yet classified it as a broader project issue.

docs.title: Issue Log
docs.text:
On this page
  1. Definition and purpose
  2. Creation, updates, and authority
  3. Typical content
  4. Lifecycle and state
  5. Relationships and downstream use
  6. Delivery approach applicability
  7. Illustrative example
  8. References

The Issue Log records problems, decisions, or conditions that exist now and require action.

An issue is not an uncertain future event. “The vendor may miss the date” is a risk. “The vendor missed today’s delivery date” is an issue. When a risk occurs, the team may close or update the risk entry and create a linked issue so the current problem has an owner and action path.

docs.title: What the log needs to show
docs.text:
A useful issue entry states the current condition, when it was identified, its effect and urgency, the owner, planned action, due date, escalation threshold, decisions, related risks or changes, and current status.

These fields make responsibility visible. A description without an owner does not show who will act. An owner without a due date does not show when the response is expected. A due date without an escalation threshold can leave a material problem unresolved until it is too late.

For ServiceBridge, a test reveals that migrated records have missing consent dates. The issue entry identifies affected data, compliance and schedule effects, the remediation owner, the next decision date, and the threshold for escalating a transition delay or change request.

docs.title: How issues are managed
docs.text:
Issues can be identified during any process. The owner analyzes and coordinates action within available authority. The project manager monitors cross-project effects and escalates decisions outside the team’s limits. A material issue may create a change request, update forecasts, require risk reassessment, or affect a contract or compliance decision.

An impediment is anything blocking or slowing flow. Teams often resolve impediments quickly on a board. A persistent or significant impediment may be entered in the Issue Log when it needs broader ownership, escalation, or a durable decision trail.

The Issue Log does not replace the Risk Register, Change Log, defect record, or action list. Those records answer different questions, although links preserve the full path from uncertainty to current problem, decision, implementation, and resolution.

Predictive projects may review issues at regular status and governance meetings. Adaptive teams expose blockers daily and escalate them quickly. Hybrid work connects rapid team action with formal organizational decisions when baselines, contracts, funding, compliance, or acceptance are affected.

On the exam, address the current problem, analyze its impact, act within authority, and escalate when necessary. Do not keep treating a realized risk as merely uncertain.

docs.title: A lesson connects experience to a future action
docs.text:
A lessons learned register records knowledge gained during the project that can improve current or future decisions. It exists because an observation such as “testing started late” has little value unless the team explains what happened, why it mattered, the conditions under which it applies, and what should be repeated or changed. The register turns experience into retrievable guidance rather than waiting for memory at closure.

A useful entry identifies the situation, evidence, consequence, contributing causes, recommendation, owner or audience, and where the lesson was applied or stored. Lessons may be positive or negative and should be captured throughout the project, not only in a final meeting. The register is a project document; an organizational knowledge repository may receive selected lessons after validation and closure. It is not an issue log because it does not manage current resolution, although one event may produce both an issue action and a lesson.

For ServiceBridge, a trial migration reveals that field owners interpret “inactive customer” differently. The team records the cause, the reconciliation delay, and a recommendation to approve business definitions before the next migration wave. The data lead applies the recommendation to upcoming work and later transfers the validated lesson to the organizational repository. In adaptive delivery, retrospectives can generate entries and experiments; in predictive work, phase reviews and control events do the same. On the exam, respond to useful knowledge by capturing, sharing, and applying it—not by postponing all learning until closure.

docs.title: The procurement SOW defines what a seller is being asked to provide
docs.text:
A procurement statement of work describes the product, service, or result to be obtained from a seller with enough clarity for sourcing, proposals, agreement, delivery, and acceptance. It exists because a seller cannot price or commit responsibly when the buyer’s need, boundaries, performance expectations, constraints, and acceptance basis are unclear.

Its major elements commonly include scope and deliverables, specifications or outcomes, interfaces, milestones, buyer-furnished information, standards and compliance, reporting, assumptions, exclusions, and acceptance criteria. The needed level of detail depends on the procurement approach. Too little detail transfers ambiguity rather than risk; excessive design prescription can prevent a seller from proposing a better solution. The procurement SOW informs solicitation and agreement but is not itself the signed agreement, source-selection method, or complete project scope statement.

For ServiceBridge, the buyer needs an accessibility-testing service. The SOW identifies the portal releases to test, required standards, environments, evidence format, reporting timing, retest rules, and acceptance authority. Sellers use the same boundary to prepare comparable proposals. After selection, the negotiated SOW becomes part of the agreement, and later changes follow contractual authority rather than an informal team request. Predictive procurement may specify a stable deliverable in detail; adaptive procurement may contract for evolving outcomes, capacity, or increments while preserving decision rights and acceptance; hybrid arrangements often combine fixed compliance obligations with iteratively selected feature work.

docs.title: Procurement strategy decides how the market will be used
docs.text:
A procurement strategy explains how an external need will be sourced, contracted, governed, and closed. It exists before solicitation so the project does not choose a contract or seller without considering capability, market conditions, risk allocation, schedule, organizational authority, and the kind of relationship the work requires.

The strategy addresses make-or-buy reasoning, packaging of the work, sourcing route, competition, contract and payment approach, risk allocation, procurement schedule, governance, performance monitoring, change rights, acceptance, and closure. These choices interact. A fixed-price structure may suit a stable, well-defined result but can create disputes when scope is uncertain. A flexible arrangement may support learning but needs clear spending boundaries and decision cadence. The strategy is not the procurement statement of work, which describes what is needed, and it is not the agreement, which creates binding obligations.

For ServiceBridge, internal teams can build the portal but lack independent accessibility certification. The project manager, procurement authority, quality lead, and compliance owner decide to source outcome-based testing in release-sized packages, retain formal evidence and acceptance requirements, and reserve contract changes to the procurement authority. That decision shapes the SOW, selection criteria, solicitation, and later control. Adaptive delivery does not remove procurement governance; it may favor capacity or incremental outcome arrangements. Hybrid procurement commonly fixes legal, commercial, security, and milestone boundaries while allowing detailed product work to evolve.
