docs.title: Project Charter
docs.text:
A project charter is the document that officially authorizes a project.

Before the charter is approved, the work may be an idea, proposal, request, or possible investment. Once the sponsor or another authorized leader approves the charter, the organization is formally agreeing that the project should begin.

The charter also gives the project manager authority to begin organizing the work and to use organizational resources within the limits established by the organization.

docs.title: What is a project?
docs.text:
A project is temporary work undertaken to create a particular product, service, result, capability, or change.

Temporary means the project has a beginning and an end. It does not mean the project must be short. A project can last weeks or years, and the result may continue long after the project ends. Project work is different from routine operations, which repeat or continue without a planned ending.

Organizations undertake projects because they expect a useful result, benefit, obligation, improvement, or change. Because a project uses time, money, people, and other resources, someone with authority must decide that it should exist. The charter records that decision.

docs.title: What does the charter do?
docs.text:
Approving the charter means that the organization has agreed, at a high level:

  • why the project is being undertaken;
  • what it is expected to accomplish;
  • what broad work is included;
  • what major limits or conditions apply;
  • who will sponsor the project;
  • who will lead it;
  • what authority the project manager has;
  • whether detailed planning may begin.

The charter gives the team enough direction to begin planning. It does not contain the complete project plan. Detailed requirements, estimates, schedules, responsibilities, and control methods are developed later.

Without a charter, the project manager may be asked to lead work without clear authority. Teams may disagree about what was approved, and resources may be committed to an effort the organization has never formally authorized.

docs.title: What is included in a project charter?
Business need and project purpose
docs.text:
The business need describes why the project is being considered. It may be:

  • a problem to solve;
  • an opportunity;
  • a legal or regulatory requirement;
  • a customer need;
  • an operational improvement;
  • a strategic objective.

The project purpose states the result or change the project is intended to produce. The organization should not authorize a project unless it knows why the project is needed.

docs.title: Measurable objectives
docs.text:
Objectives describe what the project is expected to achieve. They should be specific enough that the organization can later determine whether the project accomplished what it was authorized to do.

For example: “Reduce average customer-service response time from 48 hours to 12 hours within six months of launch.” This is more useful than a vague objective such as “improve customer service.”

docs.title: Success criteria
docs.text:
Success criteria describe how the sponsor and stakeholders will judge whether the project succeeded. Examples may include:

  • a required capability works;
  • a deadline is met;
  • a regulatory requirement is satisfied;
  • users can complete a defined task;
  • an agreed performance target is reached.

Project completion and benefit realization may not occur at the same time. A project may deliver and transition a new service before the organization can measure its longer-term benefits.

docs.title: High-level scope
docs.text:
Scope describes the broad work and results included in the project. It answers:

  • What is this project broadly responsible for?
  • What is outside the project?
  • What major result is being authorized?

For a customer-service system project, the charter may include selecting or configuring the new system, migrating customer data, integrating the system with existing tools, training users, and launching the service. It may exclude replacing the billing system, redesigning unrelated websites, and restructuring the entire customer-service department.

Scope is included so the sponsor and team share an initial boundary for the work. Detailed requirements and detailed scope are developed later during planning. The charter sets the initial boundary without pretending that all details are already known.

docs.title: Preliminary requirements
docs.text:
Preliminary requirements are the major needs already known when the project is authorized. For example:

  • the system must meet accessibility requirements;
  • customer records must be retained for a defined period;
  • the service must support a stated number of users;
  • the solution must integrate with an existing platform.

These are not the complete requirements documentation. They record the important needs that affect the decision to authorize the project.

docs.title: Major deliverables
docs.text:
Deliverables are the main products, services, or results the project is expected to produce. Examples include a configured service platform, migrated data, training materials, tested integrations, and a transition package.

Major deliverables belong in the charter because they help the sponsor and project manager agree on the main results being authorized.

docs.title: Key stakeholders
docs.text:
Stakeholders are people or groups who can affect the project, are affected by it, provide resources, make decisions, use or accept the result, or may support or resist the work.

The charter identifies the most important stakeholders known at the beginning. These may include the sponsor, customer, major departments, users, regulators, vendors, and project manager.

Stakeholders are included because their authority, needs, expectations, and involvement may affect whether the project can succeed. The charter does not replace the Stakeholder Register, which records stakeholder information in greater detail.

docs.title: Approved budget or financial boundary
docs.text:
The charter may include an approved budget, funding limit, expected cost range, or another financial boundary. The organization needs to know how much money it is willing to commit before detailed planning begins.

The charter’s budget is a high-level authorization or boundary. It is not necessarily the final cost baseline. Detailed cost estimates and the cost baseline are developed later.

For ServiceBridge, the charter may state that the project is authorized within a USD 2.4 million financial boundary. Detailed cost planning later determines how that amount is allocated.

docs.title: Summary schedule and milestones
docs.text:
The charter includes major dates or milestones that matter to the authorization decision. Examples include a regulatory deadline, planned launch, contract date, phase completion, or required transition date.

Milestones are included because a project may not be feasible if a major date cannot be met. The charter does not contain the complete project schedule.

docs.title: High-level risks
docs.text:
The charter identifies major uncertainties that could affect the decision to proceed. For example, critical technology may not work as expected, required data may be incomplete, a key resource may be unavailable, an approval may be delayed, or a vendor may miss the required timeline.

Risks are included so the sponsor understands the most important uncertainty before authorizing the project. The charter is not the full Risk Register. Detailed risk identification, analysis, ownership, and response planning occur later.

docs.title: Assumptions
docs.text:
An assumption is something treated as true for planning even though it has not yet been fully confirmed. The team may assume that a subject-matter expert will be available, existing data is usable, a vendor can meet a stated date, or required funding will be released.

Assumptions are included because a false assumption may require a different schedule, budget, scope, or decision. Initial assumptions and constraints are also recorded in the Assumption Log, where they can be checked and monitored.

docs.title: Constraints and boundaries
docs.text:
Constraints are limits the project must work within. Examples include a fixed deadline, legal requirement, approved budget, required technology, contract condition, or limited staffing. Boundaries clarify where the project begins and ends.

Constraints and boundaries belong in the charter because they prevent planning from assuming options the organization does not actually have.

docs.title: Sponsor
docs.text:
The sponsor is the person or authority that supports the project at the organizational level and normally authorizes or secures authorization for it.

Depending on the organization, the sponsor may support the business need, obtain funding, resolve major organizational obstacles, approve the charter, and support the project manager. Not every sponsor performs every task in every organization.

docs.title: Project manager and authority
docs.text:
The charter identifies the project manager or project lead and states the authority granted to that person. The authority may include organizing project planning, coordinating approved resources, convening stakeholders, making decisions within stated limits, and escalating decisions outside those limits.

The project manager is named because that person cannot be held responsible for organizing the project without enough authority to do the work. The charter does not give universal authority over funding, contracts, personnel, or governance. Those limits depend on the organization.

docs.title: Approval requirements
docs.text:
Approval requirements identify important decisions or results that require formal approval. Examples include charter approval, funding approval, design approval, regulatory approval, and final acceptance.

The charter identifies the important approval points. Detailed approval procedures may be developed later.

docs.title: Exit criteria
docs.text:
Exit criteria describe conditions under which the project or a phase may be completed, stopped, suspended, or reconsidered. Examples include:

  • required funding is not obtained;
  • the solution is no longer feasible;
  • a legal requirement cannot be met;
  • the business need disappears;
  • required acceptance is achieved.

Exit criteria belong in the charter because the organization should know not only why it is starting the project, but also what conditions may justify ending or stopping it.

docs.title: What is not in the charter?
docs.text:
The charter is high-level. It does not replace:

  • detailed requirements documentation;
  • the detailed Project Scope Statement;
  • the Work Breakdown Structure;
  • the schedule baseline;
  • the cost baseline;
  • the full Risk Register;
  • the detailed Stakeholder Register;
  • the Communications Management Plan;
  • the Procurement Management Plan;
  • the complete Project Management Plan;
  • a Sprint Backlog or detailed Product Backlog.

The charter approves the project and defines its initial boundaries. Planning later determines exactly how the work will be performed, scheduled, budgeted, monitored, and controlled.

docs.title: How is the charter created?
docs.text:
1. A business need, opportunity, obligation, or problem is identified.
  2. The Business Case and benefits information are reviewed.
  3. Agreements, major constraints, and known organizational conditions are considered.
  4. The sponsor, proposed project manager, and key contributors clarify the project’s purpose, objectives, boundaries, major requirements, budget, milestones, risks, assumptions, and authority.
  5. Important disagreements or feasibility problems are resolved or escalated.
  6. The sponsor or authorized governance body approves the charter.
  7. Detailed planning begins.

The exact procedure depends on the organization. A project manager may help prepare the charter, but the sponsor or another authorized leader issues or approves it.

docs.title: ServiceBridge example
docs.text:
A company has decided that its current customer-service system is too slow, difficult to audit, and inaccessible to some users.

The proposed ServiceBridge project would:

  • configure a replacement service platform;
  • migrate existing customer records;
  • connect the new platform to required systems;
  • train employees;
  • transition the service into operations.

The draft charter identifies:

  • Business need: improve response time, accessibility, and auditability.
  • Objective: reduce average response time and provide an accessible service before the required transition date.
  • High-level scope: platform configuration, migration, integrations, testing, training, and transition.
  • Exclusions: replacement of unrelated billing systems.
  • Budget: authorization within a USD 2.4 million financial boundary.
  • Milestones: configuration, migration testing, user testing, launch, and operational transition.
  • Stakeholders: sponsor, customer-service leadership, users, compliance staff, technology teams, seller, and operations.
  • Risks: migration quality, seller capacity, integration difficulty, and compliance delays.
  • Assumptions: required data can be migrated and key specialists will be available.
  • Project manager authority: coordinate planning and approved resources, while funding increases, contract changes, and compliance acceptance remain with the appropriate authorities.

Once the sponsor approves the charter, the project manager may begin detailed planning. The team still needs to develop the full requirements, scope baseline, schedule, budget, Risk Register, and other plans.

docs.title: Charter compared with related documents
docs.text:
The documents below support different decisions. The Business Case explains the investment, the charter authorizes the project, and planning documents develop the detail.

Document Main purpose Business Case Explains why the organization should invest in the project Project Charter Formally authorizes the project and establishes its high-level direction and authority Assumption Log Records assumptions and constraints that must be checked or monitored Stakeholder Register Records detailed information about stakeholders Project Management Plan Explains how the authorized project will be planned, executed, monitored, controlled, and closed Project Scope Statement Defines the detailed project and product scope developed during planning Scope Baseline Contains the approved scope statement, WBS, and WBS dictionary used for scope control

docs.title: Predictive
docs.text: The charter authorizes the project before detailed requirements, scope, schedule, and cost baselines are developed.

docs.title: Adaptive
docs.text:
An adaptive project still needs purpose, authorization, funding, stakeholders, authority, and boundaries. The charter may be shorter and may describe the product vision, desired outcomes, major constraints, funding boundaries, key stakeholders, and who may make which decisions.

Detailed scope may be developed through a Product Backlog rather than fixed completely at the start. Scrum does not require a Project Charter, although the organization may still require one to authorize and fund the work.

docs.title: Hybrid
docs.text: A hybrid project may use the charter to establish funding, governance, contracts, compliance obligations, major milestones, high-level scope, and project authority. Adaptive teams may then develop and deliver detailed product work iteratively.

docs.title: Common exam distinctions
docs.text:
These distinctions separate the charter’s authorization purpose from the detailed plans, baselines, registers, and team-level work records developed after approval.

  • The Project Charter formally authorizes the project.
  • The sponsor or another authorized leader approves or issues it; the project manager does not normally self-authorize the project.
  • The charter gives the project manager authority to apply organizational resources within defined limits.
  • The charter contains high-level scope, requirements, budget, milestones, risks, assumptions, stakeholders, and authority.
  • The charter is not the Project Management Plan.
  • The charter budget is not necessarily the final cost baseline.
  • High-level risks in the charter are not the full Risk Register.
  • Initial stakeholders in the charter do not replace the Stakeholder Register.
  • The charter is created before detailed planning.
  • The Assumption Log is also produced or initiated during Develop Project Charter.

docs.text: →Predictive↻Adaptive⇄Hybrid Predictive treatmentThe predictive variant uses greater upfront definition, formal approval, baselining, or controlled updates where appropriate. Adaptive equivalent or treatmentThe adaptive variant preserves the management purpose while using iterative, incremental, backlog-based, or team-owned treatment where appropriate. Hybrid treatmentThe hybrid variant connects adaptive working detail with predictive governance, funding, compliance, contract, milestone, or approval needs. docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text: Business evidence informs the charter; approval changes the effort from proposed to authorized. The charter then constrains integrated planning and remains part of the closure record.

docs.text: The charter is not the business case and is not the detailed Project Management Plan. It authorizes; the plan explains how the authorized work will be managed.

docs.text:
• Treating informal agreement as project authorization.
  • Expanding the charter into a complete management plan.
  • Assuming the project manager alone authorizes the project.

docs.text: A sponsor approves a charter for a customer-portal project, names the project manager, records the expected service outcome, and establishes the initial budget boundary. Detailed scope and delivery planning follow.

docs.title: Project Management Plan
docs.text:
A Project Management Plan explains how the authorized project will be executed, monitored, controlled, and closed.

It is not a schedule, a folder containing every project file, or a longer version of the Project Charter. The Charter authorizes the project and states its high-level direction. The Project Management Plan integrates the approved methods and commitments the team will use to manage that project.

docs.title: What the plan brings together
docs.text:
The plan may contain subsidiary management plans for scope, requirements, schedule, cost, quality, resources, communications, risk, procurement, stakeholder engagement, change, configuration, and other needs selected for the project. Each subsidiary plan answers management questions for its subject: what will be planned, who is responsible, how performance will be measured, what records will be maintained, and which changes require approval.

The plan also contains or incorporates the approved baselines used for control. The scope baseline states the approved scope, WBS, and WBS dictionary. The schedule baseline records the approved schedule model used for comparison. The cost baseline records the approved time-phased budget used to measure cost performance.

These components must agree. A scope baseline cannot authorize work that the schedule omits. A cost baseline cannot ignore the resources required by the schedule. A quality method must produce the evidence required for acceptance. Procurement dates must support delivery milestones. Risk responses must appear in the work, funding, and ownership model where appropriate.

docs.title: Plans, baselines, and project documents
docs.text:
A management plan defines how an area will be managed. A baseline records an approved expectation used for comparison and control. A project document records working information produced and updated during the project.

For example, the Risk Management Plan explains the risk method and responsibilities. The Risk Register records individual risks and their current status. The cost baseline records the approved budget for performance measurement. These records relate to one another but are not interchangeable.

Not every document update changes the Project Management Plan. A new risk can be added to the Risk Register under the approved risk method. A proposed change to the scope baseline follows the change process because it would alter an approved commitment.

docs.title: How the plan is developed and used
docs.text:
The project manager coordinates planning, but specialists, team members, functional leaders, customers, sellers, governance roles, and other stakeholders contribute the information and decisions within their authority. The designated sponsor or governance role approves the integrated plan according to organizational policy.

For ServiceBridge, planning connects data migration, accessibility testing, seller work, training, operations readiness, milestones, and the USD 2.4 million boundary. If these parts cannot coexist, the conflict is resolved before the plan is approved rather than hidden in separate documents.

Predictive projects commonly approve more detailed plans and baselines before execution. Adaptive projects may use lighter project-level plans while refining product and iteration detail continuously. Hybrid projects often keep formal funding, contract, compliance, and milestone controls while product teams plan detailed work iteratively.

On the exam, distinguish the Project Charter from the Project Management Plan, the plan from its subsidiary plans, management plans from project documents, and approved baselines from current forecasts.

docs.title: The project schedule is the current model of when work can occur
docs.text:
A project schedule is the output of the schedule model showing planned activities, dates, durations, dependencies, resources, and milestones. It exists so the team can coordinate work, forecast completion, expose dependency conflicts, and communicate when decisions or deliverables are needed. It is more than a list of target dates: changing one activity can alter successors, resource demand, float, and the critical path.

The schedule combines defined activities, sequencing, duration estimates, calendars, resource assumptions, constraints, leads and lags, and selected milestones. It may be shown as a network, bar chart, milestone view, release plan, or other usable representation. The current project schedule is not necessarily the schedule baseline. The baseline is the approved reference used to measure variance; the current schedule also reflects actual progress and the latest forecast. A milestone marks a significant point and has zero duration, while an activity consumes time and resources.

For ServiceBridge, the schedule links data cleansing, trial migration, accessibility testing, training, release, and operational transition. When the trial migration takes five extra days, the scheduler recalculates downstream dates and finds that training still has float but accessibility testing now governs release. The team updates the forecast and assesses whether a baseline change is required. Predictive projects often maintain detailed networks; adaptive teams forecast iterations and releases with shorter planning horizons; hybrid projects connect those team cadences to contractual, regulatory, and transition milestones.

docs.title: Project Scope Statement
docs.text:
On this page
  1. Definition and purpose
  2. Creation, updates, and authority
  3. Typical content
  4. Lifecycle and state
  5. Relationships and downstream use
  6. Delivery approach applicability
  7. Illustrative example
  8. References

The Project Scope Statement defines the detailed boundary of the project and the product, service, or result it will create.

The Project Charter contains high-level scope so the organization can authorize the project. The scope statement develops that boundary during planning after requirements have been analyzed. It gives the team enough clarity to decompose and plan the work without claiming that every future detail is fixed.

docs.title: What the statement explains
docs.text:
The statement describes the product scope, major project deliverables, acceptance criteria, exclusions, assumptions, and constraints that define the approved boundary.

Deliverables show the main results the project must produce. Acceptance criteria explain the conditions under which those results can be accepted. Exclusions make clear which related work is not included. Assumptions identify beliefs that planning currently treats as true. Constraints identify limits the team must work within.

Each element prevents a different misunderstanding. Without deliverables, the boundary remains abstract. Without acceptance criteria, completion can be disputed. Without exclusions, reasonable but unauthorized expectations can enter the project. Without visible assumptions and constraints, estimates may rely on options the project does not have.

For ServiceBridge, the statement includes platform configuration, data migration, integrations, accessibility testing, training, and transition. It excludes replacing the billing system and long-term operation after handoff. It records the required transition date and retention obligations as constraints and identifies data usability as an assumption to be validated.

docs.title: Relationship to the scope baseline
docs.text:
The scope statement is one component of the Scope Baseline. The Work Breakdown Structure decomposes its approved scope, and the WBS dictionary explains the components. Together they support schedule, cost, resources, procurement, quality, risk, and control.

A scope statement is not a list of activities. Activities are developed later from work packages. It is not Requirements Documentation, although approved scope is based on requirements. It is not the Product Backlog, which can hold evolving product detail in adaptive work.

Predictive work may approve a detailed scope statement and control changes formally. Adaptive work may keep the project-level boundary outcome-focused while the Product Backlog refines product detail. Hybrid work protects fixed contract, compliance, funding, or milestone boundaries while allowing selected solution details to evolve.

On the exam, distinguish the Charter’s high-level scope from the detailed scope statement, and distinguish the scope statement from the complete scope baseline.

docs.title: Measurements are observations, not conclusions
docs.text:
Quality control measurements record the actual results produced by inspection, testing, sampling, or other control activity. They exist so the team can compare observed performance with a defined metric or acceptance condition and preserve the evidence behind a conformity decision. A statement such as “quality is good” cannot be analyzed or audited; a result such as “99.4 percent of migrated records reconciled” can.

Each measurement needs the item or process measured, metric and method, units, sample or population, date, environment, expected threshold, actual result, status, and evidence reference. Those elements make results comparable and reproducible. Quality metrics define what will be measured and how; control measurements are the observed values. Test documents contain detailed test cases and results, while a quality report summarizes patterns and decisions. A measurement alone does not verify a deliverable until the authorized control activity evaluates all applicable criteria.

For ServiceBridge, the migration metric requires at least 99.5 percent field-level reconciliation with zero critical identity mismatches. A controlled test records 99.2 percent and three critical mismatches, links the result to the trial data set, and creates a defect action. After correction and authorized retest, new measurements show conformance and support verified-deliverable status. Adaptive teams collect these results continuously within the Definition of Done; predictive teams may collect them at planned control points; hybrid work connects continuous evidence to formal release and acceptance gates.

Adaptive equivalent or treatmentThe same core record supports adaptive decisions with timing, ownership, granularity, and update cadence tailored to the team. Hybrid treatmentThe same core form can cross governance and delivery cadences when ownership and decision rights remain clear. Why these badgesThe canonical artifact resource provides one common example because the decision purpose and structure do not materially differ by approach.

The Quality Management Plan explains how the project will define, create, check, and improve quality.

It turns broad statements such as “the system must be reliable” into a manageable approach: which standards and requirements apply, what measurements will be used, which reviews or tests will produce evidence, who performs them, who decides on exceptions, and how failed results are handled.

DRAFT — Pending Editorial Review

docs.title: Why its major elements are included
docs.text:
Applicable standards and quality objectives define what conformance means. Metrics and tolerances make expectations measurable. Roles separate creation, review, verification, and acceptance. Planned assurance and control activities show when process reviews, audits, inspections, and tests will occur. Reporting and record rules preserve evidence. Improvement and defect procedures explain how causes are addressed rather than merely counted.

The plan also connects requirements to acceptance. A requirement that has no verification method or acceptance route may be impossible to prove complete.

For ServiceBridge, the plan identifies accessibility, migration accuracy, availability, retention, and security requirements. It assigns automated tests, migration reconciliation, accessibility review, compliance evidence, acceptance roles, defect handling, and reporting thresholds. This lets the team plan the necessary work and cost instead of discovering quality obligations at the end.

docs.title: Plan, metrics, reports, and results
docs.text:
The plan defines the method. Quality Metrics define specific measurements. Quality-control measurements record observed results. Quality reports interpret trends, findings, and recommended action. Test and evaluation documents preserve the evidence for particular checks.

Manage Quality examines whether processes and the quality approach are suitable and being followed. Control Quality checks deliverables and produces verified results. Validate Scope obtains formal acceptance from the authorized stakeholder. These activities are connected but make different decisions.

Predictive work may plan formal stages, inspections, and gates. Adaptive teams build quality into each increment through acceptance criteria, automation, review, and a Definition of Done. Hybrid projects can combine continuous testing with formal compliance, contract, release, and acceptance evidence.

On the exam, distinguish quality from grade, the Quality Management Plan from quality metrics, assurance from control, verification from acceptance, and prevention from the cost of correcting failures.

docs.title: A quality metric makes an expectation measurable
docs.text:
A quality metric defines an attribute to measure, the method and units used, and the threshold or target that determines how results will be interpreted. It exists because words such as reliable, fast, complete, or accessible mean different things to different people. A metric converts an important expectation into a testable condition before the team produces the evidence.

A usable metric identifies the subject, operational definition, calculation or test method, data source, units, frequency, threshold, tolerance, owner, and reporting or escalation rule. The threshold must match the decision it supports. Averages can hide severe failures, percentages require a defined denominator, and a target without a measurement boundary invites manipulation. The Quality Management Plan explains how quality will be managed; metrics define specific measures; quality control measurements record actual results. Acceptance criteria may use a metric but also include business or contractual conditions.

For ServiceBridge, “migration accuracy” is defined as correctly reconciled required fields divided by required fields tested, using the approved reconciliation script on the release data set. The threshold is at least 99.5 percent with zero critical identity errors. The data lead owns measurement and the quality authority decides conformity. A failed result triggers analysis and correction rather than automatic customer rejection. Adaptive teams may attach metrics to backlog items and the Definition of Done; predictive work may establish them in planning; hybrid work preserves stable compliance metrics while refining product-level measures through feedback.

docs.title: A quality report turns evidence into a management view
docs.text:
A quality report summarizes quality performance, significant findings, trends, causes, recommendations, and decisions for the people who must act. It exists because raw test results and individual measurements are too detailed to show whether quality is improving, where systemic problems are emerging, or which matters require management attention.

The report identifies the reporting period and scope, metrics and thresholds, actual results, defects or nonconformities, trends, root-cause findings, corrective actions, owners, forecast effects, and escalations. It should preserve links to the underlying evidence rather than replacing it. Quality control measurements are individual observations; test documents contain execution detail; the quality report synthesizes them. The report does not itself accept a deliverable or approve a baseline change. Those decisions remain with their designated authorities and processes.

For ServiceBridge, three test cycles show migration accuracy rising from 98.7 to 99.6 percent, while accessibility defects remain concentrated in one seller component. The quality lead reports the trend, identifies the common cause, recommends seller correction and targeted regression tests, and flags a release risk. The project manager assesses schedule effects and the procurement authority addresses seller performance. Once evidence meets the criteria, Control Quality can verify the deliverable for later acceptance. Adaptive teams may review quality information each iteration; predictive projects may use scheduled reports; hybrid programs combine rapid team feedback with formal governance summaries.

docs.title: Requirements Documentation
docs.text:
Requirements Documentation records the needs, capabilities, conditions, and obligations that the project or product must satisfy.

It exists because a request such as “make customer service better” is not specific enough to design, estimate, test, or accept. The team must clarify what result is needed, who needs it, why it matters, and how the result will be evaluated.

docs.title: What useful requirements explain
docs.text:
A requirement should identify the needed condition or capability at the right level of detail. The documentation may include business requirements, stakeholder requirements, solution requirements, transition requirements, quality requirements, compliance obligations, assumptions, constraints, and acceptance information.

These categories help the team ask different questions. A business requirement explains an organizational outcome. A stakeholder requirement explains what a person or group needs. A solution requirement describes a capability or quality of the result. A transition requirement covers temporary needs such as data conversion or training that are necessary to move from the current state to the future state.

Requirements are accompanied by attributes such as source, owner, priority, rationale, status, version, acceptance method, and relationships to other requirements. Those attributes make change analysis and traceability possible; they are not administrative decoration.

docs.title: How requirements are developed
docs.text:
The team reviews the Charter, business case, benefits information, stakeholder information, agreements, assumptions, and existing product or operational evidence. Interviews, workshops, observation, prototypes, surveys, document analysis, decision techniques, and other methods are selected for the situation.

Conflicts and ambiguity must be resolved. If customer-service leaders request fast access while compliance requires stronger controls, both needs must be analyzed rather than recorded as if they already agree.

For ServiceBridge, requirements include accessible scheduling, record retention, secure access, migration accuracy, service capacity, and integration with existing systems. “Use vendor X” is a solution constraint, not a substitute for explaining the capability or obligation it must satisfy.

docs.title: What happens next
docs.text:
The Requirements Traceability Matrix connects each important requirement to its origin, objective, approved scope, delivery work, test, acceptance evidence, and current status. The Project Scope Statement uses the analyzed requirements to define the detailed project and product boundary.

In predictive work, a broad set of requirements may be documented before the scope baseline is approved. Adaptive teams keep detailed requirements in an ordered Product Backlog and refine them as feedback arrives. Hybrid work may keep compliance, contract, and outcome requirements under formal control while refining solution detail iteratively.

Requirements Documentation is not the Project Scope Statement, the WBS, a test plan, or a Product Backlog, although information may be linked or represented in those forms. On the exam, first understand the need and stakeholder source, then trace it into scope, delivery, verification, and acceptance.

docs.title: Traceability shows why a requirement exists and where it goes
docs.text:
A Requirements Traceability Matrix connects each approved requirement to its origin, business reason, planned scope, delivery work, verification evidence, acceptance evidence, owner, and current status. It exists because requirements can be lost, duplicated, changed without impact analysis, or declared complete without evidence when they live only in separate documents or backlog items.

Stable identifiers are essential: they allow the matrix to connect records without relying on wording that may change. Source and rationale show why the requirement matters. Links to scope and work show where it will be delivered. Verification and acceptance links show how completion will be demonstrated and who decides. Status and change references preserve the history. The matrix is not Requirements Documentation, which explains the requirements themselves, and it is not a test plan, although it links to test evidence.

For ServiceBridge, requirement REQ-ACC-014 originates in an accessibility obligation and requires keyboard completion of appointment scheduling. The matrix links it to portal scope, two backlog items, the accessibility test case, the quality result, and customer acceptance evidence. When a proposed design change affects the keyboard sequence, the team follows the links to identify impacted work and evidence before a decision. Predictive projects may build broad traceability during planning; adaptive teams can trace backlog items and increments continuously; hybrid work links evolving detail to stable contractual and compliance obligations. On the exam, traceability supports coverage and change-impact analysis—it is not merely a checklist of requirement names.

docs.title: Risk Register
docs.text:
The Risk Register records individual project risks and the information needed to understand, assign, respond to, and monitor them.

A risk is uncertain. If the event or condition already exists, it belongs in the Issue Log, although the records may remain linked. This distinction prevents a current problem from being monitored as if it might never happen.

Stakeholder resistance or insufficient involvement may create uncertainty recorded here as a risk. Use the Stakeholder Engagement Assessment Matrix for the separate current-versus-desired engagement assessment.

docs.title: What a useful risk record contains
docs.text:
A clear risk statement describes a cause, the uncertain event or condition, and its possible effect on objectives. The register may also record category, probability, impact, urgency, proximity, owner, response strategy, response actions, triggers, contingency plans, residual risk, secondary risk, and current status.

The fields are included for decisions, not for completeness. Probability and impact support prioritization. The owner is accountable for monitoring the risk and coordinating the response. A trigger tells the team when action is required. Residual risk remains after the response. Secondary risk is created by the response itself.

For ServiceBridge: “Because legacy records contain inconsistent formats, migration validation may fail, causing rework and delaying transition.” The data lead owns the risk, profiling results provide triggers, cleansing and trial migration reduce probability, and a contingency plan defines what happens if error rates exceed the agreed threshold.

docs.title: How the register changes
docs.text:
Identify Risks creates the first entries. Qualitative analysis updates priority. Quantitative analysis may add modeled effects when useful. Plan Risk Responses adds strategies and actions. Implement Risk Responses records action progress. Monitor Risks reassesses exposure, closes obsolete risks, identifies new risks, and links realized risks to issues.

The Risk Register is not the Risk Management Plan. The plan explains the method, roles, scales, thresholds, categories, reporting, and cadence. The register applies that method to specific uncertainties. It is also not the Risk Report, which summarizes overall exposure and trends for decision-makers.

Adaptive teams may keep risks close to backlog items, boards, experiments, or impediment records, but material uncertainty still needs ownership and a visible response. Hybrid projects connect team-level risk action with formal funding, contract, compliance, or milestone decisions.

On the exam, distinguish risk from issue, risk owner from response-action owner, planned response from implemented response, residual risk from secondary risk, and individual register entries from the overall Risk Report.

docs.title: The risk report explains overall exposure and its direction
docs.text:
A risk report presents a management-level view of individual and overall project risk, important trends, concentrations, response effectiveness, and matters needing decisions. It exists because a long Risk Register can describe many separate uncertainties without showing whether aggregate exposure is rising, which sources dominate, or whether the project remains within agreed thresholds.

The report commonly includes overall exposure, major individual risks, distribution by category, trends, emerging risks, response performance, reserve or forecast implications, and escalations. Its audience and cadence should match decision needs. The Risk Register remains the working record for individual risks, owners, triggers, and responses; the risk report synthesizes that information for governance and stakeholder decisions. It is not a status report for issues that have already occurred, although realized risks may affect the reported outlook.

For ServiceBridge, the register contains separate seller-capacity, migration-quality, and adoption risks. The monthly report shows that total technical exposure has fallen after a successful trial, while commercial exposure has risen because two seller milestones are slipping. The project manager recommends intensified contract monitoring and a contingency decision; the sponsor sees the change in overall exposure rather than three disconnected entries. Adaptive teams may review exposure at iteration or release cadence, predictive projects may use scheduled risk reviews, and hybrid governance combines both. A favorable trend does not close individual risks automatically; owners still monitor triggers and residual exposure.

docs.title: The schedule baseline is the approved time reference
docs.text:
A schedule baseline is the approved version of the schedule model used to compare actual and forecast timing with the authorized plan. It exists so the project can distinguish ordinary forecast movement from a change to the commitment against which performance is measured. Without that stable reference, every updated date could erase evidence of variance.

The baseline includes approved start and finish dates, milestones, and the underlying model at the level selected for control. It is created from the developed project schedule and changed only through the applicable control authority. The current schedule continues to show actual progress and the latest forecast; it may differ from the baseline without the baseline being replaced. A target date, release forecast, or informal promise is not automatically a baseline. Schedule variance signals a condition to analyze, not automatic permission to rebaseline.

For ServiceBridge, the approved baseline sets transition for September 30. A seller delay moves the current forecast to October 10. The project manager records the variance, examines float and downstream effects, and evaluates recovery options. If governance approves an accessibility-related scope change with a new October 7 commitment, the baseline is updated through integrated change control and the decision is preserved. Predictive projects commonly maintain a detailed baseline; adaptive teams may baseline release or governance commitments while refining iteration detail; hybrid work connects evolving team forecasts to controlled external milestones. On the exam, update the forecast when evidence changes, but change the baseline only with authorization.

docs.title: Scope Baseline
docs.text:
The Scope Baseline is the approved version of the Project Scope Statement, Work Breakdown Structure, and WBS dictionary.

It exists so the project has one controlled reference for what scope was approved. Without that reference, teams can argue about whether requested work is already included, whether a deliverable is complete, and whether a change affects an approved commitment.

docs.title: Why all three components are needed
docs.text:
The Project Scope Statement defines the detailed project and product boundary, deliverables, acceptance criteria, exclusions, assumptions, and constraints.

The Work Breakdown Structure, or WBS, organizes the complete approved project scope into a hierarchy. Its lowest planned components are work packages that can be estimated and managed.

The WBS dictionary explains what each WBS component means. It may record boundaries, deliverables, responsibilities, assumptions, milestones, acceptance information, and related control details. The dictionary prevents short labels in the diagram from becoming ambiguous.

The three parts solve different problems. A scope statement alone does not decompose the work. A WBS alone may use labels too short to define the boundary. A dictionary without the approved hierarchy has no controlled structure to explain.

docs.title: How the baseline is used
docs.text:
Schedule activities, resource needs, cost estimates, quality methods, procurements, and risk analysis are developed from the approved scope. During delivery, completed work and requested changes are compared with the baseline.

For ServiceBridge, a request to replace the billing system is compared with the exclusions in the scope statement and the WBS. If it is outside the baseline, the team analyzes the effect and submits the appropriate change request rather than silently adding the work.

The baseline is not a forecast. It records the approved scope used for comparison. Current conditions and forecasts may differ; changing the baseline requires the authorized control process.

Predictive projects commonly establish a formal scope baseline for a broad project boundary. Adaptive projects may control outcomes, releases, or other commitments while refining detailed Product Backlog items. Hybrid projects map evolving backlog work to the controlled scope that supports funding, contracts, compliance, and integrated reporting.

On the exam, remember that the scope baseline contains three parts. A work package is scope, not an activity; a control account is a management control point; and a planning package represents known work that will be detailed later.

docs.title: How engagement gaps support decisions
docs.text:
The Stakeholder Engagement Assessment Matrix makes a different problem visible from stakeholder classification. It compares the stakeholder’s current engagement toward the project or change with the engagement state needed for project success. The gap helps the team decide whether to build awareness, understand resistance, invite participation, sustain support, or strengthen active leadership.

The state labels describe engagement, not rank, power, authority, or personality. A powerful regulator can be Neutral, a low-power user can be Supportive, and a sponsor can be Supportive without yet providing the Leading advocacy needed to remove organizational barriers. The matrix therefore complements rather than replaces the Power–Interest Grid.

docs.title: Evidence and reassessment
docs.text:
Current-state assessment should come from observable evidence: participation, decisions, feedback, advocacy, questions, objections, follow-through, demonstrations, interviews, surveys, or direct collaboration. Desired state follows from project needs rather than a wish that every stakeholder become Leading. Some stakeholders only need awareness or neutral cooperation; forcing a higher desired state can waste attention or damage trust.

The team records the evidence, gap, action, owner, and review date, then reassesses after engagement activity or material context change. Sensitive judgments should use stable identifiers, professional language, and access controls. A changed attitude is not automatically a formal change request, though its consequences may create a risk, issue, or controlled change decision.

The desired state should be tied to a needed behavior. “Supportive” might mean timely participation in validation, while “Leading” might mean visible advocacy and removal of cross-functional barriers. Without that behavioral definition, reviewers can agree on a label while expecting different actions. A review date makes the assessment testable: the team can examine whether the chosen engagement action produced observable change.

Causes matter more than labels. Resistance can arise from credible workload, safety, privacy, job-impact, feasibility, or trust concerns. The response should investigate and address those causes within the stakeholder’s context. Persuasion is not automatically the right action; changing scope, supplying evidence, resolving an issue, escalating an authority gap, or accepting a neutral position may be more responsible.

Reassessment occurs at a useful cadence and after triggers such as a governance decision, demonstration, rejected deliverable, organizational change, new risk, or transition event. The owner records evidence rather than merely changing C and D markers. Where the desired state is not achieved, the team decides whether to revise the action, change the desired state, escalate, or alter the project decision that depended on engagement.

Matrix ownership does not create authority over the stakeholder. The project manager or engagement lead may maintain the record, while relationship owners and decision authorities contribute evidence and approve actions within their remit. Privacy, labor, legal, or cultural constraints may limit what can be recorded or shared, so professional judgment and access control remain part of the method.

docs.title: ServiceBridge interpretation
docs.text:
ServiceBridge records STK-01, the sponsor, as Supportive with a desired state of Leading. The evidence shows approval and barrier removal but limited advocacy. The selected action is not “send more status”: the sponsor is asked to lead a governance briefing and reinforce the service outcome with functional leaders.

STK-04, the support-team representative, is Resistant because of credible workload, training, and support-procedure concerns. The action is a workflow walkthrough and co-design of training and escalation, not an attempt to suppress resistance. STK-02 is already Leading, so the strategy sustains decision access rather than manufacturing a gap.

docs.title: How the stakeholder records fit together
docs.text: The Stakeholder Register answers who is involved and what is known. The Power–Interest Grid helps prioritize attention. This matrix asks what engagement exists and what is needed. The Stakeholder Engagement Plan defines strategies and actions, and the Communications Management Plan defines information delivery. Each record should link to the others without becoming a duplicate master spreadsheet.

docs.title: Failure modes
docs.text:
The matrix fails when states are assigned from rumor, personal liking, or a single meeting; when every desired state is Leading; or when sensitive assessments circulate as a public ranking. It also fails when the team updates labels without changing an engagement strategy or recording evidence.

Consequences include damaged trust, ineffective actions, overlooked causes of resistance, and false confidence. Useful assessment separates observation from interpretation, chooses a proportionate desired state, assigns action and review responsibility, and treats resistance as information rather than misconduct.

docs.title: Exam distinctions
docs.text: Engagement state is not power, authority, interest, or formal project role. Resistant does not mean low power; Leading does not grant project-management authority. The matrix supports Plan, Manage, and Monitor Stakeholder Engagement but is not the formal Stakeholder Engagement Plan or the Communications Management Plan.

docs.title: Sources and synthesis status
docs.text: Lesson 3 directly supports the five current/desired states, C and D markers, continuing engagement, feedback, and reassessment. The ServiceBridge interpretation, failure modes, privacy application, and record-family explanation are Atlas synthesis. The Atlas does not prescribe a universal approval authority, numeric scale, or mandatory matrix format.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Compares each stakeholder's current engagement state with the desired state needed for project success so engagement gaps can inform strategy and monitoring.

It is an assessment and data-representation tool that may be maintained as a working project artifact. It is not the formal output of Plan Stakeholder Engagement; that output remains the Stakeholder Engagement Plan.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The matrix makes the difference between actual stakeholder engagement and the engagement needed for project success visible. The gap informs engagement strategy, actions, communication choices, ownership, and review cadence; the matrix does not contain the complete strategy.

!!! warning "Sensitive stakeholder assessment" Stakeholder-engagement assessments may contain sensitive judgments. Use stakeholder numbers or identifiers rather than names where appropriate; restrict access when necessary; use professional, factual language; avoid insulting or speculative descriptions; separate identity data from sensitive assessments when required; and follow organizational storage and access policy.

docs.title: Where it fits in the lifecycle
docs.text:
Identify Stakeholders → Stakeholder Register → stakeholder analysis → current and desired engagement assessment → Plan Stakeholder Engagement and the Stakeholder Engagement Plan → engagement activities → monitoring of actual versus desired engagement → appropriate plan, communication, issue, risk, lesson, or change updates.

A change in attitude does not automatically require integrated change control. Formal change control applies only when a proposed response crosses a controlled commitment or decision threshold.

docs.title: Plan Stakeholder Engagement
docs.text: The matrix helps identify gaps between current and desired engagement and informs strategy; the formal process output remains the Stakeholder Engagement Plan.

docs.title: Manage Stakeholder Engagement
docs.text: Engagement actions address needs, resistance, support, and involvement; observed changes may update the working assessment.

docs.title: Monitor Stakeholder Engagement
docs.text:
Actual engagement is reassessed against desired engagement and may lead to matrix, register, plan, communication, issue, risk, lesson, or change updates without making every attitude change a formal change request.

Communication planning, management, and monitoring support the engagement strategy through appropriate information and feedback. See Plan Communications Management, Manage Communications, Monitor Communications.

Related Decision Guides: A Risk Occurs or an Impediment Exceeds Team Authority and A Stakeholder Requests a Baseline Change. These guides apply only when the observed engagement condition creates the corresponding issue, impediment, risk, or controlled-change decision.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
1. The Stakeholder Register and stakeholder classifications.
  2. The project management plan, including stakeholder and communications planning information.
  3. Observations and feedback from engagement activities, reviews, demonstrations, meetings, interviews, surveys, and direct collaboration.
  4. Issue, risk, lesson, change, governance, and organizational-context information relevant to engagement.
  5. Expert judgment, emotional intelligence, and interpersonal skills applied to factual evidence.

docs.title: Typical structure
docs.text:
1. Stakeholder identifier rather than a personal name where sensitivity requires it.
  2. Project role or group.
  3. Current engagement state and desired engagement state.
  4. Evidence supporting the assessment.
  5. The engagement gap and recommended action.
  6. Action owner, review date, and next review date.
  7. Change history and access classification where required.

docs.title: Current and desired engagement states
docs.text: C marks the current assessed engagement state. D marks the desired state needed for project success. C/D may occupy one state when no change is required. These states describe engagement toward the project or change, not formal authority. A resistant stakeholder may still have high power or influence, and Leading does not necessarily mean project leadership or management authority. Organizations may tailor the labels.

docs.title: Unaware
docs.text: The stakeholder does not know about the project or its potential effects.

docs.title: Resistant
docs.text: The stakeholder knows about the project but opposes it, its effects, or the proposed change.

docs.title: Neutral
docs.text: The stakeholder is aware but is neither actively supportive nor actively resistant.

docs.title: Supportive
docs.text: The stakeholder supports the project or change and may assist its success.

docs.title: Leading
docs.text: The stakeholder is actively engaged in helping the project succeed and influencing others positively.

docs.title: How to assess the engagement gap
docs.text:
Compare C with D, document observable evidence, identify why the gap matters, and select a proportionate engagement action. Do not assign a numeric score unless the organization deliberately adopts and documents an additional method.

Stakeholder ID Unaware Resistant Neutral Supportive Leading STK-01 C D STK-02 C,D STK-03 C D
  1. STK-01: current resistance must move toward support; the engagement strategy should address causes, not merely send more status messages.
  2. STK-02: current and desired are both Neutral, so no state movement is required, although monitoring continues.
  3. STK-03: the largest gap runs from Neutral to Leading and needs deliberate involvement and influence-building.

docs.title: How the matrix is updated
docs.text: Update the assessment regularly and when evidence changes—for example at stakeholder reviews, governance reviews, phase boundaries, major change points, iteration reviews, demonstrations, or material issue and risk events. Record the evidence, date, owner, and next review. Do not change a state solely from rumor or personal dislike.

docs.title: Project manager or stakeholder-engagement lead
docs.text: Facilitates assessment, coordinates strategies, monitors changes, protects sensitive information, and escalates matters outside delegated authority.

docs.title: Project team
docs.text: Provides factual observations, identifies emerging needs or resistance, and supports engagement actions.

docs.title: Sponsor
docs.text: May engage influential or resistant stakeholders and resolve strategic barriers but does not automatically maintain the matrix.

docs.title: Product Owner or product leadership
docs.text: May assess customer, user, and business engagement in adaptive or product-oriented delivery but does not automatically own all project stakeholder engagement.

docs.title: Scrum Team
docs.text: Gathers frequent feedback through collaboration and review and may use lighter-weight assessment; Scrum does not prescribe this matrix.

docs.title: Governance or functional leaders
docs.text: May support engagement where authority, resources, or organizational change are involved. No universal approval authority is assigned to the matrix.

docs.title: Predictive, adaptive, and hybrid treatment
docs.text:
Predictive: A formal, access-controlled matrix may be reviewed at planning updates, governance reviews, phase boundaries, major change points, and scheduled stakeholder reviews.

Adaptive: The purpose remains useful, but the representation may be lightweight and updated more frequently from iteration reviews, customer feedback, demonstrations, direct collaboration, retrospective observations, and backlog participation. A formal matrix is not universally required.

Hybrid: Formal assessment may cover sponsors, regulators, sellers, governance stakeholders, and organizational leaders while customers, users, product stakeholders, and delivery participants are assessed through a lighter and faster cadence.

docs.title: Delivery approach applicability
docs.text:
→Predictive↻Adaptive⇄Hybrid Predictive treatmentThe predictive variant uses greater upfront definition, formal approval, baselining, or controlled updates where appropriate. Adaptive equivalent or treatmentThe adaptive variant preserves the management purpose while using iterative, incremental, backlog-based, or team-owned treatment where appropriate. Hybrid treatmentThe hybrid variant connects adaptive working detail with predictive governance, funding, compliance, contract, milestone, or approval needs. Why these badgesThe canonical artifact resource provides distinct predictive, adaptive, and hybrid examples, so the badges derive from those same variants. Additional treatment context

Predictive projects may maintain a formal controlled matrix; adaptive teams may use lighter and more frequent assessment; hybrid work can combine formal governance-stakeholder assessment with rapid customer and user feedback.

docs.text:

These records work together but are not interchangeable.

docs.text:
1. The Stakeholder Register identifies and classifies stakeholders.
  2. The engagement assessment matrix compares current and desired engagement.
  3. The Stakeholder Engagement Plan defines strategies and actions.

docs.title: Stakeholder Power–Interest Grid
docs.text: Artifact type: Stakeholder analysis and data-representation tool / working artifact

docs.title: How classification supports decisions
docs.text:
The Power–Interest Grid is useful because stakeholder attention cannot be allocated from visibility or job title alone. It asks two bounded questions: how much power does the stakeholder have to affect project decisions or outcomes, and how much interest do they have in the project and its effects? Evidence-based placement helps the team decide where direct involvement, decision access, information, feedback, and monitoring deserve emphasis.

The quadrant labels are management prompts, not automatic prescriptions. Manage closely signals that both decision influence and interest are high, but it does not mean constant meetings. Keep satisfied calls for decision-relevant engagement with a high-power, lower-interest stakeholder. Keep informed recognizes that high-interest affected people deserve useful information and feedback even with limited formal power. Monitor means proportionate attention and reassessment, not neglect.

docs.title: Evidence and reassessment
docs.text:
Power evidence can include funding control, resource authority, approval or acceptance rights, legal or contractual authority, specialist decision rights, and the ability to accelerate or constrain outcomes. Interest evidence can include degree of impact, participation, information demand, concern, adoption responsibility, or attention to outcomes. Job title alone is insufficient, and a stakeholder can be highly powerful while resistant, unaware, or only intermittently involved.

Placement should be documented with a rationale and revisited when authority, impact, lifecycle stage, behavior, project conditions, or organizational structure changes. Numeric scoring can structure discussion, but the included scoring approach is optional Atlas synthesis rather than a PMI-prescribed calculation. Scores do not remove judgment or create permanent truth.

Evidence quality matters because power is contextual. A functional manager may control a specialist during planning but have little authority over customer acceptance. A regulator may rarely participate yet retain decisive release power. A community representative may lack formal authority while influencing legitimacy, adoption, or political support. The assessment should name the relevant decision or effect instead of assigning a vague global score.

Interest is also specific to the project’s current state. Someone may care intensely about a design decision and then need only exception reporting during implementation. Another stakeholder may show little early interest but become central during transition. Interviews, attendance patterns, decision records, escalation history, operational impact, and direct observation provide stronger evidence than assumptions based on title or personality.

Reassessment should be triggered by material events as well as scheduled reviews: a sponsor change, new contract, changed regulation, major risk, phase transition, release, reorganization, or newly affected user group. The analyst records why a placement changed and then checks whether engagement and communication strategies still fit. Reclassification without an action decision adds maintenance work but no management value.

Ownership should be explicit. The project manager may maintain the analysis, but contributors closest to a stakeholder supply evidence and the authority responsible for a decision confirms its governance implications. Access should be limited when disclosure could damage trust, expose personal data, or distort negotiations. The useful output is a defensible engagement decision, not a public ranking of people.

docs.title: ServiceBridge interpretation
docs.text:
ServiceBridge places the sponsor in Manage closely because funding and strategic authority combine with active outcome ownership. The compliance authority is Keep satisfied because release-gate power is high while routine design interest is intentionally limited. The frontline user representative is Keep informed: formal authority is low, but direct impact and feedback value are high.

Those placements produce different actions. The sponsor receives concise decision briefs and participates in strategic barriers. The compliance authority agrees evidence checkpoints rather than attending every workshop. The frontline representative receives accessible demonstrations and visible feedback closure. The grid informs those choices; the Stakeholder Engagement Plan and Communications Management Plan define them.

docs.title: Failure modes
docs.text:
The grid fails when teams equate organizational rank with power, treat low power as low importance, classify from personality judgments, or use one placement for the entire project. It also fails when quadrant labels are copied into a plan without explaining actual stakeholder needs, authority, evidence, or communication preferences.

Consequences include ignored affected groups, over-communication of senior stakeholders, missing approvals, privacy harm, and stale strategies. The remedy is factual evidence, professional language, restricted access where appropriate, and scheduled or event-driven reassessment.

docs.title: Exam distinctions
docs.text: The Stakeholder Register identifies and describes stakeholders. The Power–Interest Grid classifies power and interest. The engagement assessment matrix compares current and desired engagement. The engagement plan defines strategy, while communications planning defines information delivery. Power is not engagement state, interest is not approval authority, and Monitor does not mean ignore.

docs.title: Sources and synthesis status
docs.text: Lesson 3 directly supports the Power/interest axes, the four quadrant labels, identifier use, and mapping method. The content rationales, evidence examples, ServiceBridge actions, optional scoring, failure modes, and approach treatment are Atlas synthesis. The Atlas withholds any claim that numeric thresholds or one communication cadence is officially prescribed.

docs.title: Definition and purpose
docs.text:
Classifies stakeholders by evidenced power and interest so engagement and communication effort can be tailored proportionately.

The grid supports prioritization; it does not grant authority, prescribe a complete strategy, or replace professional judgment.

!!! warning "Sensitive stakeholder assessment" Use identifiers rather than personal names where appropriate, document observable evidence, restrict sensitive judgments, and follow organizational access policy.

docs.title: Axes and evidence
docs.text:
Power: Ability to influence project decisions, resources, approvals, constraints, acceptance, or outcomes.

Interest: Degree of attention, concern, involvement, or impact associated with the project and its outcomes.

Use observable authority, resource, approval, impact, participation, and feedback evidence. Do not infer placement from job title, visibility, personality, or personal preference alone.

docs.title: Four quadrants
docs.text:
Manage closely

High power · High interest

Maintain active two-way engagement, timely decision access, and frequent evidence-based review.

Keep satisfied

High power · Low interest

Provide decision-relevant information and consult at appropriate thresholds without unnecessary detail.

Keep informed

Low power · High interest

Provide useful updates, invite feedback, and make participation routes visible.

Monitor

Low power · Low interest

Watch for material changes and communicate proportionately.

The quadrant headings and explicit axis text communicate placement without relying on color.

docs.title: Qualitative method
docs.text:
1. Identify stakeholders and use identifiers rather than personal names where sensitivity requires it.
  2. Gather observable evidence for power and interest from authority, decisions, resources, impact, participation, and feedback.
  3. Assess each axis qualitatively as High or Low under documented project criteria.
  4. Place each stakeholder in one quadrant and record the rationale.
  5. Tailor communication and engagement approaches to the evidence and context.
  6. Review with appropriate contributors while protecting sensitive judgments.
  7. Reassess when authority, interest, impact, behavior, project conditions, or lifecycle stage changes.

docs.title: Optional numeric scoring — Atlas synthesis
docs.text:
!!! info "Optional Atlas implementation aid—not PMI-prescribed" Numeric scoring is an optional Atlas implementation aid, not a PMI-prescribed calculation and not required to use the grid. The downloadable workbook uses four 1–5 indicators per axis and an editable example threshold of 3.0. Define indicators and thresholds before assessment, retain the evidence, and do not imply false precision.

Power indicators: Decision authority; Resource control; Approval or acceptance authority; Ability to constrain or accelerate outcomes.

Interest indicators: Degree affected; Information demand; Participation level; Attention to outcomes.

docs.title: Lifecycle and process use
docs.text:
Identify Stakeholders establishes and initially classifies stakeholders. Planning uses the grid with the Stakeholder Register to shape stakeholder-engagement and communications strategies. Manage Stakeholder Engagement and Manage Communications apply those strategies. Monitoring reassesses the evidence and placement as power, interest, impact, or context changes.

A placement change does not automatically require integrated change control; use formal change control only when a proposed response crosses a controlled commitment or authority threshold.

docs.title: Roles and responsibilities
docs.text: The project manager or stakeholder-engagement lead facilitates and safeguards the assessment. Team members and subject-matter contributors supply factual evidence. Sponsors, product roles, functional leaders, governance bodies, and other stakeholders contribute within their authority. No universal approval owner is implied.

docs.text: Predictive work may maintain a formal controlled grid. Adaptive work may use a lighter representation and reassess it frequently. Hybrid work can combine formal governance-stakeholder assessment with rapid customer and user feedback.

Hybrid treatmentThe hybrid variant connects adaptive working detail with predictive governance, funding, compliance, contract, milestone, or approval needs. Why these badgesThe canonical artifact resource provides distinct predictive, adaptive, and hybrid examples, so the badges derive from those same variants. Additional treatment context

Predictive projects may maintain a controlled grid; adaptive teams may reassess stakeholders lightly and frequently; hybrid work can combine both cadences.
