docs.title: Plain-language meaning and function
docs.text:
A Stakeholder Register is the controlled working record of people, groups, organizations, and authorities that can affect the project, are affected by it, or believe they may be affected. It is broader than a contact list. Its purpose is to make stakeholder-related decisions traceable: whose needs and authority matter, what impact the change may create, what information is known, and what must be investigated or kept current.

Projects omit stakeholders easily because formal authority is more visible than lived impact. A regulator, sponsor, and functional manager may be obvious; frontline users, support teams, downstream operations, people represented by an advocacy group, data subjects, indirect suppliers, or a team affected by a policy change may be less visible. The register gives iterative discovery a durable home.

docs.title: Contents and rationale
docs.text:
Identification information uses a stable stakeholder ID, role or group, relationship to the project, and appropriate contact or access information. Stable IDs allow sensitive analysis to be separated from personal identity when privacy requires it. Role, authority, influence, impact, and decision rights help the team route approvals and escalation without assuming that every interested person has approval authority.

Interests, expectations, needs, requirements, concerns, and likely impacts explain what the stakeholder values and how the project may affect them. Classification information can include internal or external position, direction of influence, power and interest, or another method chosen for the context. Engagement observations and communication considerations help later planning, but the register should avoid insulting labels, unsupported speculation, or private information that the project has no legitimate reason to store.

docs.title: Creation and maintenance
docs.text:
Identify Stakeholders develops the initial register from the charter, Business Case, benefits information, agreements, organizational charts, governance records, requirements sources, operational analysis, contracts, lessons, interviews, workshops, observation, surveys, and expert judgment. The project manager coordinates the record; sponsors, business and product roles, team members, functional leaders, customer representatives, compliance or procurement authorities, and known stakeholders reveal additional relationships.

The first version is necessarily incomplete. Stakeholders emerge as requirements deepen, suppliers are selected, releases affect new groups, risks occur, teams reorganize, or operating ownership becomes clearer. Updates should record evidence and decision relevance rather than treating the original identification meeting as final.

docs.title: Lifecycle behavior
docs.text:
The register begins during initiation and feeds stakeholder-engagement and communications planning, requirements work, governance design, risk identification, acceptance, and transition. During execution and monitoring it is consulted and updated when authority, interest, impact, expectations, communication needs, or engagement evidence changes. Inactive stakeholders can be retained with an appropriate status so history is not lost.

Predictive work may maintain a formal controlled register and review it at planned governance points. Adaptive teams may keep equivalent information in a lightweight repository close to product and delivery work, revisiting it through reviews and feedback. Scrum and Kanban do not prescribe this register. Hybrid work may formally control sponsors, regulators, sellers, and acceptance authorities while updating customer and user information more frequently.

docs.title: How the stakeholder tools fit together
docs.text:
The register answers who is involved or affected and what is known about them. The Power–Interest Grid uses evidence to prioritize attention. The Stakeholder Engagement Assessment Matrix compares current and desired engagement. The Stakeholder Engagement Plan selects engagement strategies and actions. The Communications Management Plan defines information needs and delivery; a practical communications matrix can operationalize audience, owner, method, cadence, feedback, and escalation.

These records share information but are not interchangeable. A highly powerful stakeholder can be resistant, supportive, or unaware. A person who needs frequent accessible communication may have little formal authority. Classification should inform strategy, not determine it automatically.

docs.title: ServiceBridge worked example
docs.text:
ServiceBridge initially records the sponsor, customer-service director, compliance authority, support-team representative, external implementation seller, and frontline user representative as STK-01 through STK-06. It also identifies the operations owner, benefit owner, acceptance authority, functional managers, and delivery participants as the work develops.

STK-03 is recorded as the compliance authority with release-gate decision rights, an interest in evidence at agreed control points, and a need for early confirmation of accessibility, retention, and audit criteria. The register does not label that stakeholder “difficult” or expose unnecessary personal information. The Power–Interest Grid classifies the role from evidence; the engagement matrix later records current and desired involvement; communications planning defines the evidence brief and review cadence.

docs.title: Failure modes
docs.text:
A contact-list register omits impact, authority, expectations, requirements, and decision relevance. A register built only from an organization chart misses external, informal, and affected stakeholders. A register that publishes personal judgments broadly creates privacy, trust, and ethical risks; a register that is never updated causes late surprises in acceptance, compliance, adoption, and resource decisions.

The remedy is iterative discovery, factual language, explicit decision rights, proportionate access controls, and regular use. The register should improve engagement and decisions, not become a static directory or political scoring sheet.

docs.title: Exam distinctions
docs.text: The charter may name key stakeholders but does not replace the full register. The register identifies and describes stakeholders; analysis grids classify; the engagement matrix compares current and desired engagement; the engagement plan defines strategy; the communications plan defines information delivery. Stakeholder status alone does not grant approval authority, and a request is not an authorized change solely because it comes from an influential stakeholder.

docs.title: Sources and synthesis status
docs.text: The July 2026 course directly supports iterative stakeholder identification, stakeholder analysis, mapping models, privacy-conscious identifiers, engagement assessment, and communication preferences. The verified conception source supports the register’s initiation and downstream relationships. The developed rationales, ServiceBridge interpretation, privacy guidance, and approach comparison are Atlas synthesis; the Atlas does not prescribe one set of classifications or claim that Scrum or Kanban requires a Stakeholder Register.

docs.title: Test documents preserve how evidence was produced
docs.text:
Test and evaluation documents define planned evaluations and record their execution, results, defects, retests, and evidence. They exist so a conformity decision can be reproduced and traced to the requirement, configuration, environment, data, method, and result that supported it. A simple “pass” label is weak evidence when no one can tell what was tested or under which conditions.

These documents may contain test plans, cases, scripts, expected results, actual results, sampling methods, environment and version information, evaluator identity, defects, retest outcomes, and evidence links. The form varies with the product and risk. Quality metrics define the measure or threshold; test documents apply the method to a specific item; quality control measurements capture observed values; verification uses the combined evidence to decide conformity. Customer acceptance remains a separate authorized decision.

For ServiceBridge, test case TST-ACC-022 links to the keyboard-access requirement, release candidate 4.2, approved browsers, steps, expected focus order, actual results, screenshots, and a defect. After correction, the authorized evaluator records the retest and links the passing evidence to the verified deliverable. An adaptive team may automate and update tests with each increment; predictive work may plan formal qualification stages; hybrid delivery often combines continuous automated evidence with regulated or contractual evaluation packages. On the exam, testing produces evidence and may reveal defects—it does not by itself authorize acceptance or closure.

docs.title: Transition Package
docs.text:
On this page
  1. Definition and purpose
  2. Creation, updates, and authority
  3. Typical content
  4. Lifecycle and state
  5. Relationships and downstream use

A Transition Package gives the receiving organization the information, access, evidence, and ownership needed to operate or sustain an accepted result.

Transition is a transfer of responsibility, not merely a delivery of files. A technically complete system can fail after launch if operations do not know how to support it, lack access, or have not accepted ownership of unresolved risks and obligations.

docs.title: What the package may contain
docs.text:
The package may include accepted deliverables, operating procedures, configuration information, support contacts, training, access and credentials-handling instructions, data and retention requirements, warranties, licenses, compliance evidence, service levels, known defects, open risks and issues, maintenance needs, and named owners.

Each item supports readiness. Procedures explain how to run the result. Training prepares users and support staff. Configuration and access information make operation possible. Open-item records prevent unresolved work from disappearing at handoff. Ownership identifies who acts after the project team leaves.

For ServiceBridge, the package includes the accepted platform release, support model, retention and deletion procedure, accessibility evidence, data-reconciliation record, administrator training, vendor contacts, open issue list, and the operations owner’s acknowledgment.

docs.title: How transition relates to acceptance and closure
docs.text:
Acceptance confirms that the authorized recipient approves the result. Transition confirms that responsibility and capability are ready to move. Formal closure confirms that project or phase obligations have been completed, resolved, or transferred under the governing process.

A result can be accepted while transition readiness remains incomplete. A project should not claim closure merely because the system is live if ownership, support, records, contracts, or open obligations have not been addressed.

Predictive projects may prepare a consolidated handoff near the end. Adaptive teams may transition increments or releases earlier. Hybrid projects often transition product capabilities iteratively while retaining project-level operational, contractual, compliance, and closure obligations.

On the exam, distinguish deliverable acceptance from operational transition and formal project closure.

docs.title: Definition and purpose
docs.text:
Assembles accepted outputs, operating information, support arrangements, training, open obligations, readiness evidence, and transfer approvals.

Acceptance alone does not make a product operationally ready or transfer support, knowledge, access, and residual obligations.

A verified deliverable is a completed deliverable that has passed the required quality-control checks.

Verification answers whether the result conforms to requirements, specifications, quality metrics, and test expectations. It is based on evidence such as inspection results, test records, measurements, reviews, and defect status.

DRAFT — Pending Editorial Review

docs.title: How verification changes the record
docs.text:
Control Quality receives a completed deliverable and the applicable quality information. The verifier performs the planned checks and records actual results. If the result conforms, the deliverable’s state becomes verified and it can move to formal acceptance.

If it does not conform, it remains unverified. The team records defects or findings, analyzes the cause, performs authorized correction, and retests as required. A failed result should not be relabeled verified merely because the deadline is close.

For ServiceBridge, migration reconciliation shows that record counts match, required fields are preserved, and error rates are within the approved tolerance. The migration package becomes verified. The customer-service acceptance role must still decide whether to accept it under the agreed conditions.

docs.title: Verification is not acceptance
docs.text:
The verifier decides whether evidence shows conformance. The acceptance authority decides whether the verified result is accepted for the customer, sponsor, product, contract, or receiving organization. One person may hold both roles in a small project, but the decisions remain conceptually different.

A verified deliverable is not the same as a validation result in every discipline, a completed backlog item, or an accepted deliverable. The Atlas uses the predictive sequence supported by the registered quality and requirements sources; organizations may tailor the records while preserving the decisions.

Adaptive teams often verify continuously with automation, peer review, and the Definition of Done. Hybrid work may combine continuous verification with formal compliance or customer-acceptance gates.

On the exam, Control Quality produces verified deliverables; Validate Scope produces accepted deliverables.

docs.title: Information is analyzed performance data with meaning
docs.text:
Work Performance Information is performance data analyzed in context so it explains what is happening, why it matters, and what may happen next. It exists because raw observations—hours used, activities completed, defects found, dates recorded—do not by themselves support a decision. Comparison, aggregation, and analysis turn those observations into usable information.

The analysis may compare actual results with baselines, thresholds, forecasts, or prior trends; identify variances and causes; and show effects across scope, schedule, cost, quality, resources, communications, risk, procurement, or stakeholders. Work Performance Data are raw observations produced while work is performed. Work Performance Information is analyzed within control processes. Work Performance Reports package selected information for communication and decisions. Keeping these stages distinct prevents unverified data from being presented as a management conclusion.

For ServiceBridge, the team records that 6,400 of 8,000 records migrated, 96 defects were found, and USD 1.25 million was spent. Analysis compares those facts with the plan, separates expected from abnormal defects, identifies seller delay as a cause, and forecasts a release effect. That becomes information used by monitoring and control. A later report presents the relevant conclusion and recommendation to the sponsor. Adaptive dashboards can transform flow data into information continuously; predictive projects may analyze it at control dates; hybrid work reconciles rapid team signals with formal baseline and governance views.

docs.title: Delivery approach applicability
docs.text: ◎Common across approaches Predictive treatmentThe same core record supports predictive decisions; formality, approval, baselining, and storage are tailored. Adaptive equivalent or treatmentThe same core record supports adaptive decisions with timing, ownership, granularity, and update cadence tailored to the team. Hybrid treatmentThe same core form can cross governance and delivery cadences when ownership and decision rights remain clear. Why these badgesThe canonical artifact resource provides one common example because the decision purpose and structure do not materially differ by approach.

docs.title: Reports select performance information for a decision audience
docs.text:
Work Performance Reports are physical or electronic representations of analyzed project information prepared for communication, oversight, and decision making. They exist because different stakeholders need a coherent view of performance, implications, and requested decisions—not an undifferentiated export of every metric and log entry.

A report identifies its status date, audience, scope, performance against relevant commitments, trends and forecasts, significant risks and issues, changes, decisions needed, and supporting evidence. The form may be a status report, dashboard, forecast, progress presentation, or exception report. Work Performance Data are raw observations; Work Performance Information is analyzed within control work; reports communicate selected information. A report does not replace the underlying register, baseline, or approval record, and distributing a report is not the same as obtaining a decision.

For ServiceBridge, the monthly sponsor report shows that migration is behind its baseline, explains the seller-capacity cause, forecasts a ten-day release effect, states the remaining contingency, and asks whether to authorize a recovery option. Technical teams receive a more detailed defect and flow view, while operations receives readiness actions. The project manager tailors content without changing the underlying facts. Adaptive teams may use visible radiators and review outcomes; predictive work often uses scheduled reports; hybrid delivery combines team-level current information with governance-ready summaries. On the exam, communicate analyzed information through the planned channel and escalate decisions that exceed delegated authority.

Adaptive equivalent or treatmentThe adaptive variant preserves the management purpose while using iterative, incremental, backlog-based, or team-owned treatment where appropriate. Hybrid treatmentThe hybrid variant connects adaptive working detail with predictive governance, funding, compliance, contract, milestone, or approval needs. Why these badgesThe canonical artifact resource provides distinct predictive, adaptive, and hybrid examples, so the badges derive from those same variants.

docs.title: Decision Guides
docs.text:
Decision Guides start with a situation, not a process name. Use one when a scenario asks what should happen next, who can decide, what record must be updated, or when escalation is required.

A lifecycle chapter explains where work sits in the overall project story; a process page explains process mechanics; an artifact page explains a project record. A Decision Guide connects a current situation to authority → artifact → process or action → escalation without repeating those full references.

docs.title: How to use a guideQuality and AcceptanceRisk, Issues, and ImpedimentsChange and ComplianceProcurement, Transition, and ClosureBenefits
docs.text:
1. Match the facts of the scenario to the guide's current situation and immediate question.
  2. Identify the authority boundary before choosing an action.
  3. Update the relevant artifact or record and follow the applicable process or activity.
  4. Escalate only at the stated threshold, and check the common exam trap before deciding.

Decide what to do when technical verification or formal acceptance does not produce the expected result.

  • A Deliverable Fails Quality InspectionA completed deliverable fails an inspection or test and is not technically verified.
  • A Verified Deliverable Is Rejected During AcceptanceA technically verified deliverable is not accepted by the customer or designated acceptance authority.

Distinguish uncertainty from a current condition and decide when broader authority is required.

  • A Risk Occurs or an Impediment Exceeds Team AuthorityAn uncertain risk has occurred, or a blocker cannot be removed within team authority.

Route requested or required changes through the correct evidence and authority path.

  • A Stakeholder Requests a Baseline ChangeA stakeholder asks for work that may alter an approved scope, schedule, cost, or other controlled baseline.
  • A Compliance Problem Is DiscoveredTesting, audit, procurement, or operational readiness reveals a possible obligation failure.

Protect objectives and obligations when external delivery or readiness is threatened.

  • Seller Performance Threatens Project ObjectivesSeller delay, quality, capacity, or compliance performance threatens project commitments.
  • Transition or Closure Is Requested with Unresolved ObligationsTransition readiness is incomplete, or closure is requested while obligations, issues, procurement, or evidence remain unresolved.

Separate project closure from continuing operational benefits ownership and measurement.

  • Expected Benefits Are Not Yet Realized at Project ClosureOutputs are accepted and project closure is appropriate, but some expected benefits require later operational use or measurement.

docs.title: How to use this section
docs.text:
1. Read the assumption beside a formula before substituting values.
  2. Keep scope, status date, units, and calculation convention consistent.
  3. Use the interpretation to turn the result into a management question.
  4. Download the Project Quantitative Methods workbook to practice with editable inputs.
  5. Use the focused Communication Channels Calculator for participant-growth scenarios.

docs.title: Delivery-approach boundary
docs.text: Estimating applies across approaches, with differences in timing, granularity, and progressive elaboration. Network scheduling, approved baselines, and formal EVM are strongest in predictive and hybrid control structures. Adaptive delivery can estimate comparatively, elaborate detail just in time, and track iteration or release performance; formal EVM is possible only where suitable budget, scope, and performance-baseline measures exist. This does not imply every adaptive team uses EVM, or that adaptive work eliminates forecasting, budgeting, reserves, quality control, or schedule reasoning.

docs.title: Verification boundary
docs.text: Only records marked verified or supplemental official-PMI coverage are published. PERT variance and crash cost slope remain withheld pending direct source verification; neither appears in the workbook.

docs.title: Adaptive Metrics and Visual Management
docs.text:
Velocity, flow measures, burn charts, cumulative flow, and visual tools for adaptive and hybrid delivery.

Download the editable workbook See every course source mapped

!!! note "Source boundary" The July 2026 course supports these measures and visualizations. The current Scrum Guide does not prescribe velocity or a particular chart. The May 2025 Kanban Guide requires teams using its minimal definition to track WIP, throughput, work item age, and cycle time. Atlas examples are original ServiceBridge illustrations.

docs.title: Choose the measure that answers the question
docs.text:
Adaptive metrics describe different parts of a delivery system. They are useful only when their boundaries, units, and decision purpose are clear.

Velocity is completed estimate units per iteration for one team. It helps that team forecast how much similarly estimated work may fit in future iterations. Story points are not hours or currency, and velocity should not be used to rank teams.

Throughput is the number of work items completed per unit of time. It depends on how a work item and completion are defined. A team that splits work into smaller items can increase item count without increasing delivered value, so interpretation needs context.

Cycle time measures elapsed time from the workflow’s defined start point to its finish point. Lead time begins at an earlier request or commitment point. Work item age measures how long unfinished work has been in progress. State the boundaries before comparing results.

docs.title: Charts answer different questions
docs.text:
A burndown chart shows remaining work decreasing toward zero. A burnup chart shows completed work rising toward total scope and makes scope changes more visible. A cumulative-flow diagram shows how work accumulates across workflow states; a widening band can reveal growing work in progress or a bottleneck.

A control chart shows observations over time and can help distinguish stable variation from signals that merit investigation. A scatter diagram examines the relationship between two variables; it does not prove causation.

An information radiator is a visible, current display that helps people understand work and make decisions. A decorative dashboard with stale measures is not useful merely because it is visible.

docs.title: ServiceBridge example
docs.text:
The ServiceBridge team completes an average of 24 points per Sprint, but that average is useful only for its own similarly estimated backlog. Its support-integration flow completes eight items per week, with a median cycle time of six days. A widening review column on the cumulative-flow diagram shows that approval capacity, not development speed, is constraining flow.

The response is to investigate the review bottleneck and WIP policy, not to demand more velocity. The metric points to a question; it does not make the management decision automatically.

docs.title: Predictive and hybrid connections
docs.text:
Adaptive flow and iteration measures can coexist with milestone, cost, risk, quality, and EVM controls. Hybrid projects should connect the measures at meaningful boundaries rather than convert story points into currency or compare unrelated team estimates.

On the exam, distinguish velocity from throughput, cycle time from lead time, completed work from work in progress, burndown from burnup, and a flow signal from proof of root cause.

docs.title: Velocity
docs.text:
Velocity is the amount of estimated work fully completed by one team during one iteration, measured using that team’s chosen estimation unit, commonly story points.

Velocity = Σ estimates of items completed to the agreed Definition of Done during the iteration

Only fully completed items count. An unfinished item contributes zero for that iteration; 80% complete does not earn 80% of its points. Partially completed work remains unfinished and returns to or is replanned through the backlog. If work is split, remaining work may be re-estimated for future planning, but the unfinished original item never earns retroactive partial credit. Normally use the completed item’s original estimate unless the team has an explicit different policy, and calculate velocity only after the outcome is known.

Item Estimate End-of-Sprint status Counts toward velocity SB-101 8 Done 8 SB-102 5 Done 5 SB-103 13 80% complete 0 SB-104 3 Done 3

Iteration velocity: 8 + 5 + 0 + 3 = 16 story points. Unfinished means zero velocity credit.

docs.title: Average velocity and a bounded forecast
docs.text:
Sprint Completed points 1 21 2 25 3 23 4 27

Average velocity = Σ completed work units ÷ number of iterations = (21 + 25 + 23 + 27) ÷ 4 = 24 story points per Sprint.

For 100 estimated points remaining, 100 ÷ 24 = 4.17, so a whole-Sprint planning forecast rounds up to five Sprints. The recent observed velocities range from 21 to 27, producing approximately four to five Sprints (100 ÷ 27 through 100 ÷ 21, rounded up). Neither result is a guaranteed commitment. Inspect variation, team stability, changing estimates or membership, holidays and capacity, technical uncertainty, Definition of Done changes, dependencies, and scope change.

docs.title: Original velocity chart
docs.text:
21Sprint 125Sprint 223Sprint 327Sprint 420Sprint 528Sprint 6historical average: 24

The columns show completed estimated work, with no partial points. They can help this same team forecast. They do not prove productivity; sudden changes need context, and an upward trend may reflect changed estimating rather than better performance.

docs.title: What velocity must not be used for
docs.text:
• Velocity is team-specific because story points have no standard meaning across teams.
  • Never compare team velocities or use velocity as an individual productivity measure.
  • Higher velocity does not automatically mean more value or quality; inflating estimates creates neither.
  • Management must not impose a velocity performance quota.
  • Teams receive no credit for unfinished work.
  • Velocity does not replace inspection of outcomes, quality, customer value, or flow.
  • A substantial team-membership change can make history less predictive.

!!! tip "Exam note" When asked to calculate iteration velocity, count only work completed to the agreed Definition of Done. Story points are not hours.

docs.title: Burndown chart
docs.text:
A burndown shows work remaining vertically over time or iterations horizontally. Its endpoint is zero remaining. The actual line may be compared with an ideal or guideline line, but that guideline is not a mandatory commitment. Scope additions or re-estimation can make remaining work rise; unfinished work stays in the total. Sprint burndown focuses on one Sprint, while release or product burndown covers a broader horizon. Without a visible total-scope series, burndown can obscure why the curve changed.

ServiceBridge burndownRemaining work by period: 100, 84, 87, 70, 69, 48, 22, 0. It rises after scope is added. worktime → actual remainingguideline, not commitment

At period 2, completed work rises from 16 to 28, yet remaining work rises from 84 to 87 because total scope increases from 100 to 115. The team did work; the denominator also changed.

docs.title: Burnup chart
docs.text:
A burnup plots completed work increasing toward a separate total-scope line. Because the total line steps when scope changes, burnup often makes scope movement easier to understand than burndown.

ServiceBridge burnupCompleted work rises to 130 while total scope steps from 100 to 115 and then 130. worktime → completedtotal scope

Both burn charts use exactly the same data: remaining = scope − completed for every period.

Question Burndown Burnup What does the main line show? Work remaining Work completed Is scope change visible? Sometimes difficult to see Explicit through total-scope line Typical endpoint Zero remaining Completed line reaches scope line Common misunderstanding Flat line always means no work occurred Rising total-scope line may explain delayed completion

docs.title: Cumulative flow diagram
docs.text:
A cumulative flow diagram shows cumulative work items in workflow states over time. Band thickness represents items in that state; all unfinished bands together reflect WIP. A widening band can show accumulation or a bottleneck, horizontal distance may illustrate elapsed flow time when workflow boundaries permit, and stable parallel bands generally suggest steadier flow. Context is still required.

Period12345678Ready677888910In Progress23344443Review11235653Done123457912

Visible signal: Review widens from one to six items before recovering—investigate a possible review bottleneck.

docs.title: Task board or Kanban board
docs.text:
The simple path is Ready → In Progress → Review → Done. A board visualizes work state, blocked and aging items, ownership, and collaboration. A Kanban system additionally needs a Definition of Workflow with explicit start and finish points, states, policies, WIP controls, and a service level expectation. WIP control enables pull-based movement.

Ready

SB-120 · audit export

SB-121 · notice copy

In Progress WIP 2/3

SB-116 · identity sync BLOCKED

SB-118 · billing rules AGING 9 DAYS · MAY 19

Review WIP 2/2

SB-114 · intake form

SB-115 · search filter

Done

SB-109 · case detail

SB-112 · agent notes

Not every task board is a complete Kanban system. A board alone does not establish Kanban. Scrum teams may use boards without the full Kanban method, and hybrid projects may use a board inside broader predictive governance.

docs.title: Throughput
docs.text:
Throughput is the exact count of work items finished per unit of time. Throughput = completed work items ÷ time period. ServiceBridge completes 18 items in three weeks: 6 items per week. State the period, normally count items rather than points, and interpret changing item size carefully. Historical throughput can support contextual flow forecasting.

Velocity Throughput Often estimate units such as story points Counts completed work items Common in timeboxed planning Common in flow-based forecasting Team-specific estimated work Actual item completion count Sensitive to estimation practice Sensitive to item-size variation

docs.title: Cycle time
docs.text: Cycle time is elapsed time from the defined started point until the defined finished point. It includes active work and internal waiting after the item enters the measured workflow. A request-to-delivery interval is not cycle time unless the Definition of Workflow explicitly makes the request point its started boundary.

docs.title: Lead time
docs.text:
Lead time is elapsed time from a defined request, order, or commitment point until delivery. The label is incomplete unless its start and finish boundaries are named.

Concept Start point End point Primary use Procurement lead time Order or requisition Item available or delivered Predictive procurement and scheduling Schedule lead Relative predecessor point Earlier successor start Predictive network scheduling Customer lead time Customer request Customer delivery End-to-end responsiveness Commitment lead time Work commitment or selection Delivery Delivery forecasting Cycle time Work started Work finished Workflow performance Work item age Work started Current date while unfinished Managing aging WIP

Exact boundaries must be defined by the organization or the Kanban system’s Definition of Workflow.

docs.title: Predictive procurement lead time
docs.text:
ServiceBridge orders a specialized infrastructure appliance on March 1, 2026, and it is delivered on April 15, 2026. Using elapsed calendar days—subtract the start date from the end date, excluding the start and including the end—procurement lead time is 45 days.

The schedule models that elapsed acquisition interval or the resulting availability constraint before installation. If the plan allows too little time, the dependent installation can be delayed. This is procurement lead time, not a precedence-relationship lead. See Schedule Analysis, Risk, Compliance, and Procurement, and Plan Procurement Management.

docs.title: Predictive schedule lead
docs.text:
Coding is the predecessor and Testing is the successor. Testing may begin 2 working days before Coding is fully complete. That two-day schedule lead overlaps the activities and may shorten the modeled sequence, while increasing coordination and rework risk.

Schedule lead is a precedence-relationship adjustment. It is not customer lead time, commitment lead time, or procurement lead time. The complete network treatment remains in Schedule Analysis.

docs.title: Adaptive and Kanban boundaries
docs.text:
One ServiceBridge work item has these milestones:

Milestone Date Workflow meaning Request received May 1 Backlog; waiting outside WIP under this Definition of Workflow Committed or selected May 8 Ready; committed but still waiting outside WIP Work started May 10 Enters In Progress and becomes WIP Review started May 17 Remains WIP in Review Finished and delivered May 20 Reaches Done and leaves WIP

Date-counting convention: elapsed calendar days calculated as end date minus start date; the start date is excluded and the end date is included.

  • Customer lead time = May 20 − May 1 = 19 days.
  • Commitment lead time = May 20 − May 8 = 12 days.
  • Cycle time = May 20 − May 10 = 10 days.
  • Waiting before work starts = May 10 − May 1 = 9 days; two of those days follow commitment.
  • On May 15, while the item is still unfinished, work item age = May 15 − May 10 = 5 days.
Backlogrequest · May 1→Readycommitment · May 8→In Progressstarted · May 10 · WIP→ReviewMay 17 · WIP→Donefinished · May 20

Before In Progress, the item is waiting but is not WIP under this Definition of Workflow. From In Progress through Review it is WIP. At Done, its completed start-to-finish duration is cycle time. While started but unfinished, start-to-current duration is work item age. WIP is the number or set of started, unfinished items; it is not itself an elapsed-time metric. Do not call time spent as WIP “lead time” unless the selected lead-time boundary is also the workflow’s started point.

docs.title: Boundary visual
docs.text:
1. May 1Request
  2. May 1–8Waiting
  3. May 8Commitment
  4. May 8–10Waiting
  5. May 10Started
  6. May 10–17Active work + internal waiting
  7. May 17Review
  8. May 20Finished → delivered

Customer lead timeRequest → delivery · 19 days

Commitment lead timeCommitment → delivery · 12 days

Cycle timeStarted → finished · 10 days

Work item age on May 15Started → current measurement while unfinished · 5 days

docs.title: Work item age
docs.text:
Work item age is elapsed time from the defined started point until the current measurement date for an unfinished item. Once the item finishes, report its cycle time rather than continuing to calculate work item age. See the Task Board or Kanban Board, Cycle Time, and the current Kanban Guide.

!!! note "Why labels vary" Teams and tools sometimes use “lead time” and “cycle time” differently. The Kanban system’s Definition of Workflow must specify the measured start and finish points. The Atlas therefore names each boundary explicitly rather than treating a vendor tool’s default column calculation as universal.

docs.title: Control chart
docs.text:
A control chart plots a process measure over time and may include a center line and control limits. Cycle time is a useful adaptive example. Points or nonrandom patterns outside expected variation may suggest special-cause variation; investigate rather than blame. Control limits describe process behavior and are not specification limits.

ServiceBridge control chartCycle times [4, 5, 4, 6, 5, 12, 5, 4]; mean 5.625; supplied illustrative lower and upper limits 2 and 9. worktime → cycle timemean 5.625supplied UCL 9supplied LCL 2

The arithmetic mean is 5.625 days. The lower limit 2 and upper limit 9 are supplied illustrative inputs. The course discusses center lines, limits, and the rule of seven but does not supply an authoritative control-limit calculation, so the Atlas intentionally withholds that formula.

docs.title: Information radiator
docs.text: An information radiator is a highly visible, current display useful to the team and stakeholders—not one chart type. It can show board status, Sprint Goal, burn charts, cumulative flow, impediments, quality, release progress, or risk indicators. It should be easy to see and understand, current, and able to prompt conversation and action. A stale dashboard is not useful merely because it is visible; a current digital display can serve distributed teams.

docs.title: Impediment list and visualization
docs.text:
An impediment blocks or slows work and may be tracked in an issue-management system. A useful view names description, severity, current action, owner or escalation responsibility, age, and status.

HIGH · ESCALATEDTest environment unavailableCurrent actionInfrastructure escalation activeOwnerPlatform LeadAge4 daysStatusEscalated

Use the Impediment Record, Issue Log, Roles and Authority, and impediment escalation Decision Guide. Scrum Master accountability for team effectiveness does not mean personally removing every impediment. Never penalize a team for reporting blockers.

docs.title: Metrics in Scrum events
docs.text:
• Sprint Planning: historical velocity can inform capacity and forecasting; it does not dictate what Developers select.
  • Daily Scrum: Developers may inspect flow, blocked work, or Sprint Goal progress; this is not a management reporting session.
  • Sprint Review: stakeholders may discuss outcomes, release forecasts, progress, and Product Backlog adaptation.
  • Sprint Retrospective: the team may inspect cycle time, bottlenecks, quality, and flow patterns for improvement.

No Scrum event requires a particular chart. See Scrum Events and Adaptive Cadences.

docs.title: Roles, artifacts, and systems of record
docs.text:
Developers or delivery-team members produce the work and maintain operational data. The Product Owner uses product and progress information for value and backlog decisions. The Scrum Master can help the team improve flow. A project manager or governance role may use aggregated forecasts in hybrid contexts, but metric ownership never grants unilateral authority and management must not turn velocity into a quota. See Roles, Responsibilities, and Authority.

Product Backlog, Sprint Backlog, Increment, Definition of Done, a board, Impediment Record, Issue Log, Work Performance Information, Work Performance Reports, and a contextual release plan can supply or consume the data. Operational tool data remains in its designated system of record; reports are derived views, not competing records.

docs.title: Delivery-approach distinctions
docs.text:
• Adaptive: velocity, burn charts, flow metrics, and boards may support iterative or flow-based delivery.
  • Scrum: velocity and burn charts are common tactics, not prescribed Scrum artifacts or required measures.
  • Kanban: the current guide uses the exact flow metrics WIP, throughput, work item age, and cycle time and requires a Definition of Workflow. It does not require Scrum events.
  • Hybrid: adaptive measures may coexist with milestones, baselines, EVM, contracts, release governance, and transition dates. Do not combine unlike units without understanding their purpose.

See Adaptive and Hybrid Delivery, Reserves and Baselines, and Earned Value Management.

docs.title: Common exam traps
docs.text:
1. Unfinished story points do not count toward velocity.
  2. Velocity is neither comparable across teams nor an individual productivity metric.
  3. Story points are not hours.
  4. Burndown shows remaining work; burnup shows completed work and total scope.
  5. A rising burndown may mean scope was added.
  6. A widening cumulative-flow band can signal a bottleneck.
  7. Throughput counts completed items, not points.
  8. A predictive schedule lead overlaps predecessor and successor activities; procurement lead time is the time needed to obtain an external item or service.
  9. Adaptive lead time normally begins before active work; cycle time starts when work begins.
  10. Work item age applies only to started, unfinished work. WIP is a count or state, not elapsed time.
  11. Lead time is at least cycle time only when both share a finish and lead time starts earlier. Always identify the question’s boundaries.
  12. A board alone does not establish Kanban.
  13. Daily Scrum is not a manager status meeting, and no Scrum event requires a chart.
  14. Charts support decisions; they do not replace conversation and judgment.

docs.title: Potential Communication Channels
docs.text:
The communication-channels formula counts possible pairwise connections among a defined number of people. Use it to recognize how coordination paths grow as a group expands, not to determine the correct communication method or prove that every pair must communicate directly.

For a 12-person ServiceBridge working group, n(n-1)/2 gives 66 possible pairs. That result explains coordination complexity; the Communications Management Plan still determines who needs which information, why, through which channel, at what cadence, and with what feedback or escalation route.

Calculate possible unique pairwise communication paths without confusing paths with messages, technologies, methods, or communication quality.

PredictiveAdaptiveHybrid

docs.title: Canonical formula and source status
docs.text:
Supplemental · official PMIFRM-COM-001 Potential communication channels

C = n(n - 1) / 2

PredictiveAdaptiveHybrid

Interpretation: Counts each possible pair of people once to illustrate how communication complexity grows as participants are added.

Assumptions: n is an integer of at least 1; direction is not counted separately; the measure represents potential interpersonal paths rather than messages, technologies, methods, or required direct communications.

Units: Potential pairwise paths.

Cnumber of possible unique pairwise communication channelsnnumber of people included in the communication network

Exam note: The formula counts potential communication paths; it does not mean the project manager personally manages a separate formal communication for every pair, and it is not verified_current_course coverage.

!!! info "Supplemental official-PMI coverage" The formula is supported by official PMI Learning Library material but was not located in the July 2026 Lesson 3 handout. Its status is supplemental_official_pmi, not verified_current_course, and that status does not imply equal emphasis with every current-course formula.

docs.title: Assumptions
docs.text:
1. n is the number of people in the communication network and is an integer of at least 1.
  2. Each possible pair is counted once; direction is not counted separately.
  3. The result represents potential interpersonal paths, not required direct communication.
  4. It does not measure communication quality or effectiveness and does not replace communication planning.

docs.title: Worked examples
docs.text:
Scenario Calculation Result Five people 5(5 − 1) / 2 10 channels Six people 6(6 − 1) / 2 15 channels Add one person to a five-person group 15 − 10, or one path to each of 5 existing people 5 additional channels Grow from five to eight people 8(7)/2 − 5(4)/2 = 28 − 10 18 additional channels

Adding one person to a group with n existing people creates exactly n new pairwise paths. When several people are added, calculate the new total and subtract the old total.

docs.title: Five-person network
docs.text:
P1P2P3P4P510 potential pathsP1–P2P1–P3P1–P4P1–P5P2–P3P2–P4P2–P5P3–P4P3–P5P4–P5

The identifiers and complete pair list communicate the result without relying on color or line geometry.

docs.title: Exam distinctions
docs.text:
1. The formula counts potential communication paths. It does not mean the project manager personally manages a separate formal communication for every pair.
  2. n means people, not messages, email, meetings, dashboards, video calls, or other technologies and methods.
  3. Communication paths are not the Communications Management Plan or a communications matrix.
  4. More potential paths indicate greater possible complexity, not lower communication effectiveness by definition.

docs.title: How it connects to communication management
docs.text:
Item Purpose Communications Management Plan Defines the project’s communication approach, requirements, responsibilities, constraints, and governance. Practical communications matrix Operationalizes audiences, information, purpose, owner, method, cadence, feedback, and escalation; it may be part of or support the plan. Project communications The information actually created, distributed, received, understood, and retained as appropriate. Potential-channel formula Illustrates possible pairwise complexity from the number of people; it does not design any of the items above.

Use the grid and engagement evidence to tailor communication; do not convert every potential path into a mandatory communication.

docs.title: Earned Value Management
docs.text:
Compare authorized planned value, budgeted value earned, and actual cost at one status date, then forecast using an explicit assumption.

PredictiveAdaptiveHybrid

docs.title: What earned value compares
docs.text:
Earned Value Management compares three measures at the same status date and for the same scope.

Planned Value (PV) is the approved budgeted value of work planned by the status date. Earned Value (EV) is the approved budgeted value of work actually completed. Actual Cost (AC) is what that completed work actually cost.

The word “value” here means budgeted value, not customer benefit or market value. If a task budgeted at USD 100,000 is complete, it earns USD 100,000 of EV even if it cost more or less to perform.

docs.title: Reading the core results
docs.text:
Schedule variance is EV - PV. A negative result means less budgeted work has been completed than planned. Schedule Performance Index is EV / PV; below 1.0 indicates the same condition as a ratio.

Cost variance is EV - AC. A negative result means the completed work cost more than its budgeted value. Cost Performance Index is EV / AC; below 1.0 indicates unfavorable cost efficiency.

For ServiceBridge, PV is USD 1.20 million, EV is USD 1.00 million, and AC is USD 1.25 million. The project has completed less budgeted work than planned and spent more than the budgeted value of that completed work. This statement is more useful than saying only that SPI and CPI are below one.

docs.title: Forecasts depend on assumptions
docs.text:
Estimate at Completion is not one universal formula. BAC / CPI assumes current cost efficiency continues. AC + (BAC - EV) assumes remaining work will follow the original budget rate. A combined CPI and SPI formula assumes both cost and schedule efficiency affect remaining cost. The chosen formula must match the situation.

Estimate to Complete is the expected cost remaining. Variance at Completion compares BAC with EAC. To-Complete Performance Index states the efficiency remaining work would need to achieve against BAC or an approved EAC target.

docs.title: Boundaries and approach use
docs.text:
EVM requires a meaningful scope, schedule, and cost performance baseline. It is strongest in predictive or hybrid settings where those measures are maintained. Adaptive delivery can use EVM at a suitable release or project level, but velocity and throughput are not substitutes for EV and should not be converted casually into financial value.

An EVM schedule variance is expressed in currency units of budgeted value, not days. Critical-path and milestone analysis are still needed to understand calendar consequences.

On the exam, align PV, EV, and AC to the same status date and scope, interpret the sign or ratio before selecting a response, and choose forecast assumptions from the scenario rather than memorizing one EAC formula.

docs.title: The three measures
docs.text:
PV — Planned Value: authorized budget assigned to work scheduled for completion by the status date.

EV — Earned Value: authorized budgeted value of work actually completed by the status date. A simple example may calculate EV as percent complete × budget for the measured work, but the measured budget may be a project, control account, work package, or other defined performance scope—EV is not merely “a percentage of BAC.”

AC — Actual Cost: actual cost incurred for the completed work by the status date.

BAC — Budget at Completion: approved cost baseline at completion for the measured scope.

!!! note "Schedule variance uses cost units" SV and CV use cost units because PV, EV, and AC are monetary budget values. SV is not directly a number of calendar days ahead or behind schedule.

docs.title: Formula reference
docs.text:
Verified · current 2026 courseFRM-EVM-001 Schedule variance

SV = EV - PV

PredictiveHybrid

Interpretation: Positive is ahead of planned value; zero is on plan; negative is behind planned value.

Assumptions: EV and PV cover the same measured scope and status date.

Units: Currency or other budget units.

SVschedule variance in cost unitsEVearned valuePVplanned value

Exam note: SV is expressed in cost units, not calendar days.

Verified · current 2026 courseFRM-EVM-002 Schedule performance index

SPI = EV / PV

PredictiveHybrid

Interpretation: Above 1 is ahead of planned value; 1 is on plan; below 1 is behind planned value.

Assumptions: PV is nonzero and scope/status date are aligned.

Units: Dimensionless ratio.

SPIschedule performance indexEVearned valuePVplanned value

Exam note: SPI does not prove a specific number of days ahead or behind.

Verified · current 2026 courseFRM-EVM-003 Cost variance

CV = EV - AC

PredictiveHybrid

Interpretation: Positive is under budget; zero is on budget; negative is over budget.

Assumptions: EV and AC cover the same measured scope and status date.

Units: Currency or other budget units.

CVcost varianceEVearned valueACactual cost

Exam note: Negative CV is unfavorable.

Verified · current 2026 courseFRM-EVM-004 Cost performance index

CPI = EV / AC

PredictiveHybrid

Interpretation: Above 1 is cost efficient; 1 is on budget; below 1 is cost inefficient.

Assumptions: AC is nonzero and scope/status date are aligned.

Units: Dimensionless ratio.

CPIcost performance indexEVearned valueACactual cost

Exam note: CPI below 1 means the project earns less budgeted value per unit of actual cost.

Verified · current 2026 courseFRM-EVM-005 Estimate at completion — current CPI continues

EAC = BAC / CPI

PredictiveHybrid

Interpretation: Forecasts total cost if current cost efficiency continues.

Assumptions: Current cumulative cost efficiency is expected to continue for the remaining work; CPI is nonzero.

Units: Currency.

EACforecast total cost at completionBACBudget at CompletionCPIcost performance index

Exam note: Choose an EAC formula by its assumption, not by memorized preference.

Verified · current 2026 courseFRM-EVM-006 Estimate to complete

ETC = EAC - AC

PredictiveHybrid

Interpretation: Forecasts cost remaining from the status date.

Assumptions: EAC and AC use the same measured scope and status date.

Units: Currency.

ETCforecast remaining costEACforecast total costACactual cost to date

Exam note: EAC is total forecast; ETC is remaining forecast.

Supplemental · official PMIFRM-EVM-007 EAC — remaining work at original rate

EAC = AC + (BAC - EV)

PredictiveHybrid

Interpretation: Adds actual cost to the original budget for uncompleted work.

Assumptions: Past variance is atypical and remaining work will perform at the original budgeted rate.

Units: Currency.

EACforecast total costACactual costBACBudget at CompletionEVearned value

Exam note: The assumption distinguishes this formula from BAC divided by CPI.

Verified · current 2026 courseFRM-EVM-008 EAC — cost and schedule influence remaining work

EAC = AC + ((BAC - EV) / (CPI × SPI))

PredictiveHybrid

Interpretation: Adjusts remaining work for both cost and schedule performance.

Assumptions: Both current cost and schedule performance are expected to influence remaining cost; CPI and SPI are nonzero.

Units: Currency.

EACforecast total costACactual costBACBudget at CompletionEVearned valueCPIcost performance indexSPIschedule performance index

Exam note: Use only when the question says both performance factors continue to affect remaining work.

Verified · current 2026 courseFRM-EVM-009 EAC — bottom-up remaining estimate

EAC = AC + bottom-up ETC

PredictiveHybrid

Interpretation: Replaces statistical extrapolation with a new detailed remaining-work estimate.

Assumptions: The original estimate is no longer reliable and the remaining work has been re-estimated.

Units: Currency.

EACforecast total costACactual costbottom-up ETCnew detailed estimate of remaining work

Exam note: Bottom-up ETC is an input from re-estimating, not a value derived from CPI.

Supplemental · official PMIFRM-EVM-010 Variance at completion

VAC = BAC - EAC

PredictiveHybrid

Interpretation: Positive forecasts under BAC; zero forecasts at BAC; negative forecasts over BAC.

Assumptions: BAC and EAC cover the same measured scope.

Units: Currency.

VACvariance at completionBACBudget at CompletionEACforecast total cost

Exam note: Supplemental coverage; do not assume equal course emphasis.

Supplemental · official PMIFRM-EVM-011 To-complete performance index against BAC

TCPI(BAC) = (BAC - EV) / (BAC - AC)

PredictiveHybrid

Interpretation: Efficiency the remaining work must achieve to meet BAC.

Assumptions: BAC minus AC is positive and BAC remains the selected target.

Units: Dimensionless ratio.

TCPIrequired future cost efficiencyBACBudget at CompletionEVearned valueACactual cost

Exam note: Compare the required efficiency with demonstrated performance for realism.

Supplemental · official PMIFRM-EVM-012 To-complete performance index against approved EAC

TCPI(EAC) = (BAC - EV) / (EAC - AC)

PredictiveHybrid

Interpretation: Efficiency the remaining work must achieve to meet the approved EAC target.

Assumptions: EAC minus AC is positive and EAC is the selected approved target.

Units: Dimensionless ratio.

TCPIrequired future cost efficiencyBACBudget at CompletionEVearned valueEACapproved forecast targetACactual cost

Exam note: The numerator remains budgeted work remaining; the denominator changes to funds remaining against EAC.

Formal EVM is strongest where predictive or hybrid control structures provide the necessary baseline measures. Adaptive delivery may use EVM at a release or other suitable performance-baseline level, but not every agile team uses formal EVM.

docs.title: Estimating
docs.text:
Estimating selects a defensible way to forecast duration or cost from the information currently available. Read the techniques below as choices with different evidence needs: analogous estimating depends on meaningful similarity, parametric estimating depends on a valid scalable relationship, three-point estimating makes uncertainty visible, and bottom-up estimating depends on adequate decomposition.

The result is not a commitment merely because it is calculated. For ServiceBridge, a migration rate derived from a trial can support a parametric estimate, but the team must state the data volume, units, conditions, and uncertainty before the estimate can inform the budget or schedule.

Choose an estimating method for the information available, document its assumptions, and refine it as knowledge improves.

PredictiveAdaptiveHybrid

docs.title: Four current-course techniques
docs.text:
Technique What it does Reliability condition Analogous / top-down estimating Uses historical information from a similar project or activity; it is usually faster and less costly, but less precise than detailed estimating. The comparison is meaningfully similar and relevant historical information is available. Parametric estimating Applies a measurable statistical relationship or unit rate, such as cost per square foot, hours per unit, or cost per transaction. The parameter is valid for the work and scales across the range being estimated. Three-point estimating Uses optimistic, most-likely, and pessimistic estimates to represent uncertainty rather than relying on one point. The three inputs describe the same scope, units, and conditions. Bottom-up estimating Estimates detailed activities, work packages, or lower-level components with people closest to the work, then aggregates upward. The decomposition is adequate and component estimates use compatible units and scope boundaries.

!!! note "Top-down is not a fifth peer technique" In this course family, analogous estimating is also described as top-down estimating. Beginning with a fixed funding limit and asking what can be delivered is a top-down budgeting or scope-allocation decision—not a separate fifth estimating technique.

docs.title: Formula reference
docs.text:
Verified · current 2026 courseFRM-EST-001 Parametric estimate

Estimate = Quantity × Rate per unit

PredictiveAdaptiveHybrid

Interpretation: Multiplies a valid unit relationship by the measured quantity.

Assumptions: The rate is valid and scalable for the quantity and conditions.

Units: Output uses the rate numerator unit; quantity and rate denominator must match.

Estimateestimated duration or costQuantitynumber of unitsRateduration or cost per unit

Exam note: Test the parameter's validity before applying the arithmetic.

Verified · current 2026 courseFRM-EST-002 Triangular three-point estimate

TE = (O + M + P) / 3

PredictiveAdaptiveHybrid

Interpretation: Gives equal weight to all three estimates.

Assumptions: O, M, and P use the same scope and units.

Units: Same time, effort, or cost unit as O, M, and P.

TEexpected estimateOoptimistic estimateMmost-likely estimatePpessimistic estimate

Exam note: Keep the entire numerator in parentheses.

Verified · current 2026 courseFRM-EST-003 Beta / PERT three-point estimate

TE = (O + 4M + P) / 6

PredictiveAdaptiveHybrid

Interpretation: Weights the most-likely estimate four times as heavily.

Assumptions: O, M, and P use the same scope and units and a beta approximation is appropriate.

Units: Same time, effort, or cost unit as O, M, and P.

TEexpected estimateOoptimistic estimateMmost-likely estimatePpessimistic estimate

Exam note: The coefficient 4 applies only to M.

Verified · official PMIFRM-EST-004 PERT standard deviation

σ = (P - O) / 6

PredictiveHybrid

Interpretation: Approximates dispersion around the PERT mean.

Assumptions: The PERT beta approximation and comparable endpoints are appropriate.

Units: Same unit as P and O.

σstandard deviationPpessimistic estimateOoptimistic estimate

Exam note: This is dispersion in the estimate's unit, not a guaranteed range.

docs.title: Worked comparison
docs.text:
For a duration with O = 8 days, M = 12 days, and P = 20 days, the triangular estimate is 13.33 days, the beta/PERT estimate is 12.67 days, and the verified PERT standard deviation is 2 days. The PERT result is closer to the most-likely estimate because M receives four times the weight.

A parametric example: 320 records at 1.5 hours per record produces 480 hours, provided the rate remains valid at that volume.

docs.title: Adaptive and hybrid treatment
docs.text: Adaptive teams may estimate comparatively or at several horizons and elaborate detail just in time. Those are general adaptive practices; story points are not universal, and Scrum- or Kanban-specific techniques should not be generalized to every adaptive approach.

docs.title: Reserves and Baselines
docs.text:
Separate estimated work, identified uncertainty, the approved cost baseline, and governance-controlled management reserve.

PredictiveAdaptiveHybrid

docs.title: The financial boundaries
docs.text:
A cost estimate predicts the money required for particular work. The cost baseline is the approved, time-phased budget used to measure cost performance. The total of the cost baseline is Budget at Completion, or BAC.

The project budget includes the cost baseline plus management reserve. These numbers answer different questions, so they should not be used as synonyms.

docs.title: Contingency reserve
docs.text:
Contingency reserve covers identified uncertainty within the approved project scope. It may be estimated from specific risk responses, expected monetary value, simulation, judgment, or another approved method. Because it supports known uncertainty in the planned work, it is included in the cost baseline.

For ServiceBridge, data profiling shows a known chance that legacy records will require additional cleansing. The approved cost response for that uncertainty can be included as contingency reserve.

Using contingency reserve follows the authority and control rules in the Cost Management Plan. It is not a way to hide poor estimating or add unrelated scope.

docs.title: Management reserve
docs.text:
Management reserve covers unforeseen work that is still within project scope. It is outside the cost baseline and therefore outside BAC, but inside the total project budget.

If an unknown condition arises and the organization authorizes use of management reserve, the approved amount is brought into the cost baseline through the applicable control process. The decision and baseline history must remain traceable.

Management reserve is not automatically controlled by the project manager. Governance determines who may release it.

docs.title: Baseline and forecast
docs.text:
A baseline records the approved reference. A forecast predicts the current expected result. Estimate at Completion may show that the project is likely to exceed BAC, but that forecast does not silently change the baseline. Approved change is required when the controlled commitment itself changes.

Predictive and hybrid projects commonly use these formal financial controls. Adaptive work may fund stable teams or releases, yet a project or contract can still maintain a cost baseline and reserves at the appropriate level.

For the exam, remember: contingency reserve is inside the cost baseline; management reserve is outside the cost baseline; BAC equals the cost baseline; and total project budget includes management reserve.

docs.title: Budget relationship
docs.text:
Verified · current 2026 courseFRM-RES-001 Cost baseline / BAC

BAC = aggregated cost estimates + contingency reserves

PredictiveHybrid

Interpretation: BAC includes contingency reserve and excludes management reserve.

Assumptions: Scope and reserve treatment are authorized under project governance.

Units: Currency.

BACBudget at Completion and approved cost baselineaggregated cost estimatesapproved component estimatescontingency reservesbudget for identified uncertainty

Exam note: BAC means Budget at Completion, not Budgeted at Completion.

Verified · current 2026 courseFRM-RES-002 Total project budget

Total Project Budget = BAC + management reserve

PredictiveHybrid

Interpretation: Management reserve sits outside BAC but inside total project budget.

Assumptions: Management reserve is governed and not used for unauthorized out-of-scope work.

Units: Currency.

Total Project Budgetauthorized project budget including management reserveBACapproved cost baselinemanagement reservebudget for unforeseen in-scope work

Exam note: Moving management reserve into the baseline requires the applicable authorization.

Budget and reserves stack — management reserve is outside BAC. Aggregated cost estimates $2.20M + Contingency reserve $0.20M = BAC / cost baseline $2.40M + Management reserve $0.15M = Total project budget $2.55M

docs.title: Distinctions
docs.text:
BAC — Budget at Completion is the total approved cost baseline for the measured scope. It includes contingency reserve within the baseline and excludes management reserve.

Contingency reserve addresses identified uncertainty or known unknowns and may relate to identified risks or expected variability. It is part of the cost baseline.

Management reserve addresses unforeseen work or unknown unknowns within project scope. It is outside the cost baseline and BAC, but inside total project budget. It does not authorize out-of-scope work.

Formal baseline and reserve structures are strongest in predictive and hybrid governance. Adaptive delivery still budgets and forecasts; it may manage uncertainty at release or other suitable horizons.

docs.title: Schedule Analysis
docs.text:
Schedule analysis uses the activity network, durations, constraints, calendars, and resource assumptions to understand the earliest modeled completion and the work that governs it. The calculations below are decision aids: they show dependency effects and available float, but they do not prove that an estimate, dependency, or resource assumption is correct.

For ServiceBridge, delaying a task with five days of float by three days need not move the release; delaying a zero-float migration activity may. The team recalculates the network, checks the critical path and milestones, and then evaluates compression, resource, or change options with their cost and risk effects.

Build the network first, then calculate dates, float, and the path that governs the earliest modeled completion.

PredictiveAdaptiveHybrid

docs.title: Calculation convention
docs.text:
The Atlas begins the first activity at time zero: EF = ES + duration; a successor ES is the maximum predecessor EF; LS = LF - duration; and a predecessor LF is the minimum successor LS.

!!! warning "Exam numbering convention" Some course diagrams use inclusive day numbering and apply +1 or -1 adjustments. Follow the convention shown in the question. Do not mix conventions within one calculation.

docs.title: Formula reference
docs.text:
Verified · official PMIFRM-SCH-001 Early finish

EF = ES + Duration

PredictiveHybrid

Interpretation: Calculates earliest finish in the Atlas day-zero convention.

Assumptions: Finish-to-start logic without lag unless the network states otherwise.

Units: Consistent time units.

EFearliest finishESearliest startDurationactivity duration

Exam note: Inclusive-day diagrams may use +1 or -1; follow the question's convention.

Verified · official PMIFRM-SCH-002 Late start

LS = LF - Duration

PredictiveHybrid

Interpretation: Calculates latest start in the Atlas day-zero convention.

Assumptions: The required finish and successor logic are established.

Units: Consistent time units.

LSlatest startLFlatest finishDurationactivity duration

Exam note: Use the smallest successor late-start value at convergence.

Verified · current 2026 courseFRM-SCH-003 Total float from start dates

Total Float = LS - ES

PredictiveHybrid

Interpretation: Zero normally identifies critical work under the chosen convention.

Assumptions: Early and late dates use the same convention and calendars.

Units: Time units.

Total Floattime available before project completion is delayedLSlatest startESearliest start

Exam note: More than one zero-float critical path may exist.

Verified · current 2026 courseFRM-SCH-004 Total float from finish dates

Total Float = LF - EF

PredictiveHybrid

Interpretation: Equivalent to LS minus ES when conventions are consistent.

Assumptions: Early and late dates use the same convention and calendars.

Units: Time units.

Total Floattime available before project completion is delayedLFlatest finishEFearliest finish

Exam note: Do not mix inclusive and day-zero calculations.

Verified · official PMIFRM-SCH-005 Free float

Free Float = earliest ES of immediate successors - EF

PredictiveHybrid

Interpretation: Measures flexibility before the next activity's early start is affected.

Assumptions: Use the earliest ES when there are multiple immediate successors.

Units: Time units.

Free Floattime available before an immediate successor is delayedESearliest start of a successorEFearliest finish of the current activity

Exam note: Free float protects successor early starts; total float protects project completion.

docs.title: Critical path and float
docs.text:
The critical path is the longest-duration path through the network and determines the shortest calculated project duration. Critical-path activities normally have zero total float under the selected convention; more than one critical path may exist. A noncritical delay changes completion only after available float is exhausted or the critical path changes.

A · Confirm scope

Duration 3 days · predecessor none

ES0EF3LS0LF3TF0 B · Configure service

Duration 5 days · predecessor A

ES3EF8LS3LF8TF0 C · Prepare training

Duration 3 days · predecessor A

ES3EF6LS5LF8TF2 D · Validate release

Duration 4 days · predecessor B, C

ES8EF12LS8LF12TF0

Result: A → B → D is the 12-day critical path. C has two days of total float. The labels and table values—not color alone—identify critical work.

docs.title: Compression and resource optimization
docs.text:
Technique Primary constraint Likely cost effect Schedule effect Key risk Fast tracking Dependency flexibility Usually neutral directly Shortens when overlap is feasible Rework and coordination Crashing Critical-path duration Usually increases Shortens only if critical work changes Cost, risk, complexity Resource smoothing Available float Usually limited Completion unchanged May leave overallocations Resource leveling Resource availability May increase May extend or change critical path Milestone delay

Crashing is broader than simply adding people: it may use resources, spending, procurement, technology, or another cost-bearing intervention. It must reduce critical-path duration to shorten project completion.
