docs.title: AI Semantic Reference
docs.text:
Semantic contract for AI agents, retrieval systems, generators, validators, and advanced readers.

!!! info "Purpose"

This page defines the preferred terminology, conceptual boundaries, ownership rules, precedence, applicability, and verification status used throughout The Project Management Knowledge Atlas. It is designed primarily for AI agents and retrieval systems, while remaining readable to advanced human users. It is not a narrative PMP study chapter.

The Atlas is an independent study resource. Source status must be respected, and an Atlas synthesis must not be presented as official PMI guidance. Linked canonical pages contain the full reader-facing explanation. For operational role assignments, use the Roles Reference and its 49-process role map; this semantic contract remains concise.

Contract version: 1.3.0 · Last reviewed: 2026-08-01

Machine-readable JSON Machine-readable YAML

docs.title: How to resolve conflicts
docs.text:
1. PRE-001: A dedicated canonical registry has precedence over a cross-reference record.
  2. PRE-002: The Formula registry owns formula expressions and verification status.
  3. PRE-003: The Roles registry owns public role definitions; the Process Role Map owns contextual process assignments and authority boundaries.
  4. PRE-004: Artifact definitions own structure and state; the Artifact Role Map owns contextual creation, custody, review, approval, verification, acceptance, and receipt assignments.
  5. PRE-005: Lifecycle definitions own sequence, handoffs, and lifecycle context.
  6. PRE-006: Decision Guides own scenario-specific action and escalation paths.
  7. PRE-007: Shared semantic records define cross-cutting terminology and interpretation.
  8. PRE-008: Current verified source material has precedence over Atlas synthesis.
  9. PRE-009: Source-limited or synthesized material must be labeled as such.
  10. PRE-010: When authority varies by organization, do not invent a universal rule.

docs.title: Recommended behavior
docs.text:
• Follow canonical links for full explanations.
  • Preserve verification labels.
  • Distinguish official source material from Atlas synthesis.
  • State uncertainty when a record is source-limited.
  • Do not infer that missing applicability means prohibition.
  • Do not treat commercial templates as PMI-prescribed forms.
  • Do not treat process groups as sequential lifecycle phases.
  • Do not equate waterfall with every form of predictive delivery.
  • Do not equate Scrum or Kanban with all adaptive delivery.

docs.title: Avoid
docs.text:
• Inventing authority.
  • Merging risk, issue, and impediment.
  • Stating earned value as merely a percentage.
  • Placing management reserve inside BAC.
  • Describing all hybrid work as a separate standardized framework.
  • Presenting Atlas-generated crosswalks as official PMI mappings.

docs.title: Sponsor
docs.text:
Source-limited SEM-ROL-SPONSOR

Champions the initiative and connects it to authorization, funding, strategic direction, and escalation authority.

Scope: Commonly associated with authorization, strategic alignment, funding sponsorship, and decisions beyond delegated project authority.

Aliases: project sponsor

Distinctions:

  • The sponsor is not automatically the customer, acceptance authority, operational owner, or benefits owner.
  • Specific approval rights come from the organization's governance model.

Does not mean: Universal owner of every project decision

Applicability: organization specific, common across approaches

Interpretation note: Exact sponsor authority varies by organization and initiative governance.

Canonical public pages: Open reference

Related processes: Develop Project Charter (PRC-DEVELOP-PROJECT-CHARTER); Perform Integrated Change Control (PRC-PERFORM-INTEGRATED-CHANGE-CONTROL); Close Project or Phase (PRC-CLOSE-PROJECT-OR-PHASE)

Related artifacts: Project Charter (ART-CHR-001); Benefits Management Information (ART-BEN-001); Formal Closure Record (ART-CLS-002)

Related lifecycle chapters: Conception and Authorization (LFC-001); Monitoring and Change (LFC-008); Verification, Acceptance, Transition, and Closure (LFC-010)

Related Decision Guides: A Stakeholder Requests a Baseline Change (DEC-CHG-001); Transition or Closure Is Requested with Unresolved Obligations (DEC-CLS-001); Expected Benefits Are Not Yet Realized at Project Closure (DEC-BEN-001)

AI guidance:

  • Use when: Identifying authorization, strategic direction, funding sponsorship, or an escalation destination.
  • Avoid: Do not assign the sponsor every approval or post-project ownership duty.
  • Answer pattern: State the commonly associated purpose, then qualify the exact authority as governance-dependent.

docs.title: Project manager
docs.text:
Source-limited SEM-ROL-PROJECT-MANAGER

Integrates project work, information, and decisions within delegated authority.

Scope: Commonly coordinates planning, execution, monitoring, communication, and escalation across the project system.

Aliases: PM

Distinctions:

  • Integration responsibility does not automatically grant specialist, sponsor, procurement, compliance, or acceptance authority.
  • Matters outside delegated limits are escalated through the governing route.

Does not mean: Universal approver; Sole producer of project work

Applicability: common across approaches, organization specific

Interpretation note: The extent of project-manager decision rights depends on delegated governance.

Canonical public pages: Open reference

Related processes: Develop Project Management Plan (PRC-DEVELOP-PROJECT-MANAGEMENT-PLAN); Direct and Manage Project Work (PRC-DIRECT-AND-MANAGE-PROJECT-WORK); Monitor and Control Project Work (PRC-MONITOR-AND-CONTROL-PROJECT-WORK)

Related artifacts: Project Management Plan (ART-PLN-001); Work Performance Reports (ART-WPR-001); Issue Log (ART-ISS-001)

Related lifecycle chapters: Integrated Planning (LFC-002); Execution and Team Leadership (LFC-007); Monitoring and Change (LFC-008)

Related Decision Guides: A Stakeholder Requests a Baseline Change (DEC-CHG-001); A Risk Occurs or an Impediment Exceeds Team Authority (DEC-ISS-001); Transition or Closure Is Requested with Unresolved Obligations (DEC-CLS-001)

AI guidance:

  • Use when: Explaining integration, coordination, analysis, routing, and escalation.
  • Avoid: Do not infer unrestricted authority from the role title.
  • Answer pattern: Describe integration responsibility and name the authority boundary relevant to the scenario.

docs.title: Project team
docs.text:
Source-limited SEM-ROL-PROJECT-TEAM

Performs and coordinates project work, contributes estimates and evidence, and resolves matters within team authority.

Scope: Commonly owns execution details, collaboration, learning, and evidence produced by the work.

Aliases: team, delivery team

Distinctions:

  • Self-management may shape how work is performed without removing external governance or acceptance limits.

Does not mean: Freedom from governance; Automatic formal acceptance authority

Applicability: common across approaches, organization specific

Interpretation note: Team composition and decision rights are tailored to the delivery and governance model.

Canonical public pages: Open reference

Related processes: Direct and Manage Project Work (PRC-DIRECT-AND-MANAGE-PROJECT-WORK); Develop Team (PRC-DEVELOP-TEAM); Manage Team (PRC-MANAGE-TEAM)

Related artifacts: Deliverables (ART-DEL-001); Lessons Learned Register (ART-INT-002); Impediment Record (ART-ISS-002)

Related lifecycle chapters: Execution and Team Leadership (LFC-007); Adaptive and Hybrid Delivery (LFC-009)

Related Decision Guides: A Deliverable Fails Quality Inspection (DEC-QLT-001); A Risk Occurs or an Impediment Exceeds Team Authority (DEC-ISS-001)

AI guidance:

  • Use when: Explaining who performs work, estimates, collaborates, or removes team-level constraints.
  • Avoid: Do not treat self-management as unlimited organizational authority.
  • Answer pattern: State the team's work purpose and separate team authority from external decision rights.

docs.title: Product owner
docs.text:
Source-limited SEM-ROL-PRODUCT-OWNER

In product-oriented adaptive contexts, orders value-focused work and makes product decisions within the governing model.

Scope: Most precise as a Scrum accountability; other adaptive approaches may use different product roles.

Aliases: PO

Distinctions:

  • Product prioritization is separate from technical verification and formal acceptance unless governance explicitly combines them.

Does not mean: Generic name for every adaptive leader; Automatic formal acceptance authority

Applicability: scrum specific, adaptive, hybrid, organization specific

Interpretation note: Product-role naming and authority vary outside Scrum and across organizations.

Canonical public pages: Open reference

Related processes: Direct and Manage Project Work (PRC-DIRECT-AND-MANAGE-PROJECT-WORK); Manage Stakeholder Engagement (PRC-MANAGE-STAKEHOLDER-ENGAGEMENT)

Related artifacts: Requirements Documentation (ART-REQ-001); Deliverables (ART-DEL-001); Impediment Record (ART-ISS-002)

Related lifecycle chapters: Execution and Team Leadership (LFC-007); Adaptive and Hybrid Delivery (LFC-009)

Related Decision Guides: A Risk Occurs or an Impediment Exceeds Team Authority (DEC-ISS-001); A Verified Deliverable Is Rejected During Acceptance (DEC-ACC-001)

AI guidance:

  • Use when: A Scrum or product-oriented context explicitly assigns value ordering or product decisions.
  • Avoid: Do not generalize the accountability to all adaptive delivery or formal acceptance.
  • Answer pattern: Name the framework or governance context before describing product-owner authority.

docs.title: Customer or acceptance authority
docs.text:
Source-limited SEM-ROL-ACCEPTANCE-AUTHORITY

Formally accepts verified deliverables or scope results under the applicable agreement or governance model.

Scope: Commonly associated with the decision that completed, verified results satisfy agreed acceptance criteria.

Aliases: customer, acceptance authority, accepting authority

Distinctions:

  • Technical verification and formal acceptance are separate states and decisions.

Does not mean: Quality inspector; Automatic sponsor or product owner

Applicability: common across approaches, organization specific

Interpretation note: The accepting party and evidence required depend on governance and agreements.

Canonical public pages: Open reference

Related processes: Validate Scope (PRC-VALIDATE-SCOPE); Control Quality (PRC-CONTROL-QUALITY); Close Project or Phase (PRC-CLOSE-PROJECT-OR-PHASE)

Related artifacts: Verified Deliverables (ART-QLT-004); Accepted Deliverables (ART-QLT-005); Formal Closure Record (ART-CLS-002)

Related lifecycle chapters: Quality (LFC-005); Verification, Acceptance, Transition, and Closure (LFC-010)

Related Decision Guides: A Verified Deliverable Is Rejected During Acceptance (DEC-ACC-001); Transition or Closure Is Requested with Unresolved Obligations (DEC-CLS-001)

AI guidance:

  • Use when: Explaining formal acceptance after technical verification.
  • Avoid: Do not collapse verification into acceptance or invent the accepting role.
  • Answer pattern: Identify the verified state, acceptance criteria, and governance-designated decision maker.

docs.title: Governance body
docs.text:
Source-limited SEM-ROL-GOVERNANCE-BODY

Provides organizational direction and decisions under the initiative's governance model.

Scope: May decide funding, continuation, exceptions, baselines, escalation, or closure when those rights are explicitly assigned.

Aliases: steering committee, governing body

Distinctions:

  • Its mandate is defined by organizational governance rather than by a universal Atlas rule.

Does not mean: A required committee with identical powers in every organization

Applicability: organization specific, common across approaches

Interpretation note: Governance structures and mandates are organization-specific.

Canonical public pages: Open reference

Related processes: Develop Project Charter (PRC-DEVELOP-PROJECT-CHARTER); Perform Integrated Change Control (PRC-PERFORM-INTEGRATED-CHANGE-CONTROL); Close Project or Phase (PRC-CLOSE-PROJECT-OR-PHASE)

Related artifacts: Project Charter (ART-CHR-001); Project Management Plan (ART-PLN-001); Formal Closure Record (ART-CLS-002)

Related lifecycle chapters: Conception and Authorization (LFC-001); Monitoring and Change (LFC-008); Verification, Acceptance, Transition, and Closure (LFC-010)

Related Decision Guides: A Stakeholder Requests a Baseline Change (DEC-CHG-001); A Compliance Problem Is Discovered (DEC-CMP-001); Transition or Closure Is Requested with Unresolved Obligations (DEC-CLS-001)

AI guidance:

  • Use when: A decision exceeds delegated project, team, or specialist authority.
  • Avoid: Do not assume a committee exists or assign it unstated powers.
  • Answer pattern: Refer to the designated governance route and qualify its authority as organization-specific.

docs.title: Change-control authority or CCB
docs.text:
Source-limited SEM-ROL-CHANGE-AUTHORITY

Evaluates and disposes controlled changes within an approved mandate.

Scope: Commonly decides changes that affect controlled commitments, baselines, or other governance thresholds.

Aliases: change authority, change control board, CCB

Distinctions:

  • A standing CCB is one governance design; change authority may be assigned differently.

Does not mean: Required review body for every adaptive reprioritization

Applicability: predictive, hybrid, organization specific

Interpretation note: Thresholds and decision rights are defined by the governing change-control model.

Canonical public pages: Open reference

Related processes: Monitor and Control Project Work (PRC-MONITOR-AND-CONTROL-PROJECT-WORK); Perform Integrated Change Control (PRC-PERFORM-INTEGRATED-CHANGE-CONTROL)

Related artifacts: Change Requests (ART-CHG-001); Change Log (ART-CHG-004); Project Management Plan (ART-PLN-001)

Related lifecycle chapters: Monitoring and Change (LFC-008); Adaptive and Hybrid Delivery (LFC-009)

Related Decision Guides: A Stakeholder Requests a Baseline Change (DEC-CHG-001); A Compliance Problem Is Discovered (DEC-CMP-001)

AI guidance:

  • Use when: A proposed action may alter a controlled baseline or commitment.
  • Avoid: Do not require CCB review for every work-level adjustment.
  • Answer pattern: Identify the controlled commitment, threshold, and designated change authority.

docs.title: Operational owner
docs.text:
Source-limited SEM-ROL-OPERATIONAL-OWNER

Accepts operational responsibility for transferred outputs, support, controls, and residual obligations.

Scope: Commonly associated with transition readiness and continuing operation after handoff.

Aliases: operations owner, receiving owner

Distinctions:

  • Operational ownership is distinct from formal project closure and benefits ownership.

Does not mean: Universal post-project benefits owner

Applicability: organization specific, common across approaches

Interpretation note: The receiving organization and its authority are organization-specific.

Canonical public pages: Open reference

Related processes: Close Project or Phase (PRC-CLOSE-PROJECT-OR-PHASE)

Related artifacts: Transition Package (ART-TRN-001); Final Report (ART-CLS-001); Formal Closure Record (ART-CLS-002)

Related lifecycle chapters: Verification, Acceptance, Transition, and Closure (LFC-010)

Related Decision Guides: Transition or Closure Is Requested with Unresolved Obligations (DEC-CLS-001); Expected Benefits Are Not Yet Realized at Project Closure (DEC-BEN-001)

AI guidance:

  • Use when: Explaining transition, operational readiness, or post-transfer support responsibility.
  • Avoid: Do not assume operations also owns every intended benefit.
  • Answer pattern: Name the receiving role, transferred responsibilities, evidence, and unresolved obligations.

docs.title: Benefits owner
docs.text:
Source-limited SEM-ROL-BENEFITS-OWNER

Owns defined benefit measures, dependencies, reviews, and continuing action after explicit handoff.

Scope: Commonly associated with measurement and action after outputs transition into use.

Aliases: benefit owner

Distinctions:

  • The project manager does not universally retain this role after formal closure.

Does not mean: A universal authority model prescribed by the Atlas

Applicability: organization specific, common across approaches

Interpretation note: Post-project benefits authority depends on the organizational operating model.

Canonical public pages: Open reference

Related processes: Develop Project Charter (PRC-DEVELOP-PROJECT-CHARTER); Close Project or Phase (PRC-CLOSE-PROJECT-OR-PHASE)

Related artifacts: Benefits Management Information (ART-BEN-001); Benefits Handoff Record (ART-BEN-002); Formal Closure Record (ART-CLS-002)

Related lifecycle chapters: Conception and Authorization (LFC-001); Verification, Acceptance, Transition, and Closure (LFC-010)

Related Decision Guides: Expected Benefits Are Not Yet Realized at Project Closure (DEC-BEN-001)

AI guidance:

  • Use when: Explaining who continues measurement after project closure.
  • Avoid: Do not assign continuing benefits ownership to the project manager by default.
  • Answer pattern: Identify the explicit owner, measures, dates, dependencies, and escalation route.

docs.title: Quality authority
docs.text:
Source-limited SEM-ROL-QUALITY-AUTHORITY

Determines or advises whether defined quality criteria and verification requirements are satisfied within an assigned mandate.

Scope: May be advisory, performing, approving, or auditing depending on the quality system.

Aliases: quality approver, quality reviewer

Distinctions:

  • Technical verification does not itself create formal customer acceptance.

Does not mean: Acceptance authority; Universal owner of corrective action

Applicability: organization specific, common across approaches

Interpretation note: The quality role's mandate depends on the organization's quality system.

Canonical public pages: Open reference

Related processes: Plan Quality Management (PRC-PLAN-QUALITY-MANAGEMENT); Manage Quality (PRC-MANAGE-QUALITY); Control Quality (PRC-CONTROL-QUALITY)

Related artifacts: Quality Management Plan (ART-QLT-001); Quality-Control Measurements (ART-QLT-003); Verified Deliverables (ART-QLT-004)

Related lifecycle chapters: Quality (LFC-005); Verification, Acceptance, Transition, and Closure (LFC-010)

Related Decision Guides: A Deliverable Fails Quality Inspection (DEC-QLT-001); A Verified Deliverable Is Rejected During Acceptance (DEC-ACC-001); A Compliance Problem Is Discovered (DEC-CMP-001)

AI guidance:

  • Use when: Explaining technical criteria, inspection, testing, or verification decisions.
  • Avoid: Do not equate verification authority with formal acceptance authority.
  • Answer pattern: State the quality decision and then identify any separate acceptance or change decision.

docs.title: Risk authority
docs.text:
Source-limited SEM-ROL-RISK-AUTHORITY

Owns or decides risk action, acceptance, escalation, or reporting within an assigned risk-governance mandate.

Scope: May include individual risk owners, project risk leadership, or governance-level risk decision makers.

Aliases: risk owner, risk approver

Distinctions:

  • Risk ownership and authority to accept exposure may be assigned to different roles.

Does not mean: One universal role for every risk decision

Applicability: organization specific, common across approaches

Interpretation note: Risk thresholds, ownership, and acceptance authority vary by governance model.

Canonical public pages: Open reference

Related processes: Plan Risk Management (PRC-PLAN-RISK-MANAGEMENT); Identify Risks (PRC-IDENTIFY-RISKS); Monitor Risks (PRC-MONITOR-RISKS)

Related artifacts: Risk Register (ART-RSK-001); Risk Report (ART-RSK-003); Issue Log (ART-ISS-001)

Related lifecycle chapters: Risk, Compliance, and Procurement (LFC-006); Monitoring and Change (LFC-008)

Related Decision Guides: A Risk Occurs or an Impediment Exceeds Team Authority (DEC-ISS-001); A Compliance Problem Is Discovered (DEC-CMP-001)

AI guidance:

  • Use when: Explaining risk ownership, escalation, response, or exposure acceptance.
  • Avoid: Do not assume the named risk owner can accept every level of exposure.
  • Answer pattern: Separate action ownership from the authority to accept or escalate exposure.

docs.title: Compliance authority
docs.text:
Source-limited SEM-ROL-COMPLIANCE-AUTHORITY

Determines the sufficiency of compliance evidence or routes exception decisions within the applicable legal, regulatory, contractual, and organizational environment.

Scope: Authority may be internal, external, advisory, approving, auditing, or controlling.

Aliases: regulatory authority, compliance approver

Distinctions:

  • Compliance obligations can affect scope
  • risk
  • quality
  • procurement
  • acceptance
  • transition
  • and closure.

Does not mean: Quality-team preference; Universal permission to waive an obligation

Applicability: organization specific, context specific

Interpretation note: Exact authority comes from the obligation and governing environment.

Canonical public pages: Open reference

Related processes: Control Quality (PRC-CONTROL-QUALITY); Control Procurements (PRC-CONTROL-PROCUREMENTS); Validate Scope (PRC-VALIDATE-SCOPE)

Related artifacts: Compliance Evidence and Traceability (ART-CMP-001); Test and Evaluation Documents (ART-QLT-007); Issue Log (ART-ISS-001)

Related lifecycle chapters: Quality (LFC-005); Risk, Compliance, and Procurement (LFC-006); Verification, Acceptance, Transition, and Closure (LFC-010)

Related Decision Guides: A Compliance Problem Is Discovered (DEC-CMP-001); Transition or Closure Is Requested with Unresolved Obligations (DEC-CLS-001)

AI guidance:

  • Use when: An obligation, evidence gap, exception, release, or stop-work decision is involved.
  • Avoid: Do not invent an exception right or treat compliance as optional quality guidance.
  • Answer pattern: Trace the obligation and evidence, then name the designated decision or escalation route.

docs.title: Procurement authority
docs.text:
Source-limited SEM-ROL-PROCUREMENT-AUTHORITY

Exercises sourcing, agreement, remedy, change, or closure rights within an assigned commercial mandate.

Scope: Commonly associated with procurement strategy, source selection, agreements, seller administration, and commercial closure.

Aliases: contract authority, commercial authority

Distinctions:

  • The project manager integrates project impacts but does not automatically hold commercial authority.

Does not mean: Universal owner of seller work; Automatic project change authority

Applicability: organization specific, context specific

Interpretation note: Commercial decision rights depend on agreements and organizational delegation.

Canonical public pages: Open reference

Related processes: Plan Procurement Management (PRC-PLAN-PROCUREMENT-MANAGEMENT); Conduct Procurements (PRC-CONDUCT-PROCUREMENTS); Control Procurements (PRC-CONTROL-PROCUREMENTS)

Related artifacts: Agreements (ART-PRC-003); Procurement Strategy (ART-PRC-004); Closed Procurement (ART-PRC-007)

Related lifecycle chapters: Risk, Compliance, and Procurement (LFC-006); Verification, Acceptance, Transition, and Closure (LFC-010)

Related Decision Guides: Seller Performance Threatens Project Objectives (DEC-PRC-001); A Compliance Problem Is Discovered (DEC-CMP-001); Transition or Closure Is Requested with Unresolved Obligations (DEC-CLS-001)

AI guidance:

  • Use when: A sourcing, agreement, remedy, seller, or commercial closure decision is involved.
  • Avoid: Do not assign contract rights to the project manager without evidence.
  • Answer pattern: Identify the agreement right, commercial mandate, and project-impact coordination required.

docs.title: Stakeholder Engagement Assessment Matrix
docs.text:
Verified SEM-STK-ENGAGEMENT-ASSESSMENT-MATRIX

A working assessment that compares each stakeholder identifier's current and desired engagement state so the team can identify gaps and tailor engagement actions.

Scope: The matrix uses Unaware, Resistant, Neutral, Supportive, and Leading states with C for current, D for desired, and C/D when the states are the same; identifiers should replace personal names where assessment information is sensitive.

Aliases: stakeholder engagement assessment, current-and-desired engagement matrix

Distinctions:

  • The matrix assesses engagement state; the Stakeholder Register owns stakeholder identity, influence, authority, and broader profile information.
  • The matrix informs the Stakeholder Engagement Plan but is not the plan itself.
  • The matrix may inform communication choices but is not the Communications Management Plan.
  • A power-interest or similar stakeholder grid classifies influence or interest; it does not show current-versus-desired engagement.
  • The matrix is a working assessment tool and is not asserted as a formal process output.

Does not mean: Stakeholder Register; Stakeholder Engagement Plan; Communications Management Plan; Power-interest grid; Formal process output

Applicability: predictive, adaptive, hybrid, context specific

Interpretation note: Lesson 3 supports the five-state current-versus-desired model; the extended evidence, action, owner, and review fields are clearly identified as an Atlas working-resource design.

Canonical public pages: Open reference

Related processes: Identify Stakeholders (PRC-IDENTIFY-STAKEHOLDERS); Plan Stakeholder Engagement (PRC-PLAN-STAKEHOLDER-ENGAGEMENT); Manage Stakeholder Engagement (PRC-MANAGE-STAKEHOLDER-ENGAGEMENT); Monitor Stakeholder Engagement (PRC-MONITOR-STAKEHOLDER-ENGAGEMENT); Plan Communications Management (PRC-PLAN-COMMUNICATIONS-MANAGEMENT); Manage Communications (PRC-MANAGE-COMMUNICATIONS); Monitor Communications (PRC-MONITOR-COMMUNICATIONS)

Related artifacts: Stakeholder Register (ART-STK-001); Stakeholder Engagement Plan (ART-STK-002); Communications Management Plan (ART-COM-001); Issue Log (ART-ISS-001); Risk Register (ART-RSK-001); Lessons Learned Register (ART-INT-002); Change Requests (ART-CHG-001); Stakeholder Engagement Assessment Matrix (ART-STK-003)

Related lifecycle chapters: Integrated Planning (LFC-002); Execution and Team Leadership (LFC-007); Monitoring and Change (LFC-008); Adaptive and Hybrid Delivery (LFC-009)

AI guidance:

  • Use when: Comparing observed stakeholder engagement with the engagement needed for project success or explaining the resulting engagement gap.
  • Avoid: Do not expose sensitive personal assessments, substitute the matrix for its related registers or plans, or present it as a required formal output in every delivery approach.
  • Answer pattern: Define the five states and C/D markers, explain the gap, then distinguish the matrix from the register, engagement plan, communications plan, and influence-interest grids.

docs.title: Predictive
docs.text:
Atlas synthesis SEM-DEL-PREDICTIVE

A delivery approach that establishes a comparatively broad authorized plan and baselines when work can be usefully defined in advance.

Scope: Planning and control are tailored; prediction does not eliminate iteration, learning, or change.

Aliases: predictive delivery

Distinctions:

  • Predictive is a delivery approach
  • not a claim that the future is perfectly known.

Does not mean: No iteration; No change

Applicability: predictive

Interpretation note: The concise contrast is an Atlas synthesis of the registered delivery-approach source set.

Canonical public pages: Open reference

Related processes: Develop Project Management Plan (PRC-DEVELOP-PROJECT-MANAGEMENT-PLAN); Perform Integrated Change Control (PRC-PERFORM-INTEGRATED-CHANGE-CONTROL)

Related artifacts: Project Management Plan (ART-PLN-001); Scope Baseline (ART-SCP-001); Schedule Baseline (ART-SCH-005); Cost Baseline (ART-CST-002)

Related lifecycle chapters: Integrated Planning (LFC-002); Adaptive and Hybrid Delivery (LFC-009)

AI guidance:

  • Use when: Work can be planned comparatively broadly and governed through authorized plans or baselines.
  • Avoid: Do not describe predictive delivery as non-iterative or immune to change.
  • Answer pattern: Describe the planning horizon, control model, and tailoring context.

docs.title: Waterfall
docs.text:
Source-limited SEM-DEL-WATERFALL

A familiar explanatory label for a comparatively sequential form of predictive delivery.

Scope: Useful as a plain-language label when sequence and phase completion are emphasized.

Aliases: waterfall delivery

Distinctions:

  • Waterfall is related to predictive delivery but is not a synonym for every predictive implementation.

Does not mean: Every predictive project

Applicability: predictive, context specific

Interpretation note: The registered sources support predictive terminology more directly than the informal waterfall label.

Canonical public pages: Open reference

Related lifecycle chapters: Adaptive and Hybrid Delivery (LFC-009)

AI guidance:

  • Use when: A source or user explicitly uses waterfall to describe sequential predictive delivery.
  • Avoid: Do not substitute waterfall for every predictive approach.
  • Answer pattern: Treat waterfall as a familiar related label and prefer predictive for the broader category.

docs.title: Adaptive
docs.text:
Atlas synthesis SEM-DEL-ADAPTIVE

A delivery approach using short planning and delivery horizons with frequent review when learning and change are expected.

Scope: Includes multiple frameworks and methods; form, cadence, roles, and artifacts vary.

Aliases: adaptive delivery

Distinctions:

  • Adaptive is broader than Scrum or Kanban.

Does not mean: Scrum only; Kanban only; No governance

Applicability: adaptive

Interpretation note: Cross-approach process applicability is Atlas synthesis, not an official PMI agile crosswalk.

Canonical public pages: Open reference

Related processes: Collect Requirements (PRC-COLLECT-REQUIREMENTS); Direct and Manage Project Work (PRC-DIRECT-AND-MANAGE-PROJECT-WORK); Monitor and Control Project Work (PRC-MONITOR-AND-CONTROL-PROJECT-WORK)

Related artifacts: Requirements Documentation (ART-REQ-001); Deliverables (ART-DEL-001); Impediment Record (ART-ISS-002)

Related lifecycle chapters: Adaptive and Hybrid Delivery (LFC-009)

AI guidance:

  • Use when: Learning, feedback, and changing priorities call for short planning and delivery horizons.
  • Avoid: Do not infer one mandatory framework or remove governance constraints.
  • Answer pattern: Describe the feedback cadence and tailored roles, artifacts, and controls.

docs.title: Agile
docs.text:
Source-limited SEM-DEL-AGILE

A broad family of values, principles, and practices associated with adaptive and iterative delivery.

Scope: Use as a broad orientation unless a specific framework or method is named.

Aliases: agile delivery

Distinctions:

  • Agile is not interchangeable with Scrum
  • Kanban
  • or every adaptive implementation.

Does not mean: Scrum; Kanban; Absence of planning

Applicability: adaptive, hybrid, context specific

Interpretation note: The term is used broadly; specific claims require a named framework or method source.

Canonical public pages: Open reference

Related lifecycle chapters: Adaptive and Hybrid Delivery (LFC-009)

AI guidance:

  • Use when: Referring broadly to adaptive values and practices without asserting a specific framework mechanic.
  • Avoid: Do not attribute Scrum- or Kanban-specific rules to all agile work.
  • Answer pattern: Use the broad term, then name the specific approach when mechanics matter.

docs.title: Hybrid
docs.text:
Atlas synthesis SEM-DEL-HYBRID

A delivery approach that deliberately combines cadences or governance models and defines how their evidence and decisions reconnect.

Scope: May combine adaptive product delivery with predictive funding, milestones, contracts, compliance, transition, or governance.

Aliases: hybrid delivery

Distinctions:

  • Hybrid is a delivery approach
  • not a separate standardized set of 49 PMI processes.

Does not mean: A universal framework; A separate process catalog

Applicability: hybrid

Interpretation note: Atlas mappings describe management-purpose applicability and are not official PMI framework crosswalks.

Canonical public pages: Open reference

Related processes: Develop Project Management Plan (PRC-DEVELOP-PROJECT-MANAGEMENT-PLAN); Direct and Manage Project Work (PRC-DIRECT-AND-MANAGE-PROJECT-WORK); Perform Integrated Change Control (PRC-PERFORM-INTEGRATED-CHANGE-CONTROL)

Related artifacts: Project Management Plan (ART-PLN-001); Deliverables (ART-DEL-001); Change Requests (ART-CHG-001)

Related lifecycle chapters: Adaptive and Hybrid Delivery (LFC-009)

AI guidance:

  • Use when: Different components or governance levels intentionally use different cadences or controls.
  • Avoid: Do not present hybrid as one standardized framework or a second process set.
  • Answer pattern: Name the combined approaches and explain how evidence, authority, and decisions reconnect.

docs.title: Scrum-specific
docs.text:
Source-limited SEM-DEL-SCRUM

Refers to accountabilities, events, artifacts, or rules specific to Scrum; the informal phrase Agile ceremonies often means Scrum events but is not a universal agile meeting set.

Scope: Use only when the framework context is explicit and the claim is actually Scrum-specific.

Aliases: Scrum, Agile ceremonies

Distinctions:

  • Scrum is one framework within the broader adaptive landscape.
  • Scrum defines events; backlog refinement is ongoing activity rather than a formal event.

Does not mean: All adaptive work; All agile work

Applicability: scrum specific, adaptive, hybrid

Interpretation note: Framework-specific mechanics should be verified against an applicable Scrum source before being asserted.

Canonical public pages: Open reference

Related lifecycle chapters: Adaptive and Hybrid Delivery (LFC-009)

AI guidance:

  • Use when: The framework is explicitly Scrum and the concept is one of its defined mechanics.
  • Avoid: Do not generalize Scrum accountabilities, events, or artifacts to all adaptive delivery.
  • Answer pattern: Label the statement Scrum-specific and separate it from broader adaptive guidance.

docs.title: Kanban-specific
docs.text:
Source-limited SEM-DEL-KANBAN

Refers to flow-oriented practices such as visualization, work-in-progress control, pull, and flow measures in a Kanban context.

Scope: Use when the method or practice context is explicit.

Aliases: Kanban

Distinctions:

  • Kanban is not a synonym for every visual board or every adaptive approach.

Does not mean: All adaptive work; Any task board

Applicability: kanban specific, adaptive, hybrid

Interpretation note: Method-specific mechanics require an applicable Kanban source before being asserted.

Canonical public pages: Open reference

Related lifecycle chapters: Adaptive and Hybrid Delivery (LFC-009)

AI guidance:

  • Use when: Flow, pull, WIP limits, or Kanban measures are explicitly in scope.
  • Avoid: Do not label every board or adaptive practice Kanban.
  • Answer pattern: Name the flow practice and keep it distinct from broader adaptive terminology.

docs.title: Common across approaches
docs.text:
Atlas synthesis SEM-DEL-COMMON

The management purpose remains broadly applicable even when form, cadence, ownership, or storage changes.

Scope: An Atlas applicability label used to describe a persistent management need across delivery approaches.

Aliases: common applicability

Distinctions:

  • Missing applicability means insufficient mapping
  • not prohibition.

Does not mean: Identical implementation; Official PMI process-to-agile mapping

Applicability: common across approaches

Interpretation note: Applicability mappings are an Atlas synthesis where the sources do not provide an official PMI agile crosswalk.

Canonical public pages: Open reference

Related processes: Identify Stakeholders (PRC-IDENTIFY-STAKEHOLDERS); Manage Communications (PRC-MANAGE-COMMUNICATIONS); Monitor Risks (PRC-MONITOR-RISKS)

Related lifecycle chapters: Project Start to Completion (LFC-000); Adaptive and Hybrid Delivery (LFC-009)

AI guidance:

  • Use when: The underlying management purpose persists across approaches with tailored implementation.
  • Avoid: Do not imply identical artifacts, roles, cadence, or storage.
  • Answer pattern: State the common purpose and then describe how implementation may vary.

docs.title: Velocity
docs.text:
Verified SEM-MET-VELOCITY

Estimated work fully completed by one team during one iteration in that team's chosen estimation unit.

Scope: Concise semantic entry only; the Adaptive Metrics registry owns calculation, examples, and misuse boundaries.

Aliases: iteration velocity, Sprint velocity

Distinctions:

  • Only Done work counts.
  • Team-specific story points are not hours or comparable across teams.

Does not mean: Productivity; Partial-completion credit

Applicability: adaptive, scrum specific, hybrid, context specific

Canonical public pages: Open reference

AI guidance:

  • Use when: Same-team iteration forecasting is in scope.
  • Avoid: Never compare teams or count unfinished work.
  • Answer pattern: Define the team and iteration and link to the canonical metric page.

docs.title: Throughput
docs.text:
Verified SEM-MET-THROUGHPUT

The exact count of work items finished per unit of time.

Scope: Canonical mechanics and example remain in the Adaptive Metrics registry.

Aliases: delivery rate

Distinctions:

  • Counts items rather than story points.
  • The time period must be stated.

Does not mean: Velocity

Applicability: adaptive, kanban specific, hybrid

Canonical public pages: Open reference

AI guidance:

  • Use when: Finished-item flow rate is in scope.
  • Avoid: Do not omit the time unit.
  • Answer pattern: State the item count and observation period.

docs.title: Cycle time
docs.text:
Verified SEM-MET-CYCLE-TIME

Elapsed time from when a work item started until it finished.

Scope: Requires explicit workflow start and finish points.

Aliases: cycle time

Distinctions:

  • Includes active work and waiting inside the measured workflow.

Does not mean: Lead time with an earlier request start

Applicability: adaptive, kanban specific, hybrid

Canonical public pages: Open reference

AI guidance:

  • Use when: Flow elapsed time is discussed.
  • Avoid: Do not compare undefined endpoints.
  • Answer pattern: Name the workflow start and finish.

docs.title: Lead time
docs.text:
Verified SEM-MET-LEAD-TIME

Elapsed time from a defined request, order, or commitment point until delivery.

Scope: The selected start and finish points must be stated; the Adaptive Metrics registry separately owns customer, commitment, procurement, and schedule-lead distinctions.

Aliases: customer lead time, commitment lead time

Distinctions:

  • May include waiting before active work.
  • It is at least cycle time only when the finish is shared and its start is earlier.
  • Predictive schedule lead is a precedence adjustment rather than this elapsed metric.

Does not mean: Cycle time unless endpoints match; Schedule lead

Applicability: adaptive, hybrid, context specific

Canonical public pages: Open reference

AI guidance:

  • Use when: Customer commitment or procurement responsiveness is discussed.
  • Avoid: Do not leave boundaries implicit or confuse elapsed lead time with schedule lead.
  • Answer pattern: State start finish and time convention.

docs.title: Burndown
docs.text:
Verified SEM-MET-BURNDOWN

A chart of work remaining over time.

Scope: Canonical chart mechanics and shared example data remain in the Adaptive Metrics registry.

Aliases: burndown chart

Distinctions:

  • Scope additions can make the remaining-work line rise.

Does not mean: A mandatory commitment line

Applicability: adaptive, scrum specific, hybrid, context specific

Canonical public pages: Open reference

AI guidance:

  • Use when: Remaining work over time is discussed.
  • Avoid: Do not hide changing total scope.
  • Answer pattern: Name the work unit horizon and scope convention.

docs.title: Burnup
docs.text:
Verified SEM-MET-BURNUP

A chart of completed work increasing toward a separately displayed total-scope line.

Scope: Canonical chart mechanics and shared example data remain in the Adaptive Metrics registry.

Aliases: burnup chart

Distinctions:

  • A separate scope line makes scope change explicit.

Does not mean: Burndown

Applicability: adaptive, scrum specific, hybrid, context specific

Canonical public pages: Open reference

AI guidance:

  • Use when: Completed work and total scope are plotted together.
  • Avoid: Do not omit the total-scope series.
  • Answer pattern: Distinguish completed work from current total scope.

docs.title: Cumulative flow diagram
docs.text:
Verified SEM-MET-CFD

A stacked view of cumulative work-item counts in workflow states over time.

Scope: Canonical interpretation and example remain in the Adaptive Metrics registry.

Aliases: CFD

Distinctions:

  • Band thickness represents inventory in a state.
  • A widening band can signal accumulation.

Does not mean: Proof of a bottleneck cause

Applicability: adaptive, kanban specific, hybrid

Canonical public pages: Open reference

AI guidance:

  • Use when: Workflow-state accumulation over time is discussed.
  • Avoid: Do not infer causation from one diagram.
  • Answer pattern: Name the state band and the observed pattern.

docs.title: Information radiator
docs.text:
Verified SEM-MET-RADIATOR

A highly visible and current display of information useful to a team and stakeholders.

Scope: A category of visual management rather than one required chart type.

Aliases: visible information display

Distinctions:

  • It should support conversation and action.
  • Digital displays can serve distributed teams.

Does not mean: One specific chart; A useful display when stale

Applicability: common across approaches, adaptive, hybrid, context specific

Canonical public pages: Open reference

AI guidance:

  • Use when: Highly visible current team information is discussed.
  • Avoid: Do not define it as one chart type.
  • Answer pattern: Name audience currency and intended action.

docs.title: Risk
docs.text:
Verified SEM-STATE-RISK

An uncertain event or condition that can affect objectives.

Scope: Tracked while uncertainty remains and analyzed, owned, responded to, and monitored according to the risk approach.

Aliases: project risk

Distinctions:

  • A realized risk may become an issue; not every issue began as a risk.

Does not mean: A current problem already requiring corrective action

Applicability: common across approaches

Canonical public pages: Open reference

Related processes: Identify Risks (PRC-IDENTIFY-RISKS); Plan Risk Responses (PRC-PLAN-RISK-RESPONSES); Monitor Risks (PRC-MONITOR-RISKS)

Related artifacts: Risk Register (ART-RSK-001); Risk Report (ART-RSK-003); Issue Log (ART-ISS-001)

Related lifecycle chapters: Risk, Compliance, and Procurement (LFC-006); Monitoring and Change (LFC-008)

Related Decision Guides: A Risk Occurs or an Impediment Exceeds Team Authority (DEC-ISS-001)

AI guidance:

  • Use when: The event or condition is still uncertain.
  • Avoid: Do not keep describing an occurred condition only as uncertain.
  • Answer pattern: State the uncertainty, objective effect, owner, response, and monitoring route.

docs.title: Issue
docs.text:
Verified SEM-STATE-ISSUE

A current condition requiring action, ownership, and possibly escalation or change.

Scope: Captures current problems, decisions, or conditions that need resolution and traceability.

Aliases: current issue

Distinctions:

  • A realized risk may create an issue
  • but not every issue began as a risk.

Does not mean: An uncertain future event

Applicability: common across approaches

Canonical public pages: Open reference

Related processes: Monitor and Control Project Work (PRC-MONITOR-AND-CONTROL-PROJECT-WORK); Manage Team (PRC-MANAGE-TEAM)

Related artifacts: Issue Log (ART-ISS-001); Risk Register (ART-RSK-001); Change Requests (ART-CHG-001)

Related lifecycle chapters: Execution and Team Leadership (LFC-007); Monitoring and Change (LFC-008)

Related Decision Guides: A Risk Occurs or an Impediment Exceeds Team Authority (DEC-ISS-001); A Compliance Problem Is Discovered (DEC-CMP-001)

AI guidance:

  • Use when: A present condition requires action or a decision.
  • Avoid: Do not require every issue to have originated as a registered risk.
  • Answer pattern: State the current condition, owner, action, due route, and escalation threshold.

docs.title: Impediment
docs.text:
Verified SEM-STATE-IMPEDIMENT

Something currently blocking or slowing work.

Scope: May be removed within team authority or tracked through issue management when broader action or traceability is required.

Aliases: blocker, flow constraint

Distinctions:

  • Impediment terminology is not exclusive to Scrum.

Does not mean: Every risk; Scrum-only record

Applicability: common across approaches, adaptive, hybrid

Canonical public pages: Open reference

Related processes: Manage Team (PRC-MANAGE-TEAM); Monitor and Control Project Work (PRC-MONITOR-AND-CONTROL-PROJECT-WORK)

Related artifacts: Impediment Record (ART-ISS-002); Issue Log (ART-ISS-001); Change Requests (ART-CHG-001)

Related lifecycle chapters: Execution and Team Leadership (LFC-007); Monitoring and Change (LFC-008); Adaptive and Hybrid Delivery (LFC-009)

Related Decision Guides: A Risk Occurs or an Impediment Exceeds Team Authority (DEC-ISS-001)

AI guidance:

  • Use when: Something presently blocks or slows work.
  • Avoid: Do not restrict the term to Scrum or treat every impediment as a baseline change.
  • Answer pattern: State the constraint, owner, removal path, and when it becomes a broader issue.

docs.title: Compliance traceability
docs.text:
Atlas synthesis SEM-CMP-TRACEABILITY

A cross-cutting evidence chain connecting an obligation to implementation, verification, acceptance, transition, and closure records.

Scope: Obligation or requirement → scope and acceptance criteria → risk and planning → quality and test evidence → procurement or agreement obligation where relevant → verification → acceptance → transition and closure evidence.

Aliases: compliance evidence chain

Distinctions:

  • Compliance is not one isolated process.
  • Exact authority depends on the regulatory, contractual, and organizational environment.

Does not mean: One universal compliance framework; Permission to omit specialist review

Applicability: context specific, common across approaches

Interpretation note: The chain organizes registered evidence without claiming one universal compliance method.

Canonical public pages: Open reference

Related processes: Collect Requirements (PRC-COLLECT-REQUIREMENTS); Plan Quality Management (PRC-PLAN-QUALITY-MANAGEMENT); Control Quality (PRC-CONTROL-QUALITY); Control Procurements (PRC-CONTROL-PROCUREMENTS); Validate Scope (PRC-VALIDATE-SCOPE); Close Project or Phase (PRC-CLOSE-PROJECT-OR-PHASE)

Related artifacts: Requirements Documentation (ART-REQ-001); Requirements Traceability Matrix (ART-REQ-002); Risk Register (ART-RSK-001); Test and Evaluation Documents (ART-QLT-007); Compliance Evidence and Traceability (ART-CMP-001); Agreements (ART-PRC-003); Accepted Deliverables (ART-QLT-005); Transition Package (ART-TRN-001); Formal Closure Record (ART-CLS-002)

Related lifecycle chapters: Requirements and Scope (LFC-003); Quality (LFC-005); Risk, Compliance, and Procurement (LFC-006); Verification, Acceptance, Transition, and Closure (LFC-010)

Related Decision Guides: A Compliance Problem Is Discovered (DEC-CMP-001); Transition or Closure Is Requested with Unresolved Obligations (DEC-CLS-001)

AI guidance:

  • Use when: Explaining how an obligation remains traceable through delivery and closure.
  • Avoid: Do not isolate compliance in one process or invent authority to waive obligations.
  • Answer pattern: Walk the obligation through criteria, plans, evidence, verification, acceptance, transition, and closure.

docs.title: Closure and benefits handoff
docs.text:
Source-limited SEM-CLS-BENEFITS-HANDOFF

The explicit separation and connection among formal acceptance, transition, formal project closure, operational ownership, benefits ownership, and continuing benefits measurement.

Scope: Formal acceptance confirms agreed results; transition transfers readiness and responsibility; formal closure completes project or phase obligations; operational and benefits owners continue assigned post-project responsibilities.

Aliases: benefits transition, post-project benefits handoff

Distinctions:

  • Formal project closure may occur before all benefits are realized.
  • Continuing measurement requires an explicit handoff.
  • Operational ownership and benefits ownership may be assigned to different roles.
  • The Atlas does not assert a universal benefits-authority model.

Does not mean: All benefits must be realized before closure; The project manager owns benefits indefinitely

Applicability: organization specific, common across approaches

Interpretation note: Post-project operational and benefits authority depends on the receiving organization.

Canonical public pages: Open reference

Related processes: Validate Scope (PRC-VALIDATE-SCOPE); Close Project or Phase (PRC-CLOSE-PROJECT-OR-PHASE)

Related artifacts: Accepted Deliverables (ART-QLT-005); Transition Package (ART-TRN-001); Benefits Management Information (ART-BEN-001); Benefits Handoff Record (ART-BEN-002); Formal Closure Record (ART-CLS-002)

Related lifecycle chapters: Verification, Acceptance, Transition, and Closure (LFC-010)

Related Decision Guides: Transition or Closure Is Requested with Unresolved Obligations (DEC-CLS-001); Expected Benefits Are Not Yet Realized at Project Closure (DEC-BEN-001)

AI guidance:

  • Use when: Explaining acceptance, transition, closure, or responsibility after project completion.
  • Avoid: Do not delay closure until every benefit occurs or assign universal post-project ownership.
  • Answer pattern: Separate each state and name the explicit operational and benefits handoffs.

docs.title: Formula registry ownership
docs.text:
Verified SEM-FRM-OWNERSHIP

The Formula registry is the canonical structured owner for formula expressions and verification status; this semantic reference only points to that owner.

Scope: Formula and Quantitative Methods is the canonical public explanation for estimating, schedule, reserves, earned-value, and communication-channel formula families.

Aliases: quantitative-method ownership, formula precedence

Distinctions:

  • Formula verification status must come from the Formula registry.
  • Shared semantics never independently assigns a formula-family verification status.
  • When records conflict, the Formula registry has precedence.

Does not mean: A second formula registry; Independent formula verification

Applicability: common across approaches, context specific

Canonical public pages: Open reference; Open reference

Related processes: Estimate Activity Durations (PRC-ESTIMATE-ACTIVITY-DURATIONS); Develop Schedule (PRC-DEVELOP-SCHEDULE); Estimate Costs (PRC-ESTIMATE-COSTS); Determine Budget (PRC-DETERMINE-BUDGET); Control Costs (PRC-CONTROL-COSTS); Plan Communications Management (PRC-PLAN-COMMUNICATIONS-MANAGEMENT); Manage Communications (PRC-MANAGE-COMMUNICATIONS); Monitor Communications (PRC-MONITOR-COMMUNICATIONS)

Related artifacts: Project Schedule (ART-SCH-004); Schedule Baseline (ART-SCH-005); Cost Estimates (ART-CST-001); Cost Baseline (ART-CST-002); Communications Management Plan (ART-COM-001); Project Communications (ART-COM-002)

Related lifecycle chapters: Integrated Planning (LFC-002); Schedule, Resources, and Cost (LFC-004); Execution and Team Leadership (LFC-007); Monitoring and Change (LFC-008)

Related formula families: Estimating (estimating); Schedule Analysis (schedule); Reserves and Baselines (reserves); Earned Value (evm); Communication Channels (communications)

AI guidance:

  • Use when: Resolving where formula expressions, examples, or verification status are owned.
  • Avoid: Do not infer a formula's status from this semantic record or duplicate an expression here.
  • Answer pattern: Follow the Formula and Quantitative Methods link and preserve the registry's current status label.

docs.title: Project Start to Completion
docs.text:
Project Lifecycle Guide

Project Start to Completion

A relational route through project conditions, decisions, handoffs, concurrent work, and feedback—from an observed need to formal closure and continuing benefits ownership.

Recurring role, authority, delivery-approach, issue, compliance, and benefits terms use the AI Semantic Reference.

docs.title: Lifecycle phases are not process groups
docs.text:
A project lifecycle describes how the project and its results change state over time. PMI process groups classify management activity by purpose: initiating, planning, executing, monitoring and controlling, and closing. Those purposes can recur within a phase, release, iteration, or workstream. They are not five consecutive project phases.

Planning continues as uncertainty is reduced. Execution produces information that monitoring interprets. Risk, quality, stakeholder engagement, communications, knowledge, and change work cross most of the lifecycle. Closing can apply to a phase or terminated effort as well as to the entire project.

docs.title: End-to-end sequence
docs.text:
1. Business need and intended value establish why action may be warranted.
  2. Authorization creates a recognized project or phase with accountable sponsorship.
  3. Stakeholder identification reveals affected people, expectations, influence, and decision authority.
  4. Delivery approach and governance establish cadence, controls, roles, and escalation.
  5. Integrated and detailed planning reconcile scope, schedule, cost, quality, resources, communications, risk, procurement, and engagement.
  6. Authorized execution coordinates people and resources to create deliverables.
  7. Deliverables and performance information provide results and evidence for control.
  8. Monitoring, issue resolution, and change decisions compare conditions with intent and authorize responses.
  9. Verification confirms that completed deliverables meet defined quality requirements.
  10. Formal acceptance records the authorized stakeholder's decision.
  11. Transition moves accepted results and operating responsibility to the receiving environment.
  12. Closure completes administrative, contractual, knowledge, archive, and release work.
  13. Continuing benefits ownership and measurement remain with a designated post-project owner; the exact relationship to formal closure remains a documented source conflict.

docs.title: How delivery approaches change the route
docs.text: Predictive work tends to authorize broader baselines before major execution. Adaptive work uses shorter planning-and-delivery cycles, a prioritized work queue, frequent review, and continuing refinement. Hybrid work deliberately assigns different components or governance levels to different cadences. None removes the need to establish purpose, authority, quality, risk treatment, stakeholder feedback, decision rights, acceptance, and responsible transition.

docs.text:

docs.title: Verification, Acceptance, Transition, and Closure
docs.text:
Lifecycle chapter 10

Verification, Acceptance, Transition, and Closure

Finishing production is not the end: results must be verified, accepted by the proper authority, transitioned responsibly, and closed with ownership intact.

Lifecycle orientation

docs.title: Finished work passes through several decisions
docs.text:
Producing a deliverable does not finish the project. The result must move through distinct states, each created by different evidence and authority.

A deliverable is a product, service, or result produced by the project. Control Quality inspects or tests completed work. If it conforms, it becomes a Verified Deliverable. Validate Scope then asks the authorized customer or acceptance role to decide whether the verified result meets the agreed acceptance conditions. Approval makes it an Accepted Deliverable.

Verification answers “does the result conform?” Acceptance answers “does the authorized recipient accept it?” The same evidence may support both decisions, but the decisions and authorities are not interchangeable.

docs.title: Transition moves responsibility
docs.text:
Transition prepares accepted results for sustained use. The Transition Package may include operating procedures, training, access, support arrangements, unresolved items, configuration information, data, compliance evidence, and named owners.

Transition is not merely sending files. The receiving operation must be ready and must know what responsibility it is accepting. ServiceBridge cannot be treated as transitioned if the platform is live but operations lack access, support procedures, retention instructions, trained staff, or ownership of open risks.

docs.title: Closure confirms that project work may end
docs.text:
Close Project or Phase confirms completion or authorized termination, resolves or transfers remaining obligations, closes procurements as applicable, finalizes records and lessons, releases resources, archives information, and obtains formal closure from the proper authority.

Procurement closure and project closure are different. A contract can close while the project continues, and a project cannot ignore open contractual obligations merely because delivery work is finished. Phase closure confirms a phase boundary; project closure ends the authorized project.

A terminated project still needs closure. The reason for termination, completed and incomplete work, financial and contractual status, records, assets, lessons, and continuing obligations must be handled deliberately.

docs.title: Benefits may continue after closure
docs.text:
Project completion and benefit realization do not always occur together. A project can deliver and transition a capability before enough operational data exists to measure the expected benefit. The Benefits Handoff Record identifies the benefit owner, measure, baseline, target, review dates, dependencies, and escalation route for continuing work.

The registered sources contain an unresolved difference about whether benefit realization defines project completion. The Atlas therefore does not claim one universal rule. It separates formal project closure from continuing benefits ownership and records the source gap rather than guessing.

Predictive closure may follow a final phase or release. Adaptive projects may accept and transition increments throughout delivery but still need project-level closure. Hybrid work can close individual contracts or releases at different times while preserving one coordinated record of remaining obligations.

For the exam, separate completion from verification, verification from acceptance, acceptance from transition, transition from formal closure, project closure from procurement closure, and closure from later benefits measurement.

docs.title: Process Phases
docs.text:
These process groups overlap and repeat; the emphasis shows where this chapter most often concentrates.

  1. InitiatingProcess group
  2. PlanningProcess group
  3. ExecutingProcess group · emphasized
  4. Monitoring and ControllingProcess group · emphasized
  5. ClosingProcess group · emphasized

docs.title: Local sequence
docs.text:
1. Submit completed deliverables to Control Quality for inspection and testing.
  2. Move conforming work to Verified Deliverables; return failed work through defect analysis and authorized correction.
  3. Present verified deliverables to the authorized acceptance role through Validate Scope or the applicable equivalent.
  4. Record Accepted Deliverables or route rejected work through clarification, correction, or change.
  5. Confirm outstanding work, obligations, risks, issues, agreements, and readiness before transition.
  6. Transfer accepted results, operating knowledge, support information, access, and accountable ownership.
  7. Finalize lessons, reports, archives, procurement obligations, resources, and formal project or phase closure.
  8. Hand benefits information and measurement responsibility to the designated post-project owner without silently claiming that all benefits are already realized.

docs.title: Handoffs
docs.text:
What enters

Completed and verified deliverables, acceptance conditions, agreements, open items, readiness evidence, knowledge, and business intent.

What this work accomplishes

Establishes conformance, formal acceptance, operational responsibility, defensible completion, preserved knowledge, and explicit continuing ownership.

What moves next

Accepted results and operating responsibility transfer; closure records are archived; unresolved benefit measurement moves to its designated owner.

docs.title: Rejection, early termination, and authority
docs.text:
Failed verification returns to correction or authorized disposition before acceptance. Rejected acceptance returns through analysis and the applicable decision route. Transition readiness gaps can delay handoff or require a controlled exception. A terminated project still requires orderly closure of obligations, records, knowledge, contracts, and resources.

Quality control verifies. The designated customer, sponsor, product, or receiving role accepts. Operational owners confirm readiness and receive responsibility. Procurement authority closes agreement obligations. The sponsor or authorized governance role confirms formal project or phase closure according to the governing model.

docs.title: Benefits conflict preserved
docs.text:
The repository's current primary-source registry supports formal completion, transition, and archival relationships but does not resolve when benefit realization defines project completion. The Confluence source states that benefit measurement may continue after formal closure; the existing Master Project Sequence previously stated that the project is complete only when intended value is realized.

This guide therefore preserves the conflict rather than claiming either rule as verified. It distinguishes formal project closure from continuing benefits ownership, requires an explicit handoff, and leaves the exact post-project authority model deferred pending current PMI or framework verification.

docs.title: Approach treatment and exam distinctions
docs.text:
Predictive closure may consolidate a broad final release or phase. Adaptive and hybrid work may transition increments earlier, but still need final project-level obligations, archives, resources, and authority addressed. Acceptance is not verification, transition is not acceptance, and completion of production is not formal closure.

docs.title: Adaptive and Hybrid Delivery
docs.text:
Lifecycle chapter 9

Adaptive and Hybrid Delivery

Adaptive and hybrid approaches alter how often work is planned, built, reviewed, and accepted; they do not eliminate purpose, risk, quality, governance, or accountability.

Lifecycle orientation

docs.title: Adaptive delivery learns through usable results
docs.text:
Adaptive delivery is used when important solution detail is expected to emerge through feedback. The team still needs purpose, funding, stakeholders, constraints, quality expectations, and authority. What changes is the timing and level of detail.

A product vision describes the desired future outcome. A roadmap shows likely outcome or capability development over a longer horizon. A release plan describes how selected value may be delivered in releases. The Product Backlog is the ordered, evolving source of product work. An iteration backlog contains the work selected for a particular iteration and the plan for delivering it.

These artifacts answer different questions. The roadmap is not a detailed commitment for every backlog item. The Product Backlog is not an iteration plan. An iteration backlog is not the complete product scope. Detail increases as work approaches delivery and evidence improves.

docs.title: Quality and acceptance in adaptive work
docs.text:
Acceptance criteria state the conditions a particular backlog item or result must satisfy. The Definition of Done is the shared quality commitment that applies to an increment. A result can satisfy its item-level acceptance criteria yet still fail the Definition of Done if required integration, testing, documentation, or other quality work is incomplete.

Review provides feedback on the working result and may change backlog ordering or future plans. A retrospective examines how the team works and identifies improvements. Review is about the product and outcomes; retrospective is about the team’s effectiveness and working system.

docs.title: Scrum accountabilities and organizational authority
docs.text:
The Product Owner is accountable for maximizing product value and effective Product Backlog management. Developers create the usable increment. The Scrum Master is accountable for establishing Scrum and improving the Scrum Team’s effectiveness.

Those accountabilities do not automatically grant organizational authority over contracts, funding, personnel, compliance, formal acceptance, or project closure. A project manager may still coordinate cross-team dependencies, governance, suppliers, budgets, and organizational reporting in an adaptive or hybrid environment. The actual arrangement must make overlaps and escalation routes clear.

docs.title: Flow measures are different
docs.text:
Velocity is the amount of estimate units completed by one team in an iteration. It supports that team’s forecasting and should not be treated as a productivity score across teams.

Throughput is the number of work items completed per unit of time. Cycle time is the elapsed time from the workflow’s defined start point to its finish point. Lead time begins at an earlier request or commitment point defined by the system. The boundaries must be stated before the numbers can be interpreted.

docs.title: What hybrid means
docs.text:
Hybrid delivery deliberately combines approaches. ServiceBridge may use fixed funding, regulatory evidence, vendor contracts, and a required transition milestone while product teams refine and deliver portal features iteratively. Hybrid does not mean using predictive documents and agile ceremonies without deciding how they connect.

The key questions are which commitments are fixed, which details may evolve, who orders product work, who controls baselines and contracts, what evidence is required, and where decisions are escalated.

For the exam, do not assume Scrum requires a project manager or Project Charter, do not confuse the Product Backlog with an iteration backlog, and do not use velocity, throughput, cycle time, and lead time as synonyms.

docs.title: Process Phases
docs.text:
These process groups overlap and repeat; the emphasis shows where this chapter most often concentrates.

  1. InitiatingProcess group
  2. PlanningProcess group · emphasized
  3. ExecutingProcess group · emphasized
  4. Monitoring and ControllingProcess group · emphasized
  5. ClosingProcess group

docs.title: Local adaptive loop
docs.text:
1. Maintain an outcome-oriented vision and prioritized work queue.
  2. Refine enough detail for the next planning horizon and agree acceptance conditions.
  3. Select work within capacity and explicit working agreements.
  4. Build, integrate, test, and make completed results visible.
  5. Review outcomes with stakeholders and capture evidence.
  6. Improve the product, process, priorities, and plans through feedback.
  7. Repeat while maintaining governance, compliance, risk, funding, and transition visibility.

docs.title: Handoffs
docs.text:
What enters

Vision, value hypotheses, constraints, prioritized needs, capacity, quality expectations, risks, and stakeholder feedback.

What this work accomplishes

Reduces uncertainty through short learning cycles and delivers inspectable results at a sustainable cadence.

What moves next

Accepted increments, evidence, learning, changed priorities, emerging risks, and improvement actions enter the next cycle or transition.

docs.title: Predictive, adaptive, and hybrid distinctions
docs.text:
Predictive approaches seek more integrated definition before broad execution when scope and path can be planned usefully. Adaptive approaches intentionally defer detail and use frequent feedback when uncertainty or change is high. Hybrid approaches assign different components, layers, or decisions to different cadences for an explicit reason.

Hybrid does not mean using inconsistent terminology or duplicating governance. It must state where priorities can change, where contracts or baselines constrain change, how evidence crosses boundaries, and who resolves conflicts between delivery systems.

docs.title: Roles, quality, risk, and change
docs.text:
Adaptive role labels vary by framework and organization. This guide uses function-first language—sponsor or governance authority, outcome or product direction, delivery facilitation, team ownership, stakeholder acceptance—so role authority does not drift across pages. Framework-specific authority claims remain source-limited until current primary references are registered.

Quality is built into working agreements and completion criteria, then supported by verification and acceptance evidence. Risks are reviewed continuously. Feedback can reprioritize work within delegated guardrails; changes outside those guardrails follow the applicable governance path.

docs.title: Business environment and continuous improvement
docs.text: External regulation, market conditions, technology, suppliers, and internal strategy or capability can change the viable approach. The team observes those conditions, evaluates their impact, and adapts through authorized decisions. Improvement actions should name an owner and affect the next working cycle rather than remain retrospective notes.

docs.title: Exam distinctions
docs.text:
Adaptive does not mean no planning or documentation. A backlog item is not automatically approved scope under every governance model. Review, verification, and acceptance are related but distinct decisions. Velocity or flow measures support forecasting and improvement; they are not universal productivity scores.
