docs.title: Conception and Authorization
docs.text:
Lifecycle chapter 1

Conception and Authorization

The project begins when evidence, sponsorship, authority, stakeholder understanding, and an initial delivery approach are connected—not merely when someone proposes work.

Lifecycle orientation

docs.title: From need to authorization
docs.text:
Initiation is the reasoning that turns a possible change into an authorized project—or decides that no project should proceed. The logical sequence is need or opportunity → evaluation and justification → sponsor or governance decision → high-level definition → stakeholder identification → authorization → detailed planning. The sequence is not a rigid waterfall: evidence can send the proposal backward, narrow it, or stop it.

A need may arise from customer difficulty, strategy, regulation, operational performance, technology, risk, or opportunity. At this point there is an idea, not a project. Needs assessment describes the current condition and desired future state and asks whether project work is a plausible response. Routine operational improvement, policy action, purchase, research, or no action may be more appropriate.

The proposal becomes a candidate investment when evidence, alternatives, feasibility, expected value, costs, uncertainty, and strategic alignment are assembled in a Business Case or equivalent decision record. An approved Business Case means the investment logic has been accepted under that governance; it does not necessarily mean project execution is authorized.

Authorization occurs when the sponsor or other designated authority approves the charter or equivalent mandate, recognizes the project’s existence, establishes high-level boundaries and funding expectations, and grants initial project-manager authority. Only then is there an authorized project. A planned project is a later state in which the authorized direction has been elaborated into an integrated management approach, requirements, scope, schedule, cost, risk, quality, resource, communications, stakeholder, procurement, and other necessary detail.

docs.title: Decision states and feedback loops
docs.text:
Initiation can end in authorization, conditional authorization, discovery authorization, revision, deferral, rejection, suspension, or cancellation. These states matter because “approved” is too vague. A governance body may approve further feasibility work but not supplier commitment; a sponsor may authorize planning within a funding ceiling but reserve delivery approval until evidence improves.

Feasibility concerns can revise the Business Case or recommended option. Stakeholder discovery can reveal an affected group, acceptance authority, compliance obligation, or operational dependency that changes scope and value. High-level risk can make exposure unacceptable or justify a smaller experiment. Unresolved funding or authority can defer the proposal even when the need is real.

These feedback loops prevent sunk-cost momentum from replacing judgment. The purpose of initiation is not to force every idea into a charter; it is to reach an informed and traceable decision about whether a temporary project organization should be created and on what terms.

docs.title: What information moves through initiation
docs.text:
The Business Case carries justification and alternatives. Benefits information carries expected outcomes, measures, timing, and ownership. Agreements contribute external obligations, acceptance terms, and commercial constraints. Enterprise environmental factors describe conditions such as culture, structure, regulation, systems, markets, and resource availability. Organizational process assets supply policies, templates, governance practices, historical information, and lessons.

The Project Charter records authorization, purpose, objectives, high-level scope and requirements, major deliverables, summary milestones and financial boundaries, high-level risks and assumptions, key stakeholders, authority, approval requirements, and exit criteria. The Assumption Log makes unproven beliefs testable. The Stakeholder Register expands beyond the charter’s key names and feeds analysis, engagement, communications, requirements, risk, governance, acceptance, and transition.

docs.title: Initiation roles and authority
docs.text:
The initiating organization or business owner proposes and explains the need. Analysts and subject-matter experts evaluate evidence and feasibility. Functional managers supply resource reality. Customer and affected representatives explain desired outcomes and impacts. Procurement, legal, security, privacy, and compliance authorities interpret obligations within their mandate.

The sponsor champions the initiative and normally exercises or obtains authorization. Governance may reserve investment, funding, risk, continuation, or exception decisions. The proposed project manager integrates the emerging project definition and identifies decision gaps, but does not normally self-authorize. The benefit owner accepts realization responsibility, and the operations owner prepares to receive a sustainable capability.

docs.title: High-level risk and feasibility
docs.text:
Risk is considered before detailed risk planning because uncertainty can change whether the project should exist. Threats include infeasible technology, unavailable resources, supplier dependency, legal exposure, weak adoption, or unacceptable migration quality. Opportunities include earlier value, reusable capability, learning, or a smaller discovery that improves the investment decision.

The initiation decision considers exposure in proportion to available evidence. The charter carries only major risks needed for authorization; later risk processes develop the fuller register, analysis, responses, owners, and monitoring. Assumptions are visible because a proposal that depends on an untested belief has conditional feasibility.

docs.title: Delivery approach and governance
docs.text:
Predictive work commonly authorizes the project before detailed plans and baselines. Adaptive work can authorize a purpose, outcome, funding horizon, discovery, product initiative, or release without fixing detailed solution scope. Scrum does not prescribe organizational project initiation, and Kanban does not supply investment authorization. Hybrid initiation often fixes funding, contracts, compliance, milestones, acceptance, and release boundaries while allowing product detail to emerge iteratively.

Selecting an approach is therefore part of governance, not a declaration that uncertainty has disappeared. The decision should reflect the nature of work, change tolerance, feedback needs, obligations, dependencies, team capability, and decision cadence.

docs.title: ServiceBridge worked example
docs.text:
Northstar Public Services begins with evidence of delayed customer service, accessibility gaps, and weak record traceability. The Business Case compares no action, procedure improvement, cloud configuration, and custom build. Benefits planning assigns post-transition service-time measurement to the Director of Customer Operations. The seller context, accessibility and retention obligations, migration uncertainty, and USD 2.4 million boundary shape feasibility.

Stakeholder discovery identifies not only the sponsor and operational director but also the compliance authority, support representative, seller, frontline user representative, operations owner, benefit owner, functional managers, and acceptance authority. Their evidence narrows requirements, reveals adoption and migration risks, and clarifies decision rights.

The Chief Customer Officer authorizes ServiceBridge through the charter, recognizes the Service Modernization Program Manager’s delegated authority, and retains sponsor-level escalation. Detailed planning then elaborates the four deliverables, 2027-11-19 transition target, 2027-12-17 close target, requirements, estimates, risks, engagement, procurement, quality, and transition. If migration rehearsal or compliance evidence later invalidates feasibility, governance can revise, suspend, or reauthorize rather than treating the original approval as unlimited.

docs.title: Failure modes
docs.text:
Initiation becomes superficial when an attractive solution replaces needs analysis, the Business Case is written to justify a predetermined purchase, benefits have no durable owner, or the charter is approved without usable authority. It also fails when affected stakeholders are discovered only after scope and contracts are fixed.

The consequences are predictable: wasted planning, unsupported resource commitments, hidden compliance and adoption work, unrealistic milestones, unclear acceptance, and projects that deliver outputs without value. Deep initiation does not mean excessive documentation. It means that the decision is evidence-based, uncertainty is visible, authority is usable, and later planning begins from shared boundaries.

docs.title: Exam distinctions
docs.text: An idea is not a proposal; a proposal is not an approved Business Case; an approved Business Case is not necessarily an authorized project; and an authorized project is not yet a fully planned project. The Business Case justifies, the charter authorizes, the Project Management Plan integrates how work will be managed, and the Stakeholder Register expands who must be considered.

docs.title: Sources and synthesis status
docs.text: The July 2026 course directly supports the shared vision, Business Case and business-needs distinction, charter authorization and contents, stakeholder identification, and movement into planning. The verified conception source supports the detailed information flow and decision sequence. Feedback loops, state labels, ServiceBridge walkthrough, failure modes, and framework boundaries are Atlas synthesis. The Atlas does not assert a universal document set, gate model, sponsor title, or linear lifecycle.

docs.title: Process Phases
docs.text:
These process groups overlap and repeat; the emphasis shows where this chapter most often concentrates.

  1. InitiatingProcess group · emphasized
  2. PlanningProcess group
  3. ExecutingProcess group
  4. Monitoring and ControllingProcess group
  5. ClosingProcess group

docs.title: Local sequence
docs.text:
1. Recognize a problem, opportunity, obligation, or strategic need.
  2. Evaluate whether a project response is justified; keep detailed business-case mechanics with the originating organization until a verified artifact owner exists.
  3. Describe intended outcomes and benefits without claiming they have already been realized.
  4. Establish agreements or constraints that precede authorization when applicable.
  5. Approve the Project Charter through the appropriate sponsor authority.
  6. Identify Stakeholders and record influence, needs, impact, and engagement information.
  7. Select and tailor a workable delivery approach and establish decision rights.

docs.title: Handoffs
docs.text:
What enters

Need evidence, strategy, constraints, agreements, initial risks, intended outcomes, and decision criteria.

What this work accomplishes

Turns an idea into an authorized, governable effort and reveals who can affect or accept its results.

What moves next

Charter, initial assumptions, stakeholder information, delivery approach, and governance expectations enter integrated planning.

docs.title: Roles and authority
docs.text: The sponsor or authorized initiating body approves the project and establishes high-level authority. The project manager supports development of the charter and organizes the authorized work; this role does not self-authorize the project. Stakeholders supply needs, constraints, expertise, influence, and acceptance expectations. Governance roles define which decisions may be made locally and which require escalation.

docs.title: Feedback and approach treatment
docs.text:
Planning may reveal that the original case is infeasible, a key stakeholder was omitted, or the proposed delivery approach does not fit the uncertainty. That information returns to the sponsor for clarification, tailoring, reauthorization, deferral, or termination.

Predictive work often establishes broader boundaries early. Adaptive work may authorize an outcome and funding guardrails while allowing scope detail to emerge through short feedback cycles. Hybrid work must state which decisions are fixed, which evolve, and who controls the boundary between them.

docs.title: Artifact states and exam distinctions
docs.text:
Need evidence supports a decision; it is not authorization. A draft charter becomes an authorization record only through approval. Stakeholder information begins early and continues to change. Delivery-approach selection is a tailoring decision, not permission to omit management purposes.

For exam reasoning, separate the business case from the charter, the sponsor's authorization from the project manager's management authority, and stakeholder identification from the later work of planning and managing engagement.

docs.title: Execution and Team Leadership
docs.text:
Lifecycle chapter 7

Execution and Team Leadership

Execution is concurrent coordination: the team creates results while learning, communicating, engaging, resolving conflict, implementing responses, and producing performance evidence.

Lifecycle orientation

docs.title: Execution turns an approved approach into coordinated action
docs.text:
Project execution is the work of producing deliverables and carrying out the approved management approach. Leadership during execution creates the conditions in which people can make sound decisions, resolve obstacles, protect quality, share knowledge, and adapt within their authority. It exists because an approved plan does not coordinate people or produce results by itself.

The project manager integrates work across teams, suppliers, stakeholders, and governance boundaries; the delivery team performs and improves the work; specialists and functional leaders contribute authority and capability. Directing work is not the same as assigning every task. Effective leadership clarifies outcomes and constraints, supplies information and resources, invites appropriate participation, addresses conflict, and escalates decisions that exceed delegated limits. Data and deliverables produced during execution become inputs to quality control, monitoring, stakeholder engagement, and change decisions.

For ServiceBridge, the migration team discovers inconsistent customer-status definitions. The project manager does not instruct a developer to choose one definition. The data owner, operations representative, and requirements lead examine the evidence, agree the authorized business rule, update the relevant documentation, and assess affected work. The team resumes with a clear decision and preserves the lesson. Predictive execution follows approved work packages and controls; adaptive execution organizes around a goal and usable increments; hybrid execution connects team autonomy to contracts, compliance, baselines, and external milestones. On the exam, lead by resolving the system around the work before defaulting to command or escalation.

docs.text:
These process groups overlap and repeat; the emphasis shows where this chapter most often concentrates.

docs.title: Local sequence
docs.text:
1. Confirm authorized work, near-term priorities, resources, decision rights, and working agreements.
  2. Direct and manage project work to create deliverables and work performance data.
  3. Acquire, develop, and support the team; address conflict at the appropriate level.
  4. Manage knowledge so experience can improve present work and future decisions.
  5. Perform quality, communications, risk-response, procurement, and stakeholder-engagement work concurrently.
  6. Route issues, impediments, defects, new risks, and proposed changes into their controlled decision paths.

docs.title: Handoffs
docs.text:
What enters

Authorized plans and changes, resources, stakeholder expectations, agreements, risk responses, and quality criteria.

What this work accomplishes

Creates deliverables, team capability, communications, knowledge, implemented responses, and observed performance.

What moves next

Completed work enters verification; data enters domain controls; issues and changes enter decisions; learning returns to current plans.

docs.title: Leadership, conflict, and feedback
docs.text:
The project manager integrates work and removes organizational friction within delegated authority. Team members own assigned work and contribute expertise. Functional managers or resource owners retain relevant people authority. Sponsors and governance bodies resolve escalated direction or funding decisions. Stakeholders participate through the planned engagement routes.

Conflict is information about competing needs, constraints, or behavior. Resolve it at the lowest responsible level that has authority and context; escalate when safety, ethics, compliance, contractual limits, or delegated authority require it. An impediment should have an owner and path to removal even though the repository does not yet have a source-verified canonical impediment artifact page.

docs.title: Approach treatment and artifact states
docs.text:
Predictive execution coordinates against approved work packages and plans. Adaptive execution selects near-term items, collaborates through short cycles, demonstrates increments, and learns from feedback. Hybrid execution must keep cross-cadence dependencies and decision rights visible.

Work performance data are observations from execution. They become Work Performance Information only after analysis. Completed deliverables are not verified or accepted merely because the team finished production.

docs.title: Exam distinctions
docs.text:
Approved changes are implemented; proposed changes are not. Manage Project Knowledge is continuous rather than a final archive task. Team development and team management are related but distinct. Servant leadership does not remove accountability, governance, or escalation.

docs.title: Integrated Planning
docs.text:
Lifecycle chapter 2

Integrated Planning

Planning becomes usable when its parts agree about scope, timing, funding, quality, people, uncertainty, information, authority, and change.

Lifecycle orientation

docs.title: What integrated planning means
docs.text:
Integrated planning is the work of turning the approved project direction into one coordinated way of managing the project. It is not the act of placing separate plans in the same folder.

Scope choices affect activities, resources, duration, cost, quality, risk, procurement, communications, and stakeholder involvement. A promised date may require more people or a smaller scope. A compliance requirement may add testing, documentation, specialist review, and procurement clauses. Integration makes those effects visible before the team treats the plans as approved commitments.

The Project Management Plan is the integrated result. Subsidiary management plans explain how a particular area will be planned and controlled. Baselines record approved expectations for scope, schedule, or cost. Project documents hold working information such as requirements, assumptions, risks, issues, estimates, and stakeholder details. A project document can change as the team learns without every update becoming a baseline change; the governing plan states which changes require formal control.

docs.title: Why the component plans are different
docs.text:
A management plan describes a method, rule, responsibility, or control approach. It answers questions such as who approves scope, how schedule progress is measured, when risk reviews occur, and which communication methods are used.

A project document records the current information produced by applying that method. The Communications Management Plan says who needs information, why, when, in what form, and through which channel. Project communications are the reports, messages, presentations, meeting records, and other information actually created and distributed under that plan.

The same distinction applies to stakeholders. The Stakeholder Register identifies people and groups, their interests, influence, expectations, and relevant authority. The Stakeholder Engagement Plan explains how the team intends to involve them. Communication and engagement cannot be planned well until the team knows who needs information, what decisions each stakeholder makes, and what participation the project requires.

docs.title: What happens during integration
docs.text:
The team reviews the charter, business case, benefits information, agreements, assumptions, stakeholder information, and the outputs of detailed planning. Conflicts are resolved or escalated. Owners and approval routes are made explicit. The project manager then assembles the coordinated plan for approval under the organization’s governance rules.

For ServiceBridge, an initial plan might promise a November transition, full data migration, accessibility conformance, and a USD 2.4 million boundary. Integration reveals whether the migration work, accessibility testing, seller capacity, training, and operational readiness can all fit that commitment. If they cannot, the plan is not “integrated” merely because every section is complete; the conflict must be resolved.

Predictive work usually establishes more detail and formal baselines before execution. Adaptive work plans in layers: outcome and governance boundaries remain visible while backlog detail is refined closer to delivery. Hybrid work connects iterative product planning to fixed obligations such as contracts, compliance, funding, and major milestones.

On the exam, distinguish the approved Project Management Plan from the process used to develop it, and distinguish management plans from the working project documents they govern.

docs.title: Process Phases
docs.text:
These process groups overlap and repeat; the emphasis shows where this chapter most often concentrates.

  1. InitiatingProcess group
  2. PlanningProcess group · emphasized
  3. ExecutingProcess group
  4. Monitoring and ControllingProcess group
  5. ClosingProcess group

docs.title: Local sequence
docs.text:
1. Use the charter and stakeholder information to establish planning boundaries.
  2. Develop detailed subsidiary approaches and baselines through the relevant planning processes.
  3. Plan stakeholder engagement, resources, team working agreements, and communications.
  4. Define how changes, configuration items, versions, approvals, and records will be controlled.
  5. Reconcile contradictions across scope, schedule, cost, quality, risk, resources, procurement, and stakeholder expectations.
  6. Approve the integrated Project Management Plan and establish shared understanding before authorized execution.

docs.title: Handoffs
docs.text:
What enters

Authorization, assumptions, stakeholder information, enterprise constraints, organizational assets, and emerging detailed plans.

What this work accomplishes

Creates coherent management direction, usable decision thresholds, information routes, and an agreed basis for action.

What moves next

Approved plans and baselines guide execution; working documents and forecasts continue to evolve within those controls.

docs.title: Concurrent planning and return loops
docs.text: Detailed planning is concurrent and iterative. Scope influences schedule and cost; resources constrain duration; risks affect reserves and responses; procurement timing affects schedule; quality and compliance criteria affect acceptance. A contradiction returns to the affected planning owners before approval. Execution evidence later returns through monitoring and may trigger replanning or formal change.

docs.title: Roles, authority, and approaches
docs.text:
The project manager integrates planning and makes conflicts visible. Subject-matter owners develop relevant components. The sponsor or governance body resolves decisions outside delegated authority. Team members and stakeholders contribute practical knowledge and commitment.

Predictive planning commonly develops more of the integrated direction before major execution. Adaptive planning establishes vision, guardrails, cadence, working agreements, and enough detail for the next horizon. Hybrid planning must explicitly reconcile rolling detail with any predictive milestones, contracts, compliance gates, or baselines.

docs.title: Artifact states and exam distinctions
docs.text:
Working drafts are progressively integrated, then approved. Once controlled, a changed forecast or document does not automatically change a baseline. A kickoff communicates and aligns around approved direction; it is not a substitute for integration or authorization.

The communication-channel formula and other formulas remain with their process or future verified formula owner; this chapter does not duplicate them.

docs.title: Monitoring and Change
docs.text:
Lifecycle chapter 8

Monitoring and Change

Monitoring explains what current evidence means; change control decides what authorized direction should change.

Lifecycle orientation

docs.title: Monitoring turns observations into decisions
docs.text:
Monitoring is not the same as collecting status data. Work performance data are raw observations such as dates, costs, defects, completed items, and test results. Analysis gives those observations context and produces work performance information. Selected information is then organized into work performance reports for stakeholders who need to understand status, forecasts, risks, or decisions.

For example, “migration test 17 failed” is data. Comparing failures across test cycles and identifying a rising error rate produces information. A report that explains the trend, its forecast effect, and the decision required gives governance a usable view.

docs.title: Issues, impediments, and risks
docs.text:
A risk is uncertain. An Issue Log records a condition that already exists, who owns the response, when action is due, and when escalation is required. An impediment is something blocking or slowing work. A team may remove a small impediment immediately; a material or persistent impediment may become a project issue and require escalation.

The label matters because the response changes. Risks are analyzed before they occur. Issues need current action. Impediments need flow restored. The records may link to one another, but they should not hide the current state of the problem.

docs.title: A change moves through distinct states
docs.text:
A Change Request is a proposal. It explains what should change, why, and what approved commitments may be affected. Impact analysis examines scope, schedule, cost, quality, resources, risk, contracts, compliance, benefits, and stakeholder effects.

The authorized change role then approves, rejects, defers, or requests more information. Approval changes the decision state; it does not implement the work. The approved change is communicated and assigned, the team implements it, affected plans and baselines are updated under control, and the result is verified. The Change Log preserves that trace.

This sequence prevents four different things from being collapsed into one word:

  1. requested change;
  2. approved change;
  3. implemented change;
  4. verified change.

For ServiceBridge, a request to strengthen encryption is analyzed for design, cost, schedule, seller, and compliance effects. The change authority approves it. The delivery team implements it. Security testing verifies the result. Only then can the log show both the decision and its completed implementation evidence.

Adaptive teams may reprioritize uncommitted backlog detail without a formal baseline change. A change to a controlled release, contract, compliance obligation, funding limit, or other approved commitment still follows the relevant authority route. Hybrid projects must make that boundary explicit.

For the exam, assess first, follow the approved change process, update affected records after the decision, and verify the implemented result. Urgency does not give the project manager unlimited authority.

docs.title: Process Phases
docs.text:
These process groups overlap and repeat; the emphasis shows where this chapter most often concentrates.

  1. InitiatingProcess group
  2. PlanningProcess group
  3. ExecutingProcess group · emphasized
  4. Monitoring and ControllingProcess group · emphasized
  5. ClosingProcess group

docs.title: Local sequence
docs.text:
1. Capture work performance data from execution and relevant external conditions.
  2. Analyze domain results into Work Performance Information.
  3. Integrate status, variance, trends, forecasts, risks, issues, and dependencies through Monitor and Control Project Work.
  4. Communicate decision-ready Work Performance Reports.
  5. Resolve issues within delegated authority or escalate through the named governance route.
  6. Document proposed changes as Change Requests, analyze impacts, and obtain an authorized disposition.
  7. Implement approved changes, update controlled records, and verify the resulting work.

docs.title: Handoffs and return loops
docs.text:
What enters

Actual results, forecasts, defects, risks, issues, stakeholder feedback, agreement performance, and current plans.

What this work accomplishes

Creates integrated understanding and authorized responses while preserving configuration and decision history.

What moves next

Actions return to execution; approved changes update affected owners; rejected requests leave baselines unchanged; verified results proceed to acceptance.

Control is continuous. A defect can return to correction and reinspection. A variance can prompt analysis, corrective action, or change. A new issue can reveal a risk response failure. Stakeholder feedback can require engagement adjustment without necessarily changing scope. Every return path needs an owner and an authority boundary.

docs.title: Issues, impediments, and configuration
docs.text:
An issue is a current condition requiring action; a risk is uncertain. An impediment blocks or slows progress and may be an issue, organizational constraint, dependency, or policy concern. The lifecycle guide makes these relationships explicit, but dedicated issue-log and impediment destinations remain deferred because current repository sources do not yet support responsible standalone pages.

Version and configuration controls preserve which approved artifact state applies. A changed working document, an approved change, and an updated baseline are different events.

docs.title: Approach treatment and exam distinctions
docs.text:
Predictive control often compares performance with broader baselines. Adaptive control uses frequent review of outcomes, flow, quality, and feedback within governance guardrails. Hybrid control must integrate both evidence types without forcing one cadence to masquerade as the other.

Data, information, and reports are not interchangeable. Corrective action is not automatic baseline change. Only the authorized role or body may approve a controlled change. Approved change implementation must be verified.

docs.title: Quality
docs.text:
Lifecycle chapter 5

Quality

Quality connects requirements to planned criteria, capable processes, inspection evidence, verified deliverables, and acceptance decisions.

Lifecycle orientation

docs.title: Quality means meeting requirements
docs.text:
Project quality is the degree to which a result and the processes used to create it satisfy stated requirements. Grade is a category or rank assigned to products that have the same general use but different features or characteristics. A lower-grade product can still be high quality if it meets its requirements; a high-grade product is poor quality if it fails them.

Quality planning decides which standards apply, what evidence will demonstrate conformance, how work will be reviewed or tested, who performs each check, and what happens when results fail. Quality metrics make expectations measurable. Acceptance criteria state the conditions a particular result must satisfy for an authorized stakeholder to accept it.

docs.title: Planning, assurance, control, and acceptance
docs.text:
Plan Quality Management establishes the quality approach and records it in the Quality Management Plan. It also defines metrics and connects requirements to verification and acceptance evidence.

Manage Quality examines whether the project’s processes and quality approach are suitable and being followed. Audits, reviews, analysis, and improvement work can reveal causes that inspection alone would miss.

Control Quality inspects or tests completed work. When the evidence shows that a deliverable conforms, its state becomes verified. If it fails, the team records the result and routes correction through the appropriate defect and change process.

Validate Scope is different. It asks the authorized customer or acceptance role to make the formal acceptance decision using the verified deliverable and the agreed acceptance conditions. A quality team may verify technical conformance without having authority to accept the result for the customer.

For ServiceBridge, an accessibility test can verify that the portal meets WCAG criteria. The customer-service acceptance authority then decides whether the verified portal satisfies the agreed business and acceptance conditions. Passing the test supports acceptance; it is not the acceptance decision itself.

docs.title: Predictive, adaptive, and hybrid treatment
docs.text:
Predictive work may plan formal inspections, audits, test stages, and acceptance gates. Adaptive teams build quality into small increments through clear acceptance criteria, automation, review, and a Definition of Done. The Definition of Done is a shared quality commitment for an increment; it is not a substitute for every product-specific acceptance criterion or external approval.

Hybrid work may use automated iterative testing inside formal compliance, contract, release, and customer-acceptance gates. The evidence can be produced continuously even when the final authority remains outside the team.

For the exam, separate quality from grade, prevention from inspection, verification from acceptance, a verified deliverable from an accepted deliverable, and the Definition of Done from item-level acceptance criteria.

docs.title: Process Phases
docs.text:
These process groups overlap and repeat; the emphasis shows where this chapter most often concentrates.

  1. InitiatingProcess group
  2. PlanningProcess group · emphasized
  3. ExecutingProcess group · emphasized
  4. Monitoring and ControllingProcess group · emphasized
  5. ClosingProcess group

docs.title: Local sequence
docs.text:
1. Use requirements, traceability, scope, risk, stakeholder, and compliance information to plan quality.
  2. Create the Quality Management Plan and Quality Metrics.
  3. Apply the planned approach during execution and improve process capability through Manage Quality.
  4. Inspect or test completed deliverables through Control Quality and record Quality-Control Measurements.
  5. Move conforming results to Verified Deliverables.
  6. Submit verified deliverables for formal acceptance, producing Accepted Deliverables when authorized acceptance is granted.

docs.title: Handoffs and return loops
docs.text:
What enters

Requirements, acceptance conditions, scope, standards, regulations, risk, stakeholder expectations, and lessons.

What this work accomplishes

Defines measurable quality, improves delivery processes, and produces evidence about deliverable conformance.

What moves next

Verified deliverables enter acceptance; defects, trends, and process findings return to execution, risk, planning, or change.

Failed inspection does not become acceptance. The team analyzes the defect, determines the authorized response, performs correction or change work, and reinspects. A stakeholder rejection after verification is different: it may reveal an expectation, scope, requirement, or acceptance problem and follows the quality inspection failure decision guide as applicable.

docs.title: Roles, authority, and approaches
docs.text:
The project manager ensures integration. Quality specialists and the delivery team plan and perform quality work. Control Quality verifies conformance. The designated customer or sponsor role accepts; quality personnel do not silently substitute for that authority.

Predictive work may establish broader criteria and planned reviews before production. Adaptive work embeds criteria, review, testing, and feedback in each increment. Hybrid work must maintain consistent evidence and acceptance authority across both cadences.

docs.title: Exam distinctions
docs.text:
Manage Quality concerns the effectiveness and improvement of processes; Control Quality concerns results and conformance evidence. Verification precedes acceptance. Grade and quality are different concepts. Commercial audit or template examples are illustrations, not PMI-prescribed formats; detailed audit claims remain source-limited where the registry lacks current primary verification.

docs.title: Requirements and Scope
docs.text:
Lifecycle chapter 3

Requirements and Scope

Needs become controllable when they can be traced through scope, decomposition, delivery, verification, and formal acceptance.

Lifecycle orientation

docs.title: From a need to controlled scope
docs.text:
A requirement states a capability or condition that a result must satisfy. A requirement may come from a customer, user, law, contract, operational need, technical constraint, or business objective. Collecting requirements is not simply writing down requests; the team must clarify meaning, resolve conflicts, test feasibility, and record how each important requirement will be evaluated.

Product scope describes the features and functions of the product, service, or result. Project scope describes the work required to create that result. For ServiceBridge, “support accessible appointment scheduling” is product scope. Designing, configuring, testing, training, migrating data, and transitioning the service are parts of project scope.

The Project Scope Statement establishes the detailed boundary developed during planning. The Scope Baseline adds the approved Work Breakdown Structure and WBS dictionary so the boundary can be planned and controlled.

docs.title: WBS terms in plain language
docs.text:
A Work Breakdown Structure, or WBS, organizes the complete project scope into a hierarchy. The team decomposes large deliverables into smaller components until the lowest planned components can be estimated, assigned, monitored, and controlled.

A work package is the lowest WBS component for which cost and duration can be estimated and managed. It is not the same as an activity. A work package describes a piece of scope; activities describe the actions needed to complete it.

A control account is a management control point where scope, schedule, and cost information are integrated and compared with performance. A planning package is known work below a control account that has not yet been decomposed into detailed work packages. It allows later detail without pretending the team knows more than it does.

The WBS dictionary explains each component’s boundary, deliverables, assumptions, responsibilities, milestones, and other planning information. Without the dictionary, short WBS labels can be interpreted differently by different people.

docs.title: Traceability, verification, and acceptance
docs.text:
The Requirements Traceability Matrix connects a requirement to its origin, business reason, approved scope, design or delivery work, test evidence, acceptance evidence, owner, and status. This connection helps the team detect omitted requirements and evaluate the effect of a requested change.

Completion does not move directly to customer acceptance. Control Quality first checks whether a completed deliverable conforms to requirements and quality criteria. Conforming work becomes a Verified Deliverable. Validate Scope then presents that verified work to the authorized customer or acceptance role. Approval creates an Accepted Deliverable.

In predictive work, the team may approve a broad scope baseline before delivery. Adaptive work develops detailed scope through a Product Backlog and short planning horizons. A backlog item’s acceptance criteria describe the conditions for that item; the Definition of Done is the shared quality commitment for an increment. Neither automatically replaces organizational authorization or formal acceptance. Hybrid work links evolving backlog items to the controlled scope, compliance, contract, and acceptance obligations that remain fixed.

For the exam, remember: requirements describe needs, the scope statement defines the detailed boundary, the WBS decomposes project scope, activities describe scheduled work, quality control verifies, and the authorized stakeholder accepts.

docs.text:

docs.title: Local sequence
docs.text:
1. Plan how requirements and scope will be developed, validated, and controlled.
  2. Elicit and analyze needs into Requirements Documentation.
  3. Connect requirements to origin and downstream evidence in the Requirements Traceability Matrix.
  4. Define product and project scope boundaries.
  5. Decompose approved scope into the WBS and WBS dictionary within the Scope Baseline.
  6. Deliver and control scope while preserving traceability.
  7. Verify completed deliverables before seeking formal acceptance.

docs.title: Handoffs
docs.text:
What enters

Charter, stakeholder needs, product information, assumptions, constraints, standards, risk, and delivery approach.

What this work accomplishes

Defines what must be satisfied, what work is authorized, and what evidence will demonstrate completion.

What moves next

Approved scope drives schedule, cost, quality, resources, procurement, delivery, verification, acceptance, and change control.

docs.title: Feedback and rejection loops
docs.text: Unclear or conflicting requirements return to stakeholders for analysis. Decomposition can reveal missing scope or infeasible assumptions. During delivery, requested scope changes enter integrated change control. A deliverable that fails inspection returns for defect analysis and authorized rework; a verified deliverable that is not accepted returns for clarification, correction, change evaluation, or another authorized disposition.

docs.title: Roles, authority, and approaches
docs.text:
Stakeholders supply needs and acceptance expectations. The project team analyzes and decomposes the work. The project manager coordinates control. An authorized customer, sponsor, product owner, or other designated role makes the applicable acceptance decision; verification by the quality function is not that formal acceptance.

Predictive work may baseline a broad scope structure. Adaptive work refines prioritized items and acceptance criteria over short horizons while preserving outcome and traceability. Hybrid work must map evolving items to controlled commitments and approval boundaries.

docs.title: Artifact states and exam distinctions
docs.text:
A need becomes a documented requirement, a requirement becomes traceable to approved scope and delivery work, a completed deliverable becomes verified through quality control, and a verified deliverable becomes accepted only through an authorized acceptance decision. The WBS organizes scope; it is not a schedule or organizational chart.

docs.title: Risk, Compliance, and Procurement
docs.text:
Lifecycle chapter 6

Risk, Compliance, and Procurement

Uncertainty, mandatory obligations, and external commitments affect one another and must remain visible from planning through closure.

Lifecycle orientation

docs.title: Risk is uncertainty; an issue exists now
docs.text:
A risk is an uncertain event or condition that could affect project objectives. It may be a threat or an opportunity. An issue is a condition that already exists and requires action or a decision. A data-migration failure that might occur is a risk; a failed migration discovered in today’s test is an issue.

Risk management gives uncertainty a repeatable path. The team decides how risk will be managed, identifies uncertainties, assesses priority, performs quantitative analysis when useful, plans responses, implements approved actions, and monitors changes. The Risk Register holds individual risks and their owners, triggers, responses, and status. The Risk Report summarizes overall exposure and trends for decision-makers.

Threat responses include avoiding, mitigating, transferring, escalating, or accepting the threat. Opportunity responses include exploiting, enhancing, sharing, escalating, or accepting the opportunity. A response is useful only when a person owns it, the timing is clear, and the team can recognize when action is required.

docs.title: Compliance changes project work
docs.text:
Compliance is not a final inspection added after delivery. A law, regulation, policy, standard, license, or contract can change requirements, design choices, evidence, supplier terms, testing, acceptance authority, record retention, and transition conditions.

For ServiceBridge, accessibility and retention obligations become requirements. They affect design, testing, procurement clauses, acceptance evidence, and operational records. If the team discovers that a requirement cannot be met, the issue follows the applicable risk, change, compliance, and governance route; the project manager does not unilaterally waive it.

docs.title: Procurement connects project needs to seller obligations
docs.text:
Procurement planning decides what to obtain externally, how the market will be approached, which contract type fits the uncertainty, how sellers will be evaluated, and who may make commercial decisions. Conduct Procurements obtains and evaluates seller responses and establishes an agreement. Control Procurements monitors performance, manages claims and changes, and closes the commercial obligations.

Contract type allocates financial risk differently. Fixed-price arrangements place more cost risk on the seller when the scope is sufficiently defined. Cost-reimbursable arrangements place more cost risk on the buyer and require suitable oversight. Time-and-materials arrangements combine fixed rates with variable quantities and need clear limits.

The project manager coordinates scope, schedule, risk, technical evidence, and stakeholder effects, but only authorized buyer and seller representatives can bind their organizations or change the agreement.

Predictive procurement often defines detailed deliverables before award. Adaptive or hybrid procurement may use outcome-based scope, short delivery increments, demonstrations, and adjustable backlogs while retaining funding limits, acceptance conditions, compliance duties, and formal contract-change authority.

On the exam, distinguish risk from issue, a planned response from an implemented response, residual risk from secondary risk, project change control from contract change, and seller performance management from informal team direction.

docs.title: Process Phases
docs.text:
These process groups overlap and repeat; the emphasis shows where this chapter most often concentrates.

  1. InitiatingProcess group
  2. PlanningProcess group · emphasized
  3. ExecutingProcess group · emphasized
  4. Monitoring and ControllingProcess group · emphasized
  5. ClosingProcess group · emphasized

docs.title: Local sequence
docs.text:
1. Plan the risk approach, identify uncertainties, and build the Risk Register.
  2. Prioritize risks and perform quantitative analysis when warranted and supported.
  3. Select responses, assign owners, implement agreed actions, and monitor residual and emerging risk.
  4. Trace compliance obligations into requirements, scope, quality criteria, risk, procurement terms, acceptance evidence, and closure records.
  5. Plan procurement, prepare solicitation information, select sellers through authorized conduct, and establish agreements.
  6. Control seller performance, changes, claims, records, and completion; close contractual obligations through the applicable authority.

docs.title: Handoffs
docs.text:
What enters

Objectives, scope, assumptions, constraints, compliance obligations, market information, risk appetite, and make-or-buy considerations.

What this work accomplishes

Makes uncertainty actionable, obligations traceable, and external commitments governable.

What moves next

Responses, owners, procurement decisions, agreements, controls, and evidence enter execution, monitoring, acceptance, and closure.

docs.title: Feedback, issues, and authority
docs.text:
A risk trigger can create response work, an issue, or a change request. A compliance finding can block acceptance or require corrective action. Seller performance can change schedule, cost, quality, and risk. These paths return through domain control and integrated change rather than bypassing authority.

Risk owners monitor assigned uncertainties; response owners perform agreed actions. Procurement authority depends on organizational policy and agreement terms. Compliance authority depends on the governing obligation. The project manager integrates impacts but does not invent authority beyond the project governance model.

docs.title: Approach treatment and exam distinctions
docs.text:
Predictive work may establish broader risk and procurement structures early. Adaptive work reviews uncertainty and obligations frequently as increments evolve. Hybrid work must connect adaptive discovery to contract, baseline, and compliance controls.

A risk is uncertain; an issue has occurred. A contingency response differs from an unapproved scope change. Contract type influences risk allocation but does not eliminate buyer oversight. Compliance is not a closing checklist: it must be traceable from requirements through evidence and handoff. Detailed contract and audit claims remain in the process references or deferred until current primary sources support them.

docs.title: Schedule, Resources, and Cost
docs.text:
Lifecycle chapter 4

Schedule, Resources, and Cost

Time, people, equipment, and funding form one constraint system; planning or controlling them independently produces an infeasible project.

Lifecycle orientation

docs.title: Scope becomes activities, time, resources, and cost
docs.text:
The schedule does not begin as a list of dates. It begins with approved scope. Work packages are examined to identify the activities needed to produce them. Activities are sequenced, resources are estimated, durations are estimated, and the schedule model is analyzed before dates are approved.

A work package is a component of scope in the WBS. An activity is a scheduled action performed to complete that scope. One work package may require several activities, and an activity should be traceable back to the scope it supports.

A milestone is a significant point or event with zero duration. It may mark approval, contract award, completion of a phase, regulatory submission, launch, or transition. A milestone is not work and does not consume duration by itself; the activities leading to it do.

Resources and duration are related but not interchangeable. Adding people does not always reduce duration because work may be sequential, specialist-limited, or slowed by coordination. Calendars, dependencies, risk, learning, and availability all affect the result.

docs.title: Estimates, baselines, and the budget
docs.text:
A cost estimate forecasts the money required for particular work. The cost baseline is the approved, time-phased budget used to measure cost performance. Budget at Completion, or BAC, is the total value of that cost baseline.

Contingency reserve covers identified uncertainty within the approved scope and is included in the cost baseline. Management reserve covers unforeseen work that is still within project scope and sits outside the cost baseline. The total project budget is the cost baseline plus management reserve. Using management reserve normally follows the organization’s authority and change rules; it is not simply extra money controlled by the project manager.

This distinction explains why the Charter’s high-level financial boundary, detailed cost estimates, cost baseline, BAC, contingency reserve, management reserve, and total funding need not be the same number.

For ServiceBridge, the charter authorizes work within a USD 2.4 million boundary. Planning estimates the work, adds contingency for identified migration uncertainty, time-phases the approved amount into the cost baseline, and records any governance-held management reserve separately. Cost performance is later compared with the baseline, not with an informal estimate.

docs.title: Approach differences
docs.text:
Predictive projects commonly establish activity networks, detailed schedules, and cost baselines for a defined scope. Adaptive teams plan near-term work in iterations or through flow, and may forecast using velocity, throughput, cycle time, or lead time. Velocity is completed estimate units per iteration for one team. Throughput is completed work items per unit of time. Cycle time measures elapsed time after work starts; lead time measures from an earlier requested or committed point defined by the system.

Hybrid projects may keep contract, funding, infrastructure, or compliance milestones under predictive control while product teams refine and deliver features iteratively. The metrics can coexist, but they should not be treated as interchangeable or compared across teams without a valid common basis.

On the exam, separate a milestone from an activity, a work package from an activity, an estimate from a baseline, BAC from total project budget, and contingency reserve from management reserve.

docs.title: Process Phases
docs.text:
These process groups overlap and repeat; the emphasis shows where this chapter most often concentrates.

  1. InitiatingProcess group
  2. PlanningProcess group · emphasized
  3. ExecutingProcess group · emphasized
  4. Monitoring and ControllingProcess group · emphasized
  5. ClosingProcess group

docs.title: Local sequence
docs.text:
1. Translate scope components into activities and milestones.
  2. Establish logical relationships and identify resource needs.
  3. Estimate durations and costs with explicit assumptions.
  4. Analyze constraints and integrate the current Project Schedule.
  5. Aggregate estimates, reconcile funding, and approve the Schedule Baseline and Cost Baseline.
  6. Acquire and coordinate resources while execution produces actuals.
  7. Compare actual and forecast conditions with authorized baselines; decide recovery, escalation, or change.

docs.title: Handoffs
docs.text:
What enters

Scope baseline, calendars, resource information, rates, constraints, risk, procurement lead times, and estimating evidence.

What this work accomplishes

Creates a feasible coordination model and authorized comparison points for time and cost.

What moves next

Schedules, assignments, estimates, and baselines guide execution; actuals and forecasts return to monitoring and decisions.

docs.title: Feedback and authority
docs.text:
Unavailable resources can force new sequencing or duration assumptions. Schedule compression can affect cost, quality, and risk. Funding limits can force scope or timing decisions. Performance variance returns through control processes; corrective action may adjust work within authority, while a baseline-affecting proposal enters integrated change control.

The project manager integrates tradeoffs. Activity owners and specialists contribute estimates. Resource managers or functional leaders commit controlled resources. Sponsors or governance bodies decide changes beyond delegated thresholds.

docs.title: Approach treatment and artifact states
docs.text:
Predictive work often models a broader activity network and baselines. Adaptive work plans near-term items and capacity in more detail, using cadence and flow evidence to forecast. Hybrid work maps iteration or flow commitments to external milestones and funding controls.

The current schedule and forecasts are working information. Baselines are approved comparison records. Variance is not permission to rewrite them. Formulas remain canonically explained in relevant process material until repository sources support a shared formula registry.

docs.title: Exam distinctions
docs.text:
Duration is elapsed working time, not effort. Estimates are not authorized budgets. A forecast is not a baseline. Resource leveling, schedule compression, reserve decisions, and earned-value interpretations must be evaluated for downstream risk and authority, not applied as isolated calculations.

docs.title: Scrum Events and Adaptive Cadences
docs.text:
What people often call “Agile ceremonies,” what Scrum actually defines, and how other adaptive approaches differ.

Terminology first

Agile ceremonies is common informal language. Agile itself does not prescribe one universal set of meetings. Scrum officially calls its five timeboxed elements events: the Sprint, Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, Sprint Review, and Sprint Retrospective. The Sprint contains the other four events. Product Backlog refinement is important ongoing activity, but it is not a formal Scrum event. Other adaptive approaches can use similar cadences without following Scrum, and Kanban does not require the Scrum event structure.

Download the editable Scrum Events quick reference

Study velocity, burn charts, flow metrics, and visual management

docs.title: A cadence creates repeated opportunities to inspect and adapt
docs.text:
Scrum events are formal opportunities for the Scrum Team to create transparency, inspect results, and adapt. Other adaptive approaches use different cadences for planning, replenishment, delivery, review, and improvement. A cadence exists to make feedback and decisions frequent enough to reduce risk; it is not a calendar of status meetings.

The Sprint contains the other Scrum events and produces a usable Increment toward the Sprint Goal. Sprint Planning establishes why the Sprint is valuable, what can be done, and how the selected work will be delivered. The Daily Scrum lets Developers inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt their plan. Sprint Review examines the outcome with stakeholders and may change future Product Backlog ordering. Sprint Retrospective examines team effectiveness and selects improvements. Backlog refinement is an ongoing activity, not an official Scrum event. Kanban cadences and flow reviews should be described by their own system rather than relabeled as Scrum events.

For ServiceBridge, a Sprint Review shows users abandoning an appointment step. The Product Owner uses the evidence to reorder a usability improvement ahead of a lower-value report. In the Retrospective, the team separately finds that late accessibility checks caused rework and changes its working agreement. One event changes product direction; the other improves the way the team works. Hybrid governance may use the same evidence at a release or compliance gate without turning the Sprint Review into formal project acceptance. On the exam, identify what is being inspected—goal progress, product outcome, or team effectiveness—before choosing the event.

docs.title: Event overview
docs.text: Event Simple purpose Primary participants Typical result Sprint Create value through a usable Increment while progressing toward the Product Goal. Scrum Team Usable Increment, Product Goal progress, and learning Sprint Planning Decide why the Sprint is valuable, what can be completed, and how the selected work will be approached. Entire Scrum Team Sprint Goal and Sprint Backlog Daily Scrum Inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the immediate plan. Developers Updated actionable plan for the next day Sprint Review Inspect the Sprint outcome with stakeholders and decide what to do next. Scrum Team, Relevant stakeholders Feedback, changed understanding, and possible Product Backlog adaptation Sprint Retrospective Increase quality and team effectiveness. Entire Scrum Team Concrete improvement actions

  3. Sprint Reviewoutcome + stakeholder feedback
  4. Sprint Retrospectivequality + effectiveness improvements

Product Backlog refinementongoing activity across the Sprint—not an official event

Feedback loopsReview adapts the Product Backlog; Retrospective improvement affects the next Sprint

docs.title: The five Scrum events
docs.text:
Official Scrum event

Sprint Official purposeCreate value through a usable Increment while progressing toward the Product Goal. ParticipantsScrum Team WhenA new Sprint begins immediately after the previous Sprint concludes. Maximum timeboxFixed length of one month or less. The Sprint retains a fixed length of one month or less; the contained events are usually shorter. Primary inputsProduct Goal, Product Backlog, Definition of Done Outputs or adaptationsIncrement, Product Backlog Related rolesProduct Owner, Scrum Master, Developers What happens

During the Sprint, the Sprint Goal is not endangered, quality does not decrease, and scope may be clarified and renegotiated with the Product Owner as learning occurs. Work needed to achieve the Product Goal happens within Sprints. Only the Product Owner can cancel a Sprint, and only when the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete.

Common misunderstanding: A Sprint is not merely a development phase. The Product Owner alone may cancel a Sprint when the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete.

PMP-style distinction: Protect the Sprint Goal and quality; clarify and renegotiate scope with the Product Owner as learning occurs.

Hybrid-project treatment

The Sprint governs adaptive delivery work; project funding, contracts, external milestones, compliance, and transition dates remain in the surrounding governance model.

Official Scrum event

Sprint Planning Official purposeDecide why the Sprint is valuable, what can be completed, and how the selected work will be approached. ParticipantsEntire Scrum Team WhenStarts the Sprint. Maximum timeboxMaximum eight hours for a one-month Sprint. Usually shorter for shorter Sprints. Primary inputsProduct Goal, Product Backlog, Definition of Done Outputs or adaptationsSprint Goal, Sprint Backlog Related rolesProduct Owner, Scrum Master, Developers What happens

The Scrum Team addresses three topics: Why is this Sprint valuable? What can be done this Sprint? How will the chosen work get done? The Product Owner brings priorities and context. Developers select and plan work using capacity and past performance, and they are responsible for sizing it. The Product Owner or a project manager does not assign Developers' detailed work.

Common misunderstanding: The Product Owner does not assign Developers' detailed work, Developers are responsible for sizing their work.

PMP-style distinction: Remember the three topics: why valuable, what can be done, and how it will get done.

Hybrid-project treatment

The team plans Sprint work within project-level release, compliance, dependency, and milestone constraints.

Official Scrum event

Daily Scrum Official purposeInspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the immediate plan. ParticipantsDevelopers WhenEvery working day of the Sprint at the same time and place to reduce complexity. Maximum timeboxFifteen minutes. The maximum remains fifteen minutes. Primary inputsSprint Goal, Sprint Backlog Outputs or adaptationsSprint Backlog Related rolesDevelopers, Scrum Master, Product Owner What happens

Developers may choose any structure that focuses on progress toward the Sprint Goal and produces an actionable plan. The former three-question format is optional. Additional discussions can follow. Product Owner or Scrum Master attendance does not convert the event into a status meeting for them.

Common misunderstanding: The old three-question format is optional. Product Owner or Scrum Master attendance does not make this their status meeting.

PMP-style distinction: A manager asking each person for status is not the purpose of the Daily Scrum.

Hybrid-project treatment

Project reporting consumes transparent Sprint information without turning the Daily Scrum into a manager-led status meeting.

Official Scrum event

Sprint Review Official purposeInspect the Sprint outcome with stakeholders and decide what to do next. ParticipantsScrum Team, Relevant stakeholders WhenNear the end of the Sprint before the Sprint Retrospective. Maximum timeboxMaximum four hours for a one-month Sprint. Usually shorter for shorter Sprints. Primary inputsProduct Goal, Product Backlog, Increment Outputs or adaptationsProduct Backlog Related rolesProduct Owner, Scrum Master, Developers, Stakeholder, Customer or Acceptance Authority What happens

The Scrum Team and key stakeholders inspect the outcome, progress toward the Product Goal, and relevant environmental or market changes. They collaborate on what to do next and may adapt the Product Backlog. It is a working session, not merely a presentation, demo, or ceremonial sign-off.

Common misunderstanding: It is a working session rather than merely a demo. It is not automatically formal acceptance.

PMP-style distinction: Focus on product outcome, Product Goal progress, environmental change, stakeholder feedback, and next steps.

Hybrid-project treatment

Review feedback may adapt the Product Backlog but does not automatically approve baseline change or constitute contractual acceptance.

Official Scrum event

Sprint Retrospective Official purposeIncrease quality and team effectiveness. ParticipantsEntire Scrum Team WhenConcludes the Sprint after the Sprint Review. Maximum timeboxMaximum three hours for a one-month Sprint. Usually shorter for shorter Sprints. Primary inputsSprint Goal, Sprint Backlog, Definition of Done Outputs or adaptationsSprint Backlog, Definition of Done Related rolesProduct Owner, Scrum Master, Developers What happens

The Scrum Team inspects people, interactions, processes, tools, and the Definition of Done. It selects the most useful improvements, which may enter the next Sprint Backlog. The event is not a blame session, performance appraisal, or product-acceptance review.

Common misunderstanding: It is not a blame session or performance appraisal. It examines how the team works rather than stakeholder satisfaction with the product.

PMP-style distinction: Inspect people, interactions, processes, tools, and Definition of Done; select useful improvements.

Hybrid-project treatment

Team improvements enter the next Sprint while project-level lessons, quality, risk, and governance records remain coordinated separately.

docs.title: Review versus Retrospective
docs.text: Distinction Sprint Review Sprint Retrospective Primary focus Product outcome and progress toward the Product Goal Quality and how the Scrum Team works Participants Scrum Team and relevant stakeholders Entire Scrum Team Typical adaptation Product Backlog, direction, or next steps People, interactions, processes, tools, Definition of Done, or next-Sprint improvement Not the purpose Merely demonstrating work or automatic contractual acceptance Blame, performance appraisal, or deciding whether stakeholders like the product

docs.title: Backlog refinement: important, but not a Scrum event
docs.text: Refinement can clarify items, split large items, add detail, revise order, estimate or size work, discuss acceptance conditions, and remove obsolete items. It occurs as needed throughout the Sprint. The Product Owner remains accountable for effective Product Backlog management, while Developers are responsible for sizing the work they will perform. Scrum prescribes neither a required refinement meeting nor a fixed cadence; a scheduled session is a team practice, not a sixth Scrum event.

docs.title: Adaptive cadences beyond Scrum
docs.text:
Adaptive teams may use the following contextual practices. They are not universal mandatory ceremonies, and their purpose matters more than copying a meeting name.

  • Release planning
  • Roadmap review
  • Iteration planning
  • Customer feedback sessions
  • Technical design discussions
  • Risk review
  • Dependency coordination
  • Demonstrations
  • Communities of practice
  • Improvement workshops

docs.title: Kanban does not prescribe the Scrum event cycle
docs.text:
The minimal Kanban Guide emphasizes:

  • Define and visualize the workflow
  • Actively manage work items
  • Control work in progress
  • Examine flow metrics
  • Improve the workflow

Kanban teams may use regular cadences or make just-in-time workflow changes. The minimal guide does not require Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, Sprint Review, or Sprint Retrospective. A team may combine Scrum events with Kanban practices, but it should label that combination accurately rather than calling every flow meeting a Scrum event.

docs.title: Scrum artifacts and commitments
docs.text:
These concepts are defined here as the Atlas's focused adaptive-artifact reference. They do not expand the predictive 41-artifact inventory.

Product Goal

The long-term objective for the Scrum Team and the commitment for the Product Backlog.

Primary ownership: Product Owner

Product Backlog

An emergent, ordered list of what is needed to improve the product.

Primary ownership: Product Owner

Sprint Goal

The single objective for the Sprint and the commitment for the Sprint Backlog.

Primary ownership: Developers, Product Owner, Scrum Master

Sprint Backlog

The Sprint Goal, selected Product Backlog items, and the Developers' actionable delivery plan.

Primary ownership: Developers

Increment

A concrete stepping stone toward the Product Goal that is usable and meets the Definition of Done.

Primary ownership: Developers

Definition of Done

A formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets required product quality measures.

Primary ownership: Developers

docs.title: Hybrid example: ServiceBridge Modernization
docs.text:
Project governance cadence

Reserved project decisions

Funding, contracts, release milestones, compliance obligations, transition dates, budget, vendor, risk, and governance reviews.

⇄evidence, thresholds, decisions

Scrum delivery cadence

Adaptive software delivery

Sprint Planning, delivery with Daily Scrum, Sprint Review, Sprint Retrospective, and ongoing Product Backlog refinement.

Sprint Planning controls iteration work; Daily Scrum coordinates Developers; Sprint Review gathers stakeholder feedback; and Sprint Retrospective improves delivery. Project milestone, vendor, risk, budget, and governance reviews continue outside Scrum. Sprint Review does not replace formal baseline change approval or contractual acceptance. Project reporting should use Scrum information without turning Scrum events into management status meetings. This arrangement is an Atlas hybrid synthesis, not an additional Scrum rule.

docs.title: Common exam traps
docs.text:
1. Daily Scrum is not a manager status meeting.
  2. Sprint Review is not merely a demo and is not automatically formal acceptance.
  3. Sprint Retrospective improves quality and team effectiveness.
  4. Product Backlog refinement is not an official Scrum event.
  5. The former three Daily Scrum questions are not mandatory.
  6. The Product Owner orders value; Developers decide how to perform the work.
  7. The Scrum Master enables effectiveness and is not the team's task manager.
  8. Agile does not mean Scrum.
  9. Kanban does not require Scrum events.
  10. Hybrid governance meetings do not replace Scrum events, and Scrum events do not replace project governance.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Obtain the people, facilities, equipment, materials, and other resources needed to perform authorized project work.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: A plan that assumes resources are available does not make them available. Acquisition reconciles project needs with organizational priorities, supplier capacity, timing, and actual assignments. Delayed or unsuitable resources can invalidate schedule, cost, and quality assumptions.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Resource estimates and the resource-management approach define the need, while procurement and organizational processes may help fulfill it. Confirmed assignments and physical resources enable execution, team development, and ongoing management; shortfalls may require replanning or escalation. Acquisition can recur as work packages start or resource needs change.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Acquire Resources secures team and physical resources. Develop Team improves team capability and cohesion after people are assigned, while Manage Team addresses ongoing performance and issues. Estimating a need is not acquiring it.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

An airport baggage-system upgrade needs controls engineers, overnight installation crews, test equipment, and temporary storage. The project manager negotiates internal assignments and contracts specialized equipment for the required windows. The confirmed resources allow detailed work to begin and the newly formed team to develop operating routines.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Look for negotiation, assignment, or obtaining resources—not training or resolving team performance.
  2. The project manager may need functional managers, procurement staff, or sellers to secure resources.
  3. If acquisition differs from the plan, assess schedule, cost, and risk effects rather than silently assuming the gap away.

docs.title: What this process does
docs.text:
Close Project or Phase confirms that an authorized project or phase may end and that remaining responsibilities have been completed, resolved, or transferred.

Finishing production is not enough. Closure addresses acceptance, transition, contracts, finances, records, knowledge, resources, unresolved items, and formal authority so the organization does not lose obligations when the team disbands.

docs.title: What is checked before closure
docs.text:
The project manager reviews the Project Management Plan, accepted deliverables, agreements, transition evidence, open risks and issues, change status, financial records, quality and compliance evidence, lessons, and other closure requirements.

Procurements are closed by the applicable commercial authority. Accepted results and operating responsibility are transferred. The final report compares intended and actual project results. Records and lessons are finalized and archived. Resources are released through the proper organizational process. The sponsor or designated governance role provides formal closure according to the governing method.

For ServiceBridge, launch does not by itself close the project. Operations must receive support procedures and access, contractual obligations must be addressed, acceptance evidence must be stored, open items must have owners, and the benefits measure must be transferred to the operations director.

docs.title: Related decisions remain distinct
docs.text:
Project closure is not procurement closure. Phase closure is not project closure. Transition is not acceptance. Releasing the team is not formal closure. A terminated project still requires an orderly record of the reason, completed work, assets, obligations, contracts, finances, and lessons.

Benefits may be measured after closure. The registered sources contain an unresolved difference about whether benefit realization defines project completion, so the Atlas separates formal closure from the continuing benefit owner rather than stating one universal rule.

Adaptive projects may transition increments during delivery but still need final project-level closure. Hybrid work can close releases, phases, and agreements at different times while preserving one coordinated view of remaining obligations.

For the exam, obtain acceptance before closure, follow the organization’s formal closure process, archive knowledge, release resources appropriately, and transfer continuing ownership explicitly.

Scope: Typical allocation only; the charter, agreements, policy, and team design determine the actual assignment and delegation.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Confirm that the project or phase is formally complete, transition its results, resolve remaining administrative obligations, and preserve useful records and learning.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: Finishing the last activity does not prove that obligations, acceptance, transition, contracts, records, and organizational learning have been addressed. Formal closure establishes a defensible end state and releases attention and resources deliberately. Skipping it leaves unresolved ownership, open commitments, and weak evidence of completion.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Closure depends on completion information, acceptance where applicable, and resolution of outstanding work. It consolidates final records and lessons, transitions the result, and closes the authorized project or phase; procurement closure may also occur as contracts reach completion. A terminated project still requires an orderly close.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Close Project or Phase is a management process, not the moment the final scheduled activity ends. Deliverable acceptance may occur earlier through Validate Scope, and individual contracts may be closed through Control Procurements while the wider project continues.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

After a university opens a new research laboratory, the team confirms acceptance, transfers operating procedures to facilities staff, closes remaining supplier obligations, archives approvals, and documents commissioning lessons. Only then does the sponsor formally close the project and release the remaining project resources.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Look for formal completion, transition, records, and lessons—not merely completed production work.
  2. Premature termination changes the reason for closing, not the need to close responsibly.
  3. Accepted deliverables support closure, but acceptance and project closure are distinct decisions.
