docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Elicit, analyze, and document stakeholder needs and conditions so later scope, design, verification, and acceptance decisions have a traceable basis.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: A solution can satisfy its stated scope and still fail if the underlying needs were incomplete, ambiguous, or attributed to the wrong stakeholders. Requirements work makes expectations examinable and exposes conflicts early. Traceability helps the team understand why each requirement exists and how it will be checked.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Stakeholder identification and the planned scope approach establish whom to involve and how to work. The resulting requirements inform Define Scope, quality planning, solution work, and eventual verification and acceptance; they may be refined as understanding grows. Collection explores needs—it does not yet settle the complete project boundary.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Collect Requirements captures and analyzes needs. Define Scope decides which requirements and constraints are included in the detailed boundary, while Validate Scope later seeks formal acceptance of completed deliverables.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

A clinic is redesigning patient intake. Interviews and observation reveal needs from patients, nurses, privacy staff, interpreters, and billing specialists, including accessibility and data-handling conditions. The team traces those needs into the proposed service scope and later test and acceptance criteria.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. If stakeholders are expressing needs or resolving requirement ambiguity, the work precedes detailed scope definition.
  2. A requested feature is not automatically approved project scope; it must be evaluated with other needs and constraints.
  3. Traceability connects a requirement to its origin and downstream verification, reducing orphan requirements.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Obtain and evaluate seller responses, select an appropriate seller, negotiate as authorized, and establish an agreement for external work.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: A sourcing strategy becomes useful only when the project applies it fairly and selects a seller whose offer can satisfy the need. This process turns market responses into a governed commercial commitment. Weak evaluation can trade a low initial price for unacceptable risk, capability, or contract ambiguity.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Procurement documents, evaluation criteria, seller responses, and organizational authority shape the selection. The resulting agreement and seller relationship enable externally supplied work and become the basis for Control Procurements. Additional procurements may be conducted as later needs are authorized.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Conduct Procurements selects and contracts with a seller. Plan Procurement Management defines the sourcing approach, while Control Procurements monitors agreement performance, changes, claims, and closure after award.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

A transit agency evaluates proposals for fare-payment equipment using technical compliance, implementation approach, support capacity, delivery risk, and total commercial terms. After clarification and authorized negotiation, it selects a seller and executes an agreement. The project team then controls performance against that agreement.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Seller selection should follow the approved evaluation approach rather than an improvised preference.
  2. Contract authority and procurement rules matter; the project manager may participate without having sole authority to bind the organization.
  3. After award, performance issues belong in Control Procurements rather than repeating source selection.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Analyze cost performance and forecasts, influence the factors causing variance, and manage changes to the approved cost baseline.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: Recording invoices does not explain whether the project is receiving the expected progress for its spending or where final cost is heading. Cost control connects actual performance, remaining work, and forecasts so management can act. It protects financial commitments while allowing justified change through governance.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Execution supplies cost and progress information that is compared with the baseline established during budgeting. Analysis may produce updated forecasts, corrective actions, or change requests, and its conclusions contribute to overall project monitoring. The process repeats as new performance evidence becomes available.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Control Costs evaluates cost performance against the baseline and forecasts outcomes. Determine Budget creates the authorized baseline, while Monitor and Control Project Work integrates cost findings with other project dimensions.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

A housing retrofit program has spent less than planned, but completed units are also below plan because specialist crews are unavailable. Cost control analyzes the relationship between spending and progress, updates the completion forecast, and recommends a staffing response rather than treating the apparent underspend as good performance.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Cost status requires context about accomplished work; lower spending alone is not necessarily favorable.
  2. Forecast updates do not automatically change the approved cost baseline.
  3. A baseline-changing response follows the project’s change-control authority.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Manage seller and buyer performance against agreements, administer changes and claims, maintain appropriate records, and close contractual relationships.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: Signing an agreement does not ensure that external work will meet project needs. Contract control connects technical progress with commercial obligations and provides a governed way to address variance, change, disputes, payment, and completion. Neglect creates both delivery and legal exposure.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Agreements, performance evidence, inspections, invoices, and correspondence provide the control basis. Findings may lead to corrective action, contractual change, claims handling, or broader project change control; completed obligations support contract closure and eventually project closure. Oversight continues for each active procurement.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Control Procurements manages the contractual relationship and agreement performance. Control Quality verifies technical conformance of results, and Close Project or Phase closes the wider project or phase. Contract closure can occur before project closure.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

A software vendor is meeting feature requirements but missing agreed response times and documentation dates. The buyer reviews evidence against the agreement, issues the required notice, agrees on a recovery action, and processes an authorized contractual change. Final completion is documented when all obligations are satisfied.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Use the agreement as the governing reference for seller obligations and buyer remedies.
  2. Technical acceptance, payment authorization, contract closure, and project closure are related but distinct decisions.
  3. A contract change may also require integrated project change control when project baselines are affected.

docs.title: What this process does
docs.text:
Control Quality checks completed work and records whether it conforms to requirements, quality metrics, specifications, and test expectations.

The process uses inspection, testing, measurement, data analysis, and other planned checks. Its purpose is not merely to find defects. It produces evidence that supports correction, process learning, release decisions, and formal acceptance.

docs.title: From completed to verified
docs.text:
The team submits a completed Deliverable with the applicable requirements and quality information. The verifier performs the planned checks and records actual results in quality-control measurements and test documents.

If the evidence demonstrates conformance, the result becomes a Verified Deliverable. If it fails, the team records defects or findings, analyzes the cause, routes any required change, performs authorized correction, and retests.

For ServiceBridge, the migration package is checked for record counts, field accuracy, retention attributes, reconciliation exceptions, and error tolerance. Passing those checks verifies the migration package. Customer acceptance still follows separately.

docs.title: Control Quality is not Validate Scope
docs.text:
Control Quality answers whether the result conforms. Validate Scope asks the authorized customer or acceptance role whether to accept the verified result. Quality specialists may verify evidence without authority to accept for the customer.

Manage Quality is also different: it examines and improves the processes and quality approach used to create results. Control Quality examines the actual deliverable and its evidence.

Predictive projects may use formal inspection and test stages. Adaptive teams verify continuously through automation, peer review, acceptance tests, and the Definition of Done. Hybrid projects may combine continuous testing with formal compliance, contractual, release, and acceptance gates.

For the exam, Control Quality produces verified deliverables, quality-control measurements, and related findings or change requests. It does not produce formal customer acceptance.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Inspect, measure, and record results to determine whether deliverables and performance conform to defined quality requirements.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: A completed item is not ready for acceptance merely because the team believes it is finished. Objective checks provide evidence of conformance and identify defects or corrective needs before stakeholder acceptance. Without verification, nonconforming work can move downstream and become more expensive to correct.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Quality metrics and completed work provide the basis for inspection and measurement. Conforming results become verified deliverables that can proceed to Validate Scope; defects may lead to rework, process improvement, or change requests. Control Quality repeats as deliverables are produced.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Manage Quality evaluates and improves the processes used to create results. Control Quality checks the results themselves. Validate Scope then obtains formal acceptance of verified deliverables from the authorized stakeholder.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

Before a new warehouse conveyor is presented to operations, the team tests throughput, safety interlocks, stopping distance, and error handling against the agreed criteria. Failed tests trigger correction and retesting. The passing system becomes a verified deliverable for the operations sponsor’s acceptance review.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Verification answers whether specified criteria were met; acceptance answers whether the authorized stakeholder accepts the result.
  2. A defect found during inspection belongs in Control Quality even if its cause later drives Manage Quality improvement.
  3. Follow the deliverable state: completed, verified, and accepted are not interchangeable.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Confirm that physical resources are available and used as planned, identify variances, and take action when equipment, materials, or facilities do not match project needs.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: Even acquired resources can be unavailable, consumed faster than expected, misallocated, or released at the wrong time. Physical-resource control protects work continuity and cost and schedule assumptions. It creates active visibility rather than relying on inventory or allocation plans that may no longer be current.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Resource plans, assignments, usage information, and execution needs provide the comparison basis. Variances may lead to reallocation, replenishment, corrective action, or change requests and inform overall monitoring. Control continues while physical resources are required.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Control Resources concerns physical resources such as equipment, materials, and facilities. Manage Team addresses people’s performance and relationships. Acquire Resources obtains resources; control checks their continuing availability and use.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

A road project discovers that aggregate is being consumed faster than planned and a shared compactor has been reassigned. The team reconciles usage, secures a replacement equipment window, and adjusts deliveries before paving stops. Cost and schedule forecasts are updated with the resulting effects.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Use Control Resources for physical availability and utilization, not personnel coaching.
  2. Acquisition success does not eliminate the need to monitor consumption, condition, allocation, and release.
  3. A material or equipment variance may require corrective action without automatically changing a baseline.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Assess schedule performance, forecast timing outcomes, and manage changes to the approved schedule baseline.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: A published schedule becomes obsolete unless actual progress and emerging constraints are analyzed. Schedule control distinguishes ordinary forecast movement from variance that requires action or formal change. It helps the team respond before missed dates cascade across dependent work.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Execution supplies progress and current forecasts, which are compared with the schedule model and baseline. Analysis may lead to corrective action, resequencing, updated forecasts, or change requests; approved baseline changes are incorporated through governance. Control recurs throughout the work rather than waiting for a missed milestone.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Control Schedule analyzes timing performance and manages the schedule baseline. Monitor and Control Project Work integrates schedule findings with the project’s overall health, and Perform Integrated Change Control decides controlled change requests.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

A public-health campaign finds that translation approvals are running two weeks late. The scheduler updates actual progress, analyzes downstream printing and distribution effects, and tests recovery options. The team resequences unaffected work and submits a baseline change only where the authorized completion commitment must move.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Updating a forecast is not necessarily the same as changing the approved schedule baseline.
  2. Use dependency logic to assess the effect of delay rather than treating every late activity as equally important.
  3. Corrective action can be proposed in schedule control but may require integrated approval before implementation.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Monitor the status of project and product scope and manage proposed or actual changes to the approved scope baseline.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: Scope can drift through informal requests, misunderstood requirements, or work that no longer matches approved boundaries. Active control detects variance, assesses its cause and impact, and routes necessary changes through the established process. It protects the baseline without assuming that all change is undesirable.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Actual work and completed deliverables are compared with approved scope information. Variances or stakeholder requests may lead to corrective action or change requests, while approved changes update the relevant baseline and plans. Control occurs throughout delivery and uses requirement traceability and acceptance information where relevant.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Validate Scope asks whether an authorized stakeholder accepts a completed deliverable. Control Scope asks whether current work and boundaries remain aligned with the approved scope baseline and manages changes to that baseline.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

During a retail-store rollout, local managers ask each site team to add custom signage not included in the approved package. The project manager identifies the cumulative scope impact, stops informal additions, and submits a consolidated change for cost, schedule, and brand review. Approved variants are then incorporated into the baseline.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Scope control does not mean refusing every change; it means preventing uncontrolled change.
  2. A rejected deliverable may trigger corrective work, while a requested boundary change may require integrated change control.
  3. Acceptance status and baseline status answer different questions.

docs.title: What this process does
docs.text:
Create WBS organizes the complete approved project scope into a hierarchy of manageable components. WBS means Work Breakdown Structure.

The process solves a planning problem: a scope statement can define the boundary without showing how the work will be estimated, assigned, scheduled, costed, and controlled. Decomposition breaks large deliverables into smaller parts until the team reaches a useful level of management detail.

docs.title: Decomposition in plain language
docs.text:
The team starts with the Project Scope Statement and Requirements Documentation. It identifies the major deliverables and project work, then divides them into smaller components. The team checks that the hierarchy includes all approved scope and does not add work outside the boundary. This is often called the 100 percent rule: the WBS should represent all project scope, including project-management work, without counting the same scope twice.

A work package is the lowest WBS component for which cost and duration can be estimated and managed. It describes scope, not the actions on the schedule. Activities are developed later from work packages.

A control account is a management control point where scope, schedule, and cost can be integrated and measured. A planning package is known work below a control account that will be decomposed later because current detail is insufficient. It makes uncertainty visible instead of forcing false precision.

The WBS dictionary explains each component’s boundary and related information. Without it, a label such as “Migration” could mean extraction only to one person and full reconciliation and cutover to another.

docs.title: ServiceBridge example
docs.text:
ServiceBridge includes a Data Migration deliverable. The team decomposes it into data profiling, cleansing, transformation, trial migration, reconciliation, production migration, and archival confirmation. A work package may cover trial migration and reconciliation. Activities later include preparing the environment, running scripts, reviewing exceptions, and approving results.

The approved Project Scope Statement, WBS, and WBS dictionary become the Scope Baseline. That baseline then supports activity definition, estimating, budgeting, procurement, risk work, and scope control.

Predictive projects commonly create a broad WBS before detailed schedule and cost planning. Adaptive teams may decompose outcomes into a product structure, roadmap, releases, and backlog items instead of fixing all detailed scope early. Hybrid projects can maintain a controlled WBS for fixed obligations while refining product detail iteratively.

For the exam, the WBS is deliverable-oriented scope decomposition. It is not a schedule, organization chart, responsibility matrix, or list of activities.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Decompose the approved project scope into manageable components that provide a structured basis for planning, responsibility, estimating, and control.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: Large deliverables are too broad to estimate, assign, or monitor reliably. Decomposition creates a complete, organized view of the authorized scope at a level the project can manage. Poor decomposition hides work, duplicates responsibility, or encourages teams to schedule activities before understanding the deliverables.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: The detailed scope description and requirements establish what must be represented. The WBS organizes that scope into progressively smaller components and supports activity definition, estimates, budgeting, responsibility decisions, and scope control. Decomposition can be elaborated as information becomes available, while the approved scope baseline remains controlled.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Create WBS decomposes deliverables and project scope into manageable components. Define Activities later identifies the actions needed to produce those components. A WBS is not a chronological task list or organization chart.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

A utility is replacing a water-treatment control system. The team decomposes the project into design, equipment, site preparation, installation, migration, testing, training, and transition components, then breaks each to a manageable level. Schedule planners use those components to define activities without losing sight of the complete authorized scope.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Think deliverable-oriented decomposition before activity sequencing.
  2. The WBS should represent the full authorized scope; omitted work will distort estimates and control.
  3. More detail is not automatically better—the useful level is one the project can estimate, assign, and monitor.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Identify the specific schedule activities needed to produce the project’s planned work packages and deliverables.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: A WBS shows what scope must be delivered but may not expose the actions needed to create it. Defining activities translates manageable scope components into work that can be ordered, estimated, assigned, and tracked. Missing activities create false confidence in dates and resource needs.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: The scope baseline and scheduling approach provide the structure for identifying work. The activity list then supports dependency sequencing, duration and resource estimates, and schedule development. Activities can be elaborated as near-term work becomes clearer, especially in rolling-wave planning.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Create WBS decomposes scope into deliverable-oriented components. Define Activities identifies the actions needed to produce those components. Sequence Activities then determines their logical relationships.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

For a pharmaceutical packaging-line upgrade, the WBS includes a validated labeling station. The team defines activities for design approval, equipment preparation, installation, software configuration, protocol execution, training, and release. Those activities can then be sequenced and estimated.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. If the work is being translated from work packages into schedulable actions, this is activity definition.
  2. Do not confuse identifying an activity with deciding its order or duration.
  3. Progressive elaboration can add detail without implying that the original scope was uncontrolled.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Develop a detailed description of the project and product boundaries by selecting and clarifying the work and results the project will include.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: A requirements set can contain competing wishes, optional features, and unresolved boundaries. Scope definition turns that information into a coherent statement of what the project will deliver and what lies outside its responsibility. Weak boundaries create expectation gaps and uncontrolled expansion.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Defined requirements, assumptions, constraints, and planning decisions provide the basis for the detailed scope. The result supports decomposition in Create WBS, schedule and cost planning, quality criteria, and later scope validation and control. It may be refined iteratively as product understanding improves through approved decisions.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Collect Requirements identifies and analyzes needs; Define Scope chooses and describes the included boundary; Create WBS decomposes that approved boundary into manageable components. Definition is not decomposition.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

A museum plans a traveling exhibition. Requirements include multilingual interpretation, educational programming, insurance, and possible augmented reality. The team defines the funded exhibition boundary, explicitly excludes a permanent gallery renovation, and passes the approved scope description into WBS development and estimating.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Look for decisions about what is included and excluded, not merely a list of stakeholder requests.
  2. The detailed scope description precedes decomposition into the WBS.
  3. Refining scope is legitimate; changing an approved baseline later requires appropriate control.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Aggregate project cost estimates into an authorized, time-aware cost baseline and establish the funding view needed to support the work.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: A collection of estimates does not show when money is needed, what performance will be measured against, or whether the project is financially authorized. Budget determination reconciles estimates with schedule, funding constraints, and governance. Without it, spending decisions lack a coherent baseline.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Cost estimates and schedule timing are consolidated, reviewed, and aligned with funding limits. The approved cost baseline supports Control Costs and overall performance reporting; later baseline changes require appropriate authorization. Budget development may iterate when estimates, timing, or funding constraints cannot be reconciled.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Estimate Costs asks what individual work is expected to cost. Determine Budget aggregates and authorizes the baseline and funding profile used to measure cost performance. A total estimate is not automatically an approved cost baseline.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

A food manufacturer combines equipment, construction, commissioning, training, and contingency estimates for a new production line. Mapping those costs to the schedule reveals a funding peak during installation, so finance and the sponsor adjust the release plan before approving the baseline. Control Costs later measures performance against it.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Look for aggregation, authorization, funding timing, or establishment of the cost baseline.
  2. The cost baseline is a performance reference; actual expenditures and forecasts are compared with it later.
  3. If funding constraints force schedule or scope tradeoffs, planning may iterate before authorization.

docs.title: Purpose and result
docs.text:
Develop Project Charter is the process used to prepare the high-level information needed for an authorized sponsor or governance body to decide whether the project should begin. Its main results are an approved Project Charter and the initial Assumption Log.

The Project Charter page is the canonical explanation of what the charter means, what it contains, how it is created, and how it differs from detailed planning documents. This process reference preserves the process relationships, roles, inputs, outputs, delivery approaches, and exam links around that explanation.

docs.title: Who authorizes the project
docs.text:
The sponsor, project initiator, or another authorized leader issues or approves the charter. The proposed project manager may help develop it, but does not normally authorize the project alone.

Approval formally authorizes the project and gives the project manager authority to apply organizational resources within the organization’s limits.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Establish that a proposed project or phase is worth undertaking, authorize it to proceed, and give the project manager authority to coordinate the work.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: A promising idea is not yet an authorized project. The charter connects the intended outcome to an organizational need and establishes enough authority and shared direction to justify detailed planning. Without that foundation, teams may spend money or make commitments without a recognized sponsor, objective, or decision boundary.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Authorization draws on the business reason for the work and the sponsor’s expectations. Once the charter exists, stakeholders can be identified more deliberately and the integrated project management plan can be developed within an approved mandate. A charter may be revisited when a phase is authorized, but it is not the detailed plan for performing the work.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Develop Project Charter authorizes and frames the project or phase; Develop Project Management Plan integrates the detailed approach for executing, monitoring, and closing it. Approval to investigate or begin is not the same as approval of every later baseline or delivery decision.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

A hospital proposes replacing its medication-dispensing system after repeated delay incidents. The sponsor confirms the safety objective, expected operational benefit, initial boundaries, and project manager authority in the charter. Department leaders then use that authorization to identify affected clinical stakeholders and begin integrated planning.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. When a scenario lacks formal authority or sponsor alignment, look to the charter before detailed planning.
  2. A charter is high-level authorization; it does not substitute for the project management plan or its subsidiary components.
  3. The project manager may help develop the charter, but authorization comes from an appropriate sponsor or initiating authority.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Combine the project’s planning decisions into a coordinated basis for directing work, measuring performance, controlling change, and closing the effort.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: Separate scope, schedule, cost, quality, resource, and risk decisions can conflict even when each looks reasonable alone. Integration exposes those conflicts and establishes how the parts will work together. Without an integrated plan, teams optimize locally and lack a common basis for execution or control.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: The charter supplies authority and high-level direction; subsidiary planning and baselines contribute progressively more detail. The resulting plan guides Direct and Manage Project Work and provides the reference used by monitoring and integrated change control. It is progressively elaborated and updated through controlled decisions rather than frozen after one planning event.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: The project charter explains why the project is authorized and establishes high-level direction. The project management plan explains how the authorized work will be executed and controlled by integrating approved planning components. Neither is simply a schedule.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

A manufacturer is preparing a new product launch. Marketing’s release date, engineering’s validation work, procurement lead times, quality reviews, and budget constraints are reconciled into one governing plan. Delivery teams use that integrated basis to coordinate work, while proposed baseline changes are evaluated across all affected areas.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Choose this process when the issue is coordination among planning components, not creation of one specialized plan.
  2. Approved baselines and subsidiary plans are components of the integrated plan; they are not unrelated documents.
  3. An approved change is incorporated through controlled updates, not by informally rewriting the plan.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Integrate activity logic, duration and resource estimates, calendars, constraints, and project objectives into an analyzed schedule model and usable timing commitments.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: Individual estimates do not reveal the combined feasibility of the project. Schedule development exposes critical relationships, resource conflicts, limited flexibility, and tradeoffs before dates are approved. Without integrated analysis, milestones may be politically attractive but operationally impossible.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Activities, dependencies, durations, resource information, and constraints converge here. The resulting schedule guides execution and becomes the reference for Control Schedule; iteration may send the team back to refine estimates, logic, or resource choices. Approved changes and actual performance later update the model through control.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Sequence Activities creates dependency logic and Estimate Activity Durations supplies time estimates. Develop Schedule combines those inputs with resources and constraints to calculate and optimize the overall model.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

A renewable-energy developer integrates permitting, equipment fabrication, site work, grid interconnection, testing, and seasonal access constraints. Analysis reveals that transformer delivery governs the target energization date, so the team adjusts procurement timing and parallel site work before approving the schedule.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Choose Develop Schedule when separate scheduling inputs are being integrated into dates and a feasible model.
  2. A schedule forecast can change with actual performance without every change becoming an unauthorized baseline change.
  3. Compression or resource adjustment should be evaluated for effects on cost, risk, and quality.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Improve team members’ capabilities, working relationships, and environment so the project team can perform effectively together.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: Assembling skilled individuals does not automatically create a capable project team. Shared practices, trust, feedback, learning, and a workable environment reduce coordination loss and improve collective performance. Development is especially important when the team is new, distributed, or working across organizational boundaries.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Acquired team members and the resource-management approach establish the starting conditions. Development activities strengthen capability during execution and can respond to observations from Manage Team; learning also supports project knowledge. Team development continues as membership and challenges change.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Develop Team builds capability and cohesion. Manage Team tracks performance, gives feedback, resolves conflict, and coordinates changes for specific performance needs. Acquire Resources obtains the people in the first place.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

A distributed product-launch team has marketing, regulatory, engineering, and regional sales members who have never worked together. They establish shared decision routines, practice handoffs through a launch simulation, and pair regional staff with subject experts. Later performance issues are handled through Manage Team.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Training, team-building, recognition, and improved working conditions point toward team development.
  2. Conflict can reveal a development need, but handling a specific performance issue is often Manage Team.
  3. Team development is iterative; it does not end after a kickoff workshop.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Lead and perform the authorized work, produce project results, and implement approved changes in accordance with the project management plan.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: Planning has value only when coordinated action turns it into deliverables and usable work results. This process aligns people, resources, and approved decisions during delivery. Without it, execution becomes a collection of disconnected tasks and unauthorized adjustments.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: The project management plan supplies the governing direction, while approved changes may alter what the team performs. Work results and performance information feed quality, knowledge, monitoring, and change-control activities. Execution and control interact continuously; discovering a variance does not itself authorize the team to change a baseline.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Direct and Manage Project Work performs authorized work and approved changes. Monitor and Control Project Work evaluates overall performance, while Perform Integrated Change Control decides what to do with change requests. Approval and implementation are separate decisions.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

During an office relocation, the team coordinates furniture installation, network cutover, staff communications, and approved floor-plan changes. Progress and issues are reported for monitoring, and only approved changes are incorporated into the work. The result is a functioning workplace ready for operational handoff.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. If the scenario says an approved change now needs to be carried out, this is the integration process that implements it.
  2. Work performance data originates from doing the work; analysis of overall performance belongs in monitoring.
  3. Do not treat execution as permission to bypass change control when a baseline would be affected.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Estimate the working time each schedule activity will require under the expected resource, productivity, calendar, and uncertainty conditions.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: Dates built from unsupported guesses cannot support commitments or meaningful forecasts. Duration estimation makes assumptions visible and relates the amount of work to the way it will be performed. Ignoring resource capability, availability, or uncertainty produces schedules that fail under ordinary conditions.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Defined and sequenced activities, resource expectations, and relevant experience inform the estimates. The durations are combined with network logic and constraints in Develop Schedule and are refined as knowledge or execution evidence improves. A duration estimate is elapsed working time, not automatically the effort hours or final calendar dates.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Estimate Activity Durations estimates how long an activity takes with expected resources. Estimate Activity Resources determines the types and quantities of resources needed, while Develop Schedule calculates dates for the connected work.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

A laboratory automation project estimates configuration, validation, and training durations using vendor experience, staff availability, test-volume assumptions, and uncertainty around regulatory review. Schedule development then combines those estimates with dependencies and calendars to forecast the go-live date.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Separate duration from effort: adding people does not always reduce elapsed time proportionally.
  2. Estimates should reflect expected resources and calendars, not an unconstrained ideal.
  3. Refinement is normal when better information becomes available; it is not evidence that planning occurred only once.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Estimate the types and quantities of team members, materials, equipment, facilities, and other resources needed for each activity.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: Duration and cost estimates are unreliable when resource assumptions remain implicit. This process tests whether planned activities can be staffed and supplied in a realistic way and exposes scarcity, capability, or availability concerns. It creates a basis for acquisition and schedule analysis without promising that every resource is already secured.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Defined activities, work requirements, organizational capacity, and the resource-management approach shape the estimates. The results inform duration and cost estimates, schedule development, procurement decisions, and Acquire Resources; they are refined as designs and availability become clearer.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Estimate Activity Resources determines what and how much an activity needs. Estimate Activity Durations estimates elapsed working time with expected resources, and Acquire Resources obtains the selected people and physical resources.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

For a stadium event, planners estimate security staff by entrance and shift, medical teams by attendance profile, generators by electrical load, and barriers by crowd-flow design. Those quantities feed vendor sourcing, staffing assignments, duration planning, and the event budget.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. An estimate of resource type or quantity is not an acquisition commitment.
  2. Resource assumptions affect both duration and cost, so those planning activities often iterate.
  3. Distinguish a capability requirement from a named assignment; acquisition happens later.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Develop reasoned estimates of the monetary resources needed to complete project activities and work.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: Funding and tradeoff decisions require more than a single optimistic total. Cost estimation makes the basis, uncertainty, and components of expected spending visible. Weak estimates obscure risk and make later budget performance difficult to interpret.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Scope, schedule, resource, procurement, and risk information provide the estimating basis. Individual estimates are aggregated and reconciled during Determine Budget and are refined as design or market information improves. Estimating predicts likely cost; it does not itself authorize the total budget.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Estimate Costs develops costs for activities or work components. Determine Budget aggregates those estimates, accounts for timing and authorized reserves as appropriate, and establishes the approved cost baseline and funding requirements.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

A municipal bridge-repair team estimates engineering, traffic control, labor, materials, equipment, environmental monitoring, and specialist subcontract costs using current quantities and market information. The estimates include stated uncertainty and are later aggregated into the funding and cost-baseline decision.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. An estimate supports a decision; it is not the same as an approved budget.
  2. Look for the basis and uncertainty of component costs before aggregation.
  3. Changes in scope, schedule, resources, or risk can require estimates to be revisited.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Discover and describe uncertain events or conditions that could affect objectives, including both threats and opportunities.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: A project can manage only the uncertainties it recognizes or remains prepared to discover. Broad identification draws on diverse perspectives and exposes causes, events, and possible effects before they become issues. Treating the first list as complete leaves the project blind to emerging risk.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: The planned risk approach and current scope, schedule, cost, procurement, stakeholder, and technical information guide the search. Identified risks move into qualitative analysis and, when warranted, quantitative analysis and response planning; identification continues throughout the project.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Identify Risks discovers and describes uncertainty. Perform Qualitative Risk Analysis prioritizes identified risks, while an issue is a condition that has already occurred and needs present action.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

Before a vaccine-storage expansion, the team identifies possible permit delay, refrigeration supply shortage, power instability, staff availability, and an opportunity to combine purchasing with another program. The risks are described with potential causes and effects, then prioritized for analysis.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Include opportunities as well as threats.
  2. Do not jump from a newly identified risk directly to an arbitrary response before assessing significance.
  3. Identification is iterative; execution, changes, and monitoring can reveal new risks.

docs.title: What the process actually does
docs.text:
Identify Stakeholders is the deliberate work of discovering who can influence the project, who is affected by it, who holds relevant knowledge or authority, and who may perceive an effect even when the project team has not recognized one. Its value lies in reducing blind spots before plans, requirements, commitments, and communication patterns harden.

The work is investigative rather than clerical. A project manager does not simply request an organization chart and copy names into a spreadsheet. The team examines the project’s purpose, intended change, boundaries, benefits, agreements, constraints, dependencies, decision rights, affected operations, customers, data, communities, sellers, regulators, and receiving organizations. It then records what is known and what requires further discovery.

docs.title: How stakeholders are discovered
docs.text:
Formal stakeholders include sponsors, governance bodies, functional managers, customers, acceptance authorities, regulators, sellers, and named decision-makers. Informal stakeholders may influence adoption, information flow, working norms, or local decisions without formal authority. Internal stakeholders work within the initiating or performing organizations; external stakeholders include customers, suppliers, partners, regulators, communities, and other affected parties.

Affected people with little formal power require particular attention. Frontline employees, service users, support groups, data subjects, or people represented through accessibility and public-interest advocates may experience the project’s greatest impact while having no budget or approval authority. Hidden and indirect stakeholders can emerge through dependencies: an upstream data owner, a downstream support team, another project competing for specialists, or an operations group expected to sustain the result.

Useful sources include the charter, Business Case, benefits information, agreements, organizational structures, governance and policy records, requirements sources, operational process maps, risk and assumption information, prior lessons, contracts, customer research, interviews, workshops, observation, surveys, and expert judgment. Existing stakeholders should be asked who else is affected or has authority; relying only on the sponsor’s first list reproduces the sponsor’s blind spots.

docs.title: Analysis and outputs
docs.text:
The process creates or updates the Stakeholder Register and may use evidence-based classification such as the Power–Interest Grid. Identification and classification are related but distinct. First determine who belongs in the stakeholder system; then assess authority, influence, impact, interest, information needs, and other context appropriate to the project.

Stakeholder discovery can change the proposed project. A compliance authority may reveal an obligation, a frontline user may expose an accessibility need, or an operations owner may show that transition is infeasible. During initiation, those findings can refine the charter, Business Case, benefits, scope boundary, assumptions, risks, funding, or authorization decision rather than merely feeding later communication.

docs.title: Lifecycle behavior
docs.text:
The initial process occurs during initiation, but identification is iterative. New stakeholders appear when requirements deepen, suppliers are selected, teams reorganize, product increments reach different users, risks occur, or operational ownership changes. The register and analyses should be consulted before major decisions and updated when evidence changes.

Responsibility for discovery is shared even when the project manager coordinates the process. Team members, business analysts, sponsors, product leaders, functional managers, and existing stakeholders each see different parts of the system. Naming an owner for follow-up prevents an uncertain stakeholder lead from disappearing merely because the first workshop could not confirm it.

Predictive projects may schedule formal stakeholder reviews and maintain controlled records. Adaptive teams may discover stakeholders through product research, reviews, demonstrations, collaboration, and incremental releases. Scrum does not prescribe Identify Stakeholders as a named process. Kanban practices can reveal service customers and dependencies but do not replace authorization and stakeholder governance. Hybrid delivery connects frequent discovery to formal sponsor, compliance, contract, milestone, and acceptance decisions.

docs.title: ServiceBridge worked example
docs.text:
ServiceBridge begins with the Chief Customer Officer, Customer-service director, and Service Modernization Program Manager. Reviewing the four deliverables and obligations reveals additional stakeholders: the compliance authority, support-team representative, external implementation seller, frontline user representative, operations owner, benefit owner, acceptance authority, functional managers, migration specialists, and customers who rely on accessible service.

The frontline representative has limited formal authority but high impact and interest. The compliance authority has release-gate authority but limited interest in day-to-day design. The seller controls capacity for an integration dependency. These are not merely contacts: each finding changes engagement, evidence, communication, risk, resource, or escalation planning.

docs.title: Failure modes
docs.text:
Omitting stakeholders creates late requirements, rejected deliverables, resistance, compliance gaps, unsupported transition, and unplanned decision paths. Over-identification without analysis creates a different problem: a large directory with no indication of relevance, authority, impact, or information need.

Other failures include treating powerful people as the only stakeholders, describing resistance as a character flaw, publishing sensitive assessments too broadly, or treating the first register as final. Effective identification uses factual evidence, proportionate privacy, stable identifiers, and repeated discovery.

docs.title: Exam distinctions
docs.text:
The charter may recognize key stakeholders; Identify Stakeholders develops the broader register. The register records identity and context; the Power–Interest Grid classifies; the engagement assessment matrix compares current and desired engagement; the Stakeholder Engagement Plan defines strategies; and the Communications Management Plan defines information delivery. Stakeholder discovery can influence authorization, not just communications.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Determine who can affect the project, who may be affected by it, and what is initially known about their interests, influence, and involvement.

The Stakeholder Engagement Assessment Matrix can summarize current and desired engagement after stakeholders are identified. It supplements the Stakeholder Register; it does not replace the register's identity, influence, authority, and communication information.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: Plans fail when important voices, decision rights, or sources of resistance remain invisible. Early stakeholder analysis lets the team recognize whose support, expertise, approval, or adaptation will matter. Missing a stakeholder can produce late requirements, blocked decisions, or avoidable opposition.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: The charter and emerging project context provide an initial boundary for the search. The results inform requirements work, communications planning, risk identification, and stakeholder engagement planning. Identification continues throughout the project because roles, influence, and affected groups can change.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Identify Stakeholders establishes who matters and why; Plan Stakeholder Engagement selects an approach for involving them; Manage Stakeholder Engagement carries out that approach. A contact list alone is not stakeholder analysis.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

A city begins a downtown bus-lane project. The team identifies transit riders, nearby businesses, emergency services, accessibility advocates, road-maintenance staff, and permitting authorities, then records their differing influence and concerns. That analysis shapes later workshops, traffic studies, and engagement plans.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Identification is not confined to Initiating; newly affected or newly influential stakeholders should be added when discovered.
  2. Separate finding and analyzing stakeholders from communicating with or actively engaging them.
  3. In situational questions, an unexpected influential party usually calls for analysis before choosing a response.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Carry out agreed risk-response actions so planned treatment changes the project’s actual exposure.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: Risk registers often contain well-designed actions that never occur because they lack follow-through, timing, or coordination. Implementation closes the gap between intention and action. It makes ownership observable and integrates responses with the work rather than treating risk management as a reporting exercise.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Approved response plans and assigned owners establish what should be performed. Execution evidence then feeds Monitor Risks, which evaluates whether the action occurred and whether it changed exposure; ineffective responses may require adjustment or new planning. Implementation happens when the planned trigger or timing requires it.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Plan Risk Responses selects and integrates the action. Implement Risk Responses performs it. Monitor Risks checks exposure, triggers, and effectiveness. Marking an action 'planned' is not evidence that it was carried out.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

A conference team planned a backup venue contract if wildfire conditions crossed an agreed trigger. When the threshold is reached, the response owner activates the reservation, redirects logistics, and updates attendee communication. Monitoring then tracks air quality and the operational effects of the move.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Look for execution of an already agreed response, not selection of a strategy.
  2. Risk owners support accountability, but response actions must still be coordinated with authorized project work.
  3. After implementation, monitor whether exposure changed as intended and whether new risks appeared.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Create, distribute, retrieve, and manage project information so stakeholders receive usable information through the planned channels and at the needed time.

Observed communication responses can provide evidence for the Stakeholder Engagement Assessment Matrix, while the Communications Management Plan continues to direct message delivery and information controls.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: Information only supports decisions when it reaches the right audience in a form they can understand and use. This process turns the communications approach into day-to-day information flow and responds to immediate communication needs. It also protects consistency, confidentiality, and accessibility where required.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: The communications plan and current project information guide production and distribution. Stakeholder responses and observed information needs feed Monitor Communications and may lead to adjustments in content or channels. Communication occurs continuously alongside execution and stakeholder engagement.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Manage Communications performs the communication work. Monitor Communications assesses whether communication is effective and whether needs are being met. Manage Stakeholder Engagement uses interaction to address expectations and involvement, not merely transmit information.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

During an enterprise policy rollout, the project team publishes role-specific guidance, gives managers briefing packs, maintains a controlled question log, and issues urgent corrections through an agreed channel. Feedback shows where messages are misunderstood, giving Monitor Communications evidence for changes.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Producing and distributing information points to Manage Communications; evaluating its effectiveness points to Monitor Communications.
  2. Communication is two-way when understanding or feedback matters; transmission alone may be insufficient.
  3. Tailor content without creating conflicting versions of the project’s current information.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Apply relevant existing knowledge to project decisions and capture new learning so it can improve current and future work.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: Teams repeatedly lose time when experience remains with individuals or lessons are recorded only after they can no longer help. Deliberate knowledge management makes expertise usable and creates feedback while work is still underway. It also reduces dependence on a few people and preserves learning beyond the project.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Knowledge is drawn from organizational experience, specialists, and current project activity. It supports execution, problem solving, quality improvement, risk responses, and later planning updates; new learning is shared back into the project and organization. The process is continuous and social, not merely a closing documentation exercise.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Manage Project Knowledge is broader than maintaining a lessons-learned record. A repository can store explicit information, but transferring tacit experience may require conversation, observation, mentoring, or collaborative review.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

A construction team encounters unexpected soil conditions similar to those on an earlier site. A geotechnical specialist from the prior project reviews the response with the current team, which adapts the excavation approach and records the reasoning. The lesson helps current risk and schedule decisions and becomes available to future projects.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Look for both using existing knowledge and creating new knowledge; the process is not limited to archiving lessons.
  2. A lesson can be useful during execution, so do not wait for Close Project or Phase to capture and share it.
  3. Tacit knowledge often requires interaction; storing a document alone may not transfer judgment.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Apply the planned quality approach to project processes and work, evaluate whether those processes are capable, and improve them where needed.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: Inspection at the end can find defects but cannot recover all wasted effort or prevent the same cause from recurring. Managing quality focuses on whether the methods used to create results are suitable and consistently applied. It turns quality planning into preventive and improvement activity during execution.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: The quality management plan and metrics establish the intended approach. Manage Quality uses execution evidence to assess and improve processes, and its findings can influence work practices, risk responses, or change requests; Control Quality separately measures specific results and deliverables. The activities recur as work and learning evolve.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Plan Quality Management defines the approach and measures. Manage Quality applies and improves the processes used to create results. Control Quality inspects results for conformance. Process capability and deliverable verification are related but different questions.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

A customer-support transformation is producing inconsistent knowledge articles. The quality lead reviews the authoring and peer-review workflow, finds that approval roles are unclear, and introduces a clearer review method with coaching. Later sampling in Control Quality checks whether completed articles meet the defined criteria.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. A scenario about process improvement, assurance, or preventing recurring defects points toward Manage Quality.
  2. Inspection results can inform process improvement, but inspecting a deliverable remains Control Quality.
  3. Quality is built through the work process; it is not created solely by final testing.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Work directly with stakeholders to address needs and concerns, manage expectations, resolve issues, and support appropriate participation in project decisions and work.

Review and update the Stakeholder Engagement Assessment Matrix when observed behavior provides new evidence. Engagement actions remain governed by the Stakeholder Engagement Plan and project context.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: Stakeholder support is not maintained through plans alone. Active engagement surfaces concerns early, builds shared understanding, and helps the project navigate competing expectations and change impacts. Avoiding difficult interactions allows resistance and misinformation to harden.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: The engagement plan and current stakeholder analysis guide day-to-day interaction. Outcomes, issues, and relationship changes feed communications, issue management, project decisions, and Monitor Stakeholder Engagement; approaches are adapted throughout the project.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Manage Stakeholder Engagement conducts the relationship work. Manage Communications handles project information flow, while Monitor Stakeholder Engagement evaluates whether the overall approach is achieving the needed involvement.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

During a factory automation project, operators fear job loss and supervisors worry about production disruption. The project manager facilitates demonstrations, listens to role concerns, involves operators in procedure design, and resolves an escalation about training time. Monitoring later checks whether participation and support improve.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Engagement focuses on relationships, expectations, participation, and issue resolution—not only message delivery.
  2. Address concerns at the appropriate level before defaulting to escalation.
  3. A changed stakeholder response may require revising the engagement strategy, not merely repeating the same communication.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Observe team performance, provide feedback, resolve issues, and coordinate changes needed to sustain effective project delivery.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: Team conditions change as pressure, assignments, conflict, and performance evolve. Active management addresses those conditions before they damage work or relationships. It balances project needs with appropriate organizational authority rather than treating every problem as a training gap.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Performance observations, issue information, and team-development results inform management action. Feedback, conflict resolution, assignment changes, or escalations affect ongoing execution and may create new development or resource needs. The process continues throughout team participation.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Develop Team builds general capability and cohesion; Manage Team responds to current performance, feedback, conflict, and assignment conditions. Control Resources focuses primarily on physical-resource availability and use, not team leadership.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

Two engineering leads on a rail project are issuing incompatible interface decisions. The project manager meets with them, clarifies decision authority, resolves the immediate conflict, and adjusts the coordination routine. A broader interface workshop is then used as a team-development response.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. A specific conflict, feedback conversation, or performance correction points to Manage Team.
  2. Use appropriate authority and escalation paths; the project manager may not control every functional assignment.
  3. Do not confuse physical-resource variance with team performance management.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Evaluate overall project performance against the integrated plan so trends, forecasts, variances, and needed action are visible to decision-makers.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: Local status reports do not automatically reveal whether the project as a whole remains viable or coordinated. Integrated monitoring turns performance information into a cross-project view and identifies where corrective, preventive, or replanning action may be needed. Passive observation would leave emerging problems unaddressed.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Execution and specialized control processes provide performance information, forecasts, and issues. This process synthesizes them, communicates the overall condition, and may produce change requests for formal review. It recurs throughout delivery and does not approve baseline changes by itself.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Monitor and Control Project Work assesses the project’s integrated health and recommends action. Perform Integrated Change Control evaluates and decides on change requests. Detecting a variance is not the same as approving its remedy.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

A regional data-center migration is on budget, but vendor delays threaten the cutover window and increase operational risk. The project manager combines schedule, cost, risk, and readiness information into an overall forecast and recommends resequencing work. Any baseline change then goes through integrated change control.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Choose overall monitoring when the question combines information from several knowledge areas.
  2. Monitoring is active analysis and forecasting, not simply collecting status.
  3. A recommended corrective action becomes a change request when formal approval is required.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Evaluate whether project communication is meeting stakeholder information needs and adjust the approach when it is not.

Use communication-effectiveness evidence alongside the Stakeholder Engagement Assessment Matrix when reassessing involvement. Communication effectiveness and engagement state are related but not interchangeable.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: A communication can be delivered on time and still fail because it is misunderstood, ignored, inaccessible, or sent through the wrong channel. Monitoring looks beyond message counts to usefulness and effect. It keeps communication aligned with changing stakeholders and project conditions.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Actual communications, feedback, issue patterns, and stakeholder behavior are compared with the planned approach. Findings can change timing, format, channel, responsibility, or escalation and then influence Manage Communications. Evaluation recurs as information needs and project risk evolve.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Manage Communications creates and distributes project information. Monitor Communications determines whether that flow is effective. Monitor Stakeholder Engagement evaluates the broader relationship and involvement, of which communication is only one part.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

A merger-integration project sends weekly updates, yet call-center supervisors continue acting on outdated procedures. Monitoring reveals that the email format is hard to use during shifts, so the team introduces supervisor huddles and a searchable change summary. Later feedback confirms fewer errors.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Evidence of delivery is not evidence of understanding or usefulness.
  2. Look for feedback, communication performance, or a need to change the communications approach.
  3. A stakeholder relationship problem may require engagement action beyond changing the message.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Track identified and residual risks, detect emerging uncertainty, evaluate response effectiveness, and assess whether the risk-management approach remains useful.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: Risk exposure changes as work proceeds, assumptions fail, responses are implemented, and new information appears. Monitoring keeps risk decisions connected to current reality and prevents closed or outdated entries from dominating attention. It also tests whether the project’s risk practices are working.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Execution evidence, risk-owner updates, response results, issues, and project forecasts provide the monitoring basis. Findings may identify new risks, close obsolete ones, trigger planned responses, revise priorities, or create change requests and feed another cycle of analysis and planning.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Monitor Risks evaluates exposure and response performance across the project. Implement Risk Responses carries out planned actions. Monitoring can trigger or adjust work, but it is not passive observation or a substitute for implementation.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

During a cloud-service transition, the team reviews migration errors, supplier capacity, security findings, and response actions. A previously minor identity risk is escalating while a data-volume risk has retired. The team reprioritizes exposure, activates an agreed test response, and identifies a new vendor-concentration risk.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Monitoring includes new-risk identification, trigger review, response evaluation, and overall process effectiveness.
  2. An issue that has occurred may require immediate management while its effects also inform risk monitoring.
  3. Risk status is dynamic; do not preserve an outdated ranking merely because it was approved during planning.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Evaluate stakeholder relationships and involvement, detect changes in support or influence, and adjust engagement strategies when needed.

The Stakeholder Engagement Assessment Matrix makes current-versus-desired engagement visible so the team can reassess gaps, record evidence, and recommend adjustments. It is a working assessment, not a formal process output.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: A strategy that worked early may fail after a decision, organizational change, or visible project impact. Monitoring compares actual involvement with what the project needs and identifies relationship risks before they block progress. It treats engagement as an adaptive management concern.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Feedback, participation patterns, issues, decisions, and stakeholder behavior provide evidence. Findings update stakeholder analysis and engagement approaches and influence Manage Stakeholder Engagement and communications; evaluation continues as the project and its environment change.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Monitor Stakeholder Engagement assesses relationship effectiveness and needed adjustment. Manage Stakeholder Engagement performs the interactions, while Monitor Communications evaluates whether information needs are being met.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

On a neighborhood flood-control project, public meeting attendance is stable but comments show that renters believe only property owners influence decisions. The team recognizes an engagement gap, adds tenant outreach through local organizations, and measures whether participation becomes more representative.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Attendance or message delivery alone does not prove effective engagement.
  2. Look for comparison between current and needed involvement followed by a strategy adjustment.
  3. Stakeholder influence and attitude can change suddenly after a project decision or external event.

docs.title: What this process does
docs.text:
Perform Integrated Change Control evaluates change requests, considers their combined effects, and routes each request to the authorized decision-maker.

“Integrated” means the decision is not made from one viewpoint alone. A scope change can alter schedule, cost, quality, resources, risk, procurement, benefits, compliance, operations, and stakeholder commitments. The process brings those effects together before an approved baseline or other controlled commitment is changed.

docs.title: The decision path
docs.text:
1. A Change Request is submitted.
  2. The team records it and checks that the request is clear enough to analyze.
  3. Relevant specialists assess effects, options, risks, and recommendations.
  4. The project manager coordinates the analysis and determines the correct authority route.
  5. The authorized role approves, rejects, defers, or requests more information.
  6. The decision is communicated and recorded in the Change Log.
  7. Approved work is assigned and implemented.
  8. Affected plans, baselines, documents, contracts, or backlog records are updated under control.
  9. The implemented result is verified before the change is closed.

Approval is not implementation. Implementation is not verification. Keeping those states separate prevents reporting an approved idea as completed work.

docs.title: ServiceBridge example
docs.text:
A compliance review requests stronger encryption. The analysis shows effects on design, vendor scope, test evidence, cost, and launch timing. The project manager coordinates the evidence but cannot waive the compliance obligation or change the contract alone. The designated authorities approve the technical and commercial changes. The team implements them, security testing verifies the result, and the log links the decision to the evidence.

Adaptive teams can adjust uncommitted backlog detail through normal product decisions. A change to a baseline, contract, funding boundary, regulatory obligation, or other controlled commitment still follows the relevant authority process. Hybrid work must define that boundary clearly.

For the exam, assess impact before action, follow the change process, and never assume urgency gives the project manager unlimited approval power.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Evaluate change requests in an integrated context, decide their disposition through the authorized governance process, and coordinate approved changes.

docs.title: Why This Process Exists
docs.text: A change that helps one objective can damage another by altering scope, schedule, cost, quality, risk, or stakeholder commitments. Integrated review makes those tradeoffs visible before authorization. Without it, local decisions can quietly invalidate baselines and create incompatible promises.

docs.title: How It Fits in the Sequence
docs.text: Change requests may arise from execution, monitoring, risk responses, quality findings, or stakeholder needs. Their impacts are assessed against the project management plan and other current information; approved changes are then incorporated and implemented through the appropriate work. The process operates whenever controlled change is needed, not only at a scheduled gate.

docs.title: Common Confusions
docs.text: Perform Integrated Change Control approves, rejects, defers, or otherwise disposes of requests. Direct and Manage Project Work implements what has been approved. A team should not begin baseline-changing work merely because a request has been submitted.

docs.title: Practical Example
docs.text:
PRACTICAL EXAMPLE

A medical-device project proposes replacing a component after a supplier warning. The change authority reviews regulatory, quality, schedule, cost, inventory, and validation impacts before approving the replacement. Planning records are updated, and the delivery team then implements the authorized design change.

docs.title: Exam Tips
docs.text:
EXAM TIP
  1. Follow the change request to the authorized decision before selecting implementation activity.
  2. Assess cross-project effects; an isolated technical benefit does not establish overall approval.
  3. Configuration and baseline updates follow the decision according to the project’s governance approach.
